speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION COMPANY LIMITED DISPOSAL AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-53, an Act to authorize the disposal of the Northern Transportation Company Limited and the forgiveness of its debt to Her Majesty and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-53 authorizes the federal Government to dispose of the Northern Transportation Company Limited. Agreement in principle has been reached with the Innuvialuit Development Corporation and the Nunasi Corporation. The agreement is being finalized this week and the enabling legislation will give the Government the authority to complete the sale.
By way of background, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the Northern Transportation Company Limited was established under private ownership in 1931 as the Northern Waterways Limited. It operated several small vessels from Waterways, Alberta to Lake Athabasca, Great Slave Lake, the Mackenzie River and Great Bear Lake. In 1934, the company was renamed the Northern Transportation Company Limited, still under private ownership. In 1936, NTCL was acquired by Eldorado Gold Mines Ltd.-later Eldorado Mining and Smelting, now Eldorado Nuclear-which was then a private company involved in mining on Great Bear Lake.
Under Eldorado ownership, the NTCL served Eldorado needs and continued to operate a common carrier service in the Athabasca and Mackenzie area. In 1944, Eldorado Mining and Smelting was nationalized under the War Measures Act because of its radium and pitchblende mining operations at Great Bear Lake. NTCL came under government ownership as part of the Eldorado package.
From 1945 to 1957, NTCL slowly grew as traffic increased. Community resupply became an important activity and thereby NTCL was fulfilling a very important public role.
In 1949, NTCL was declared an agent of Her Majesty, pursuant to the Government Companies Operations Act. In
1957, NTCL began operating into the Canadian western Arctic to resupply the Distant Early Warning Line radar stations established by the U.S. Air Force. This was a further example of NTCL's contribution to government objectives in the North.
In 1957 to 1972, NTCL traffic continued to grow, particularly in later years, as oil and gas exploration was developed in the Mackenzie Delta. In 1962, the NTCL main operating base shifted from Fort McMurray, Alberta, to Hay River, Northwest Territories, with the completion of the Great Slave Lake Railway. Athabasca operations continued but there was no operational link between the Athabasca and the remainder of the NTCL system.
In 1965, NTCL acquired the assets of Yellowknife Transportation Limited, one of its competitors on the Mackenzie River. In 1972, NTCL reached a peak of over 400,000 tonnes of cargo carried. In expectation of further increases, NTCL engaged in a major capital expenditure program involving purchase of new tugboats, barges and shore equipment. In 1973, NTCL bought Grimshaw Trucking and Distributing Ltd. of Edmonton. Between the period of 1972 and 1976, NTCL traffic declined drastically, owing to the failure of the anticipated Arctic gas pipeline to proceed and to reduce exploration activity. In that period of time NTCL suffered some severe financial losses.
In 1976, NTCL was recapitalized through conversion of some $24.9 million of federal government debt into equity. Between 1977 and 1981, NTCL recovered its financial position, which peaked in 1981 with net earnings of $4.3 million and a return on invested capital of 11 per cent.
In 1981, NTCL incorporated Nortran Offshore Ltd. and refurbished two vessels for seismographic geotechnical work under Nortran. From 1981 to the present, NTCL has remained profitable, although at a somewhat lower level than the 1981 peak.
That gives you a brief history, Mr. Speaker, of the development of the Northern Transportation Company Limited.
Presently, NTCL is a federally incorporated company under the Canada Business Corporations Act. The company's head office is in Edmonton, Alberta, with its main operating base at Hay River, Northwest Territories. It is the largest operator of tugboats and barges in northwestern Canada and is the primary means of marine transportation for residents of the Mackenzie River watershed, the western Arctic, and the Keewatin Hudson Bay coast. NTCL operates 26 tugboats and 171 barges. NTCL owns Grimshaw Trucking and Distributing Limited, a trucking company operating in Alberta and the Northwest Territories. It also owns Nortran Offshore Limited

which offers seismographic-geotechnical vessels for charter in the Beaufort Sea.
In 1984 NTCL carried 236,000 tonnes of cargo on its 5,000 mile marine system and employed 564 people during its peak summer season. Some of the highlights of its 1984 financial performance are that it generated revenue of S40.9 million and it earned $1.55 million from operations, with net earnings of $1.34 million, a return on invested capital of 5.1 per cent, and a return on equity of 3.6 per cent.
What is the justification for privatizing the Northern Transportation Company Limited? NTCL was not made a Crown corporation by design, but rather by accident through the nationalization of its then parent company, Eldorado. NTCL never had a clearly defined public policy mandate. Although the resupply activities carried out by NTCL are very important to northern residents, there is no reason why resupply operations cannot be carried out by a privately owned company. We believe that the private sector is capable of and willing to provide the service required.
NTCL itself has had aspirations in the past to diversify into related business areas. These aspirations were discouraged because it was not thought appropriate for NTCL to become involved in new areas already well served by the private sector. Privatization of NTCL would free the company to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities.
Northern Transportation Company Limited has been a candidate for privatization on several occasions already. The company was on the short list to be privatized in 1979, and in 1984 the previous Government announced plans to sell NTCL. The process for the sale of NTCL has been public for some time and there have been no expressions of public concern over the issue of privatization.

As I said, the previous administration offered NTCL for sale in August of 1984 and, after a lengthy process of providing information to interested parties, three offers were received in November of 1984 for the purchase of the company. The offers were evaluated on the basis of price, native-northern participation, and commitment to community resupply. Northern Industrial Carriers Limited of Edmonton was selected as the preferred offerer provided it could attain a satisfactory level for northern-native participation. Other offers came from the consortium of the Denendeh Development Corporation, the NWT Metis Development Corporation, and Arctic Transportation Limited, and a consortium of the Inuvialuit Development Corporation, the Nunasi Corporation, and NTCL management personnel. After lengthy negotiations, the final offer of NIC was rejected in March 1985. The rejection was on the basis of an inadequate level of native and northern participation and a reduction in price from the original tender.
It was then decided that new offers would be invited from groups that had earlier been involved in the sale process. Three
offers were received: one from the consortium and the Denendeh Development Corporation, the NWT Metis Development Corporation, and Arctic Transportation Limited; the second from the consortium of the Inuvialuit Development Corporation and the Nunasi Corporation; and the third from Arctic Offshore Limited and Northern Arc Shipbuilders Limited. Again the offers were evaluated on the basis of price, native-northern participation, and commitment to community resupply. The IDC-Nunasi offer met all of the criteria set for evaluation. In addition, it presented several other attractive features, notably the fact that IDC and the Nunasi represented the majority of NTCL's resupply customers.
At present, six Inuvialuit communities and 12 Inuit communities are served. Whether one applies revenue-tonne miles or tonnage as compared to NTCL's over-all community resupply services, the percentage attributable to these communities is in the range of 90 per cent to 95 per cent. The offering group is made up entirely of the northern Inuit.
Just to give you a brief run-down on the IDC group, this corporation was created by the Committee for Original Peoples Entitlement to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities on behalf of the Inuvialuit people of the Mackenzie Delta and the Western Arctic. These people live in communities as far east as Holman Island and Paulatuk. The IDC received its current capitalization of the Inuvialuit land claim agreement signed in 1982. This involved a number of businesses, including aviation, catering and support for the Beaufort Sea oil operation. The corporation's head office is in Inuvik, Northwest Territories. Its president is Randal Pokiak and its general manager is Peter Coolican. The Nunasi Corporation pursues entrepreneurial activities on behalf of the Inuit people of the central and eastern Arctic, and acts on behalf of Inuit living in Coppermine and east, and Keewatin, as well as throughout the eastern Arctic. Nunasi has not been the beneficiary of land claim funding since no land claims agreement has been reached with the Inuit. The company owns a small airline in the Keewatin, and until recently had a significant shareholding in a gold mine. The corporation's head office is in Ottawa and its president is John Hickes.
Also involved is the firm of Trimac. Although not a shareholder in the IDC group, Trimac will play an important role by providing administration and management advice to the company. Trimac is a large diversified Calgary-based company involved in bulk trucking, general construction, pipeline construction, oilfield drilling and consulting. The company is very well respected in the western Canadian transportation industry.
The IDC-Nunasi group has agreed to a binding commitment to maintain NTCL's community supply. The fact that the ownership will represent the majority of NTCL's customers strengthens the degree of commitment even further. In addition, NTCL's long-term debt to the Government, currently some $27 million, will be retired on closing, using cash in the company. As I said, closing of the deal is planned for the
June 25, 1985

end of June. Negotiations between Government officials and the IDC-Nunasi are going on and progressing well.
I hope that all Hon. Members of the House will agree to give this particular legislation speedy passage. I should say that I will be offering a couple of amendments at some point with respect to the impact on the company as it relates to income tax. The thrust of the amendments are that, for income tax purposes, the company will be in the same position after the sale, with the transfer of property, as if it had always owned the property. The portion of the amendment dealing with the debt recognizes that the debt, which is now owed by an agency of Her Majesty to Her Majesty, will not remain with the privately owned company. Really, what the amendments do is to clarify the technical issues involving NTCL's tax status. It is not a change in the substance of the Bill whose purpose remains unchanged.
I hope there might be some disposition to proceed with this Bill in all stages in the House. If not, I would certainly be prepared to appear before the standing committee to offer further elaboration at that time. But perhaps there may be some discussions about how we might proceed in order that we might receive passage of this legislation before the end of the week.

Mr. Speaker, let me add my words of appreciation and some sympathy to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). We know that he has had a very harrowing weekend and we recognize the difficult circumstances under which he is operating. Therefore, we appreciate his being in the House today to introduce the Bill and provide us with information related to the sale of the Northern Transportation Company Limited.
However, there are a number of questions that should be answered. Therefore, we would appreciate his appearance at the committee as well as the provision of somewhat more enlightened and expanded comments during the second reading and report stages.
We treat this Bill seriously, not only because of its importance to northern Canadians but also because it is an important precedent in the ways and means of the privatization of a
Northern Transportation Company number of Crown corporations. I would give the Minister of Transport a somewhat backhanded compliment by saying that at least he has been able to privatize one Crown corporation, while his colleague, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), has made more than enough speeches throughout the country about what he will do but has done nothing in ten months. However, while the Minister of Transport has at least been able to bring this privatization almost to fruition, I would add that one reason he has been able to do so is that it was an initiative begun by the previous Government. Obviously his achievement is a result of having a major advantage as a result of the foundations being well laid approximately a year ago. That would explain the difference between his level of accomplishment and that of his colleague, who is absolutely floundering and staggering in his attempt to accomplish his goal. I read recently a speech made by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion in October in which he said that all these Crown corporations will be signed, sealed and delivered by Christmas. However, one has yet to pass by the hallowed portals, which only shows that the large sip between the sip and the drink of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion must be carefully watched.
When our Government introduced the Crown Corporation Bill over a year ago, it was our belief that it was an important principle that any sale of a Crown corporation had to be examined by Parliament. We believed that it was an essential ingredient in a process that any Government undertook in providing for the sale of a Crown corporation. I suggest that the wisdom of that belief is borne out in today's legislation because it gives us an opportunity to have a greater degree of public scrutiny and examination of a very important issue concerning the way in which the Government sells a Crown corporation.
As the Minister pointed out, these matters should not be approached in an ideological fashion but, rather, in a pragmatic way. We must ask if the existing Crown corporation is serving a public purpose. While that may be defined in different ways by different Parties and Governments, it is a primary test.
Although most Members in the House believe that history began last September 4, that was a test which we applied in November of 1983 when we first announced that we had commissioned the board of directors of Northern Transportation Company Limited to examine the prospects or reasons for the sale of the Northern Transportation Company Limited.
I want the Minister to consider carefully the fact that we asked the board of directors to become directly involved in the assessment and evaluation and to become major partners in the sale. It is my understanding that since the new Government came to power, the board of directors has been basically frozen out of any involvement in this particular sale. That is of some concern. Under basic corporate law in this country, the board of directors, whether that of a private or of a publicly held company, has major responsibilities to act not only as stewards for the shareholders, which, in this case, is the Government, but also to provide for a more sensitive and at

The board of directors is a very important policy-making body, a very important monitoring body and a very important decision-making body. One of the key questions I want to raise and bring to the attention of the House is, why was the board of directors of this Crown corporation, which had been initially involved last year in the preliminary discussions of the sale, according to its President and chief operating officer, Mr. Cameron, not been directly involved? The experience gained and the background enjoyed in running this company has been ignored. I think it may have something to do with the fact that there was a substantial hiccup in sales when the Government made its first overture to northern carriers. It then had to withdraw and move on to a second range of buyers simply because it did not use or exploit the background information that might have been supplied by that board of directors. I do not think it is necessarily within the purview of a government Department to be in the sense the vendor of such a thing, because it is unquestionably the responsibility of the Minister. I believe the initial judgment or assessment that we have to make in this case is that when one comes to making choices about privatizing, it is very important to follow wisdom, which is to involve the interested parties who are essential to a sale. In this case to sidetrack the board of directors from the outset is a very serious mistake and one for which I hope we would receive some rationale. It suggests some of the reasons for the problems that were encountered when bringing this sale to fruition.
I am a little concerned that the Minister did not share with this House the kind of information gained by the initial assessment and evaluation done by First Boston, which had been set up to do a proper financial accounting of the company to determine its level of assets, prospects and so on, which would help Parliament, and in particular the standing committee which will be working in a very strict time frame, to get a better financial judgment as to the pluses and minuses of this sale. I go back to the Minister's own words. Is the Government undertaking the right kind of financial deal in making this sale? We do not know because we do not have First Boston's report. I do not think there is anything particularly confidential there. If there were, it could be raised, but I say to the Minister across the House that it may be of some importance to the committee to have access to the results of the First Boston study. I think it would give us some proper background as to what were the various financial statements and results. I say this in particular because it is important to go back a little in history to clear the air. Certain of the Minister's colleagues a year or so ago raised a number of questions when they were on this side of the House concerning the financial arrangements of NTC sales and made some fairly strong charges concerning the management of the company.
As we said at that time, that was something which, in a way, was an attempt to put these people into a precarious position and to assess their reputation. I think the responsibility of the
Minister should be at least to give us the results of the First Boston study to clear the air and not to leave some of those questions outstanding as they were last year. At that time when I held his position I said I could not answer those questions until we had done the proper financial study, which we were prepared to do through an independent party. Many of those individuals, among them the past President, Mr. Montpetit, deserve and have the respect of this House, and we should recognize that by attempting to come to deal with those financial issues.
I do commend the Minister of Transport for following through on the original terms of reference. They were to ensure that there was substantial participation by northerners and native people. When we initially examined the concept of the sale, we thought it was an ideal opportunity to provide incentives for the newly emerging entrepreneurial class of native people in northern Canada. We thought it would provide them with an opportunity to have a good stake in a company which directly affected their interests. At that time we had several discussions and participated in negotiations with native organizations. They made a very strong case that NTCL was a prime candidate to enable them to get a major toe-hold in a northern transportation system which they could own and operate. That was one of the primary justifications we used in November 1983 to begin the process leading toward the privatization of this particular company.
When the Minister originally made his announcement concerning the sale to Northern Industrial Carriers, at that time it did not contain participation or involvement of northern native organizations in particular. Obviously the second bid which has been accepted by the Government, at least on its face value, fully meets that test and the criteria which we put forward as being a justification for the sale.
I hope Hon. Members of the House will take full recognition of the fact that this is a very important step in northern Canada. As some Hon. Members who represent northern constituencies are fond of saying, and rightfully so, sufficient attention is not paid to the affairs and interests of northern Canada by Members of the House. They tend to be pushed off to the sidelines too often.
One of the most important and exciting developments which I witnessed when I was in the Ministry of Transport was the way in which a number of native organizations, partly using money from land claims as their basis of capital, were undertaking a new way of meeting their economic objectives. They were moving toward the notion of self-sufficiency, not only in local government terms but also in economic terms. My Party and I believe very strongly that this is one of the signposts for the future. If we are to alleviate the severe economic deprivation of northern native people, perhaps one of the most important ways in which Government can assist them is by giving them the equity, capital and operations which allow them to grow, expand and develop economic investments in their own community. As any number of groups at the bottom of the

economic ladder try to climb up it, they do so by developing a stake in their own community and by developing the ability to obtain a good capital base upon which to build.
This sale of NTCL is a very important step forward. It will enable native people in northern Canada to acquire an important company. It is an important company in that it supplies a very important service. With the right kinds of conditions, it can be a real foundation for the expansion and development of a number of other offshoots, not only in transportation. It will at least give them the basic capital and the administrative development and experience upon which they can grow and evolve into fairly major economic operations.
The Bill is important in terms of being a first step in privatization and the principles adhered to. It is a very important example of the way in which Government can assist native people-and for that matter other groups-in their economic development. Rather than divorce itself from them, it can facilitate their development of economic self-sufficiency.
This raises several questions which I hope the Minister will answer. He mentioned in his statement that the $24.5 million outstanding loan to the Government would be written off. I believe he said that it would be written off by the proceeds from the sale. If that is the case, we would want to know the sale price. Also we would want to know what kinds of conditions and arrangements have been made. Is it simply a writeoff trade? Will further equity be coming back to the Government? In other words, what kind of financial arrangement has been arrived at?
The second component would be: What kind of continuing commitments has the Government made, particularly in terms of resupply in the Keewatin area? As I recall the situation, the present contract went into 1989. I believe that is the present arrangement. In some years, in particular in 1983, the level of subsidy for that was over $600,000. I believe last year, if I am not mistaken, the company paid some money back to the Government, about $300,000. As a result of the way in which the resupply agreement has been worded, there is a back-up commitment by the Government of Canada to ensure that the resupply continues to pay any additional costs over what is returned by way of revenue. It is very important to know at this point in time whether that is simply running until 1989. Is there a long-term commitment from the Government to maintain that subsidy? In particular-and I do not believe the Minister mentioned it in his opening remarks-to what degree has a term of reference or a set of directions been given to the Canadian Transport Commission to ensure that the agreement is lived up to in terms of resupplying essential communities, to ensure that it will be honoured? I am not saying that there should be any mistrust, but we must remember that it is the only source of supply for certain parts of northern Canada, including the northern part of Manitoba, the province from which I come, and the Churchill supply area. What kind of agreements or arrangements will be made with CTC to monitor the performance of the company in its resupply commitments and in redefining its terms? What commitment is being
Northern Transportation Company made by the Government in the long-term interests of the area?
When we talk about privatization, there are many private companies which receive transport subsidies. I have heard Hon. Members opposite say that perhaps too many companies receive such subsidies. However, I want to express a note of caution. In the last Budget papers tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), there was a very clear statement that the Government intended to reduce the number of subsidies under transportation. Of course, we assume that that would primarily mean in Atlantic Canada. The key question would be: Would this affect or have an application to the Keewatin supply area under NTCL? I think it is very important for the Minister of Transport to outline clearly those conditions.
I should like to refer to another set of issues, those affecting or impacting on local residents, particularly in the Territories. As I understand it, some real concern has been expressed over the last several months about the need to undertake impact studies of both an economic and environmental kind in terms of the consequences of the sale. The Minister did not indicate whether such studies or impact assessments had been made. Some assurances should be provided to the affected communities which have a singular reliance upon the company for their well-being and livelihood. We require further information and clear guarantees from the Government as to what in fact has been done. What kind of assurances have been given to these communities as a condition of sale? Has CTC been assigned a role to determine the conditions of licence and the performance of these conditions?
Those are very clear-cut questions. When this company has been privatized, the only two areas in which the Government will be able to provide some continuing level of guaranteed assurances would be through its subsidy payments on the Keewatin supply route and through the licensing arrangements under CTC. We have not received any information from the Government in either case as to what it intends to do. There are a number of questions related to the sale, but I want to make clear that we as a caucus and as a Party support its basic principle, because in fact it was an initiative which we took. We did so because it made good sense at that time. I suspect it makes even better sense now. One clear question had to be answered at that time, and I believe the Minister referred to it in his opening address. If the company were to expand its operations, if it were to diversify and supply alternative services, it would need more equity to do so. There seems to be no good reason why the Government of Canada should be paying for that new infusion of equity capital. That comes back to what the conditions of sale are and what in fact are the financial arrangements that have been made; to what degree the reserves of the company have been used up; what kind of capital will remain and what kind of return on the capital will be allowed so that it will not be so totally stripped that it would not be able to take advantage of that area.

Mr. Speaker, 1 ordinarily would not welcome any opportunity to speak on a Bill which allows the Government to get out of its obligations to provide guaranteed and essential services to the residents of northern Canada, or to any part of the country for that matter. I am happy to say that the Government's initial plan to sell to a southern private company fell through and it is in fact now planning to sell this company to a consortium of two Inuit corporations. I want to say to the Minister that had he done otherwise, he would not be getting this Bill through in the eleventh hour of this session.
The whole issue of privatization, like deregulation, has been a matter of some debate in this House and all over the country for the last several years, ever since the Proposition 13 syndrome and Reaganomics were imported into this country and grabbed on to by both the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party.
It does provide an opportunity to consider the purpose and the value of Crown corporations, particularly in the instances where it covers part of the economy that is a natural monopoly, small markets or isolated areas where an essential public service has to be provided. Over the years, in this country as well as others, Governments of the stripe of the Liberal or Conservative Parties have got into Crown corporations, not because they believed in them, not because they thought there was an essential public service that Government could best provide through ownership by the taxpayers of the nation, but for a number of other reasons. One was to bail out some outfit that was going broke and to help out the banks and the bond holders and private investors, and the other was because the private sector could not or would not fulfil an essential public need. Where was the private sector in the 1930s when it came to fulfilling essential public need in northern Canada? It could not or would not provide that essential public service, and starting in 1934 the people of Canada began providing that essential public service in the thinly populated northern isolated area.
The other thing is that in the mindless drive toward privatization there seemed to be a strong tendency under the previous Government as there is under the present Government to sell off the winners and leave the taxpayers stuck with only the losers. Hardly anybody is going to rush forward to buy a Crown corporation that is losing its shirt, although the Government may well end up having to sell parts or all of several other Crown corporations. I am thinking of a couple of aircraft manufacturers and a few others that were taken into public ownership, not because the Government believed there was an essential need to have a Crown corporation in the aircraft industry to preserve a qualified capacity for the manufacture, production, research and development in the aircraft industry. It was done for other reasons. Those reasons were part of it, but there were other reasons as well, partly to preserve jobs and partly to bail out those who were losing their shirts and stop them from pulling out of the country or just folding up completely.
The taxpayers are just as entitled as any private investor to the opportunity to obtain a return on the investment they make. That is why I do not understand the rush to sell the winners. I know they are easier to sell because they are making money. NTCL has been very profitable, certainly for the last five or six years. Those are easier to sell. If it were only as easy to sell off the losers! There is no imperative that the Government be in the kind of business that some of those losers are in, but it is in for a variety of other reasons, and they remain losers.
Those public corporations that provide essential public services, that fill a public need and serve the national interest, and at the same time obtain a return on investment in a profitable situation for the taxpayers, are surely the kind, given the combination of all those three things, for the keeping in the public sector of which there is total justification. They should be kept as Crown corporations.
As a matter of general principle, my Party believes that there are certain sectors of the economy, and particularly in isolated or thinly populated areas or areas with a small population and small markets, where the private sector cannot or will not provide the services that people need. Those are legitimate areas for Government to establish Crown corporations on behalf of not only those people in the areas affected or in the services that they require but also to serve the national interest. Otherwise we would never have built a railroad.
We make an exception in this case because at least NTCL is being sold to the people of the North. It is too bad that all of the aboriginal groups who bid on this company could not have got together and been given joint ownership and joint control. Then they would all be involved and we could be certain that all areas of the North currently served would continue to be served as well as they are now, if not better, and that any changes in the future because of development decisions and needs of corporate development would be made by those people themselves with all the interests of the North at hand. Just the same, we believe that the IDC and Nunasi corporations will do a better job than some private sector outfit from the south who would go into it to make a buck, get rid of the parts that lose money, and give little or no attention or consideration to the needs of the people in all parts of northern Canada.
What we would really have liked to have seen in this bill are clauses which would guarantee services to the North, guaran-

tees that the purchasers, whoever they might be, would continue to provide the excellent services that the company has been providing and some guarantees that the company will continue to invest its profits. The company has been very profitable over the last number of years and its profits should continue to be invested in the further development and improvement of the Northern Transportation system.
We believe that the proposed purchasers will do all of those things because doing so affects all of them. It will be in their own best interests to reinvest profits and to improve the operations of the company so that it will be even better than it is now. There can be no question that NTCL has been doing a good job and has been meeting an essential public need that up until now the private sector has been unable and unwilling to meet. We do believe that the proposed purchasers will do these things, but we want a guarantee that they or anyone to whom they may sell all or part of the company in the future will continue to do the same. However, there is nothing in this Bill that provides for that. There may be something in the agreement of sale providing for that, and I understand that the Minister has said that there is. I wish that he would show us the agreement of sale. Perhaps he will do so later. The Bill itself is completely vague on that matter.
Over the last five years NTCL has made profits of somewhere in the order of $20 million. It has certainly made profits of over $14 million in 1979, 1980 and 1981. I do not have at hand the figures for the last couple of years but I believe the profit picture was good in both of those years as well. I also recognize that the company indicates in its annual reports an extraordinary item, it being payments of debt to the Crown. Even so, it has still reported a profit in each year. Of course, the Bill provides for the forgiveness of the Crown debt so that it will not be an expense that will have to be borne by the new owners. That brings me to two questions.
First, as I mentioned earlier, should the Government be selling a profitable operation for which there are no competitors? In fact, the economic reality is that there is no room for competition because of the high cost of providing services in the North and because of the smallness of the market. The question to be asked is, should the Government be selling the company no matter to whom, particularly when it is a winner both in terms of the services it provides and the profits it makes? Can the Government not provide this service at a reasonable rate itself and still make a return on its investment, no matter how small?
After 50 years of efforts by the Government and investment by the taxpayers, this company has finally become a very successful and worth-while operation. Then and only then does the private sector rush in saying that it cannot have all these publicly-owned corporations interfering in the private sector. The private sector wants to pick up the action and it wants the gravy off the top. This applies not only in this instance but in the case of airlines. Where the hell was Canadian Pacific when we needed it? As soon as Air Canada started making money,
Northern Transportation Company
then the pressure was on and the demand was there for the private sector to involve itself in air transportation to provide competition.

Second, if we decide to sell this corporation, will the taxpayers get fair value for their investment? After the Crown debt is forgiven-and we can only assume that the Minister plans to do so since there is a provision in the Bill to do so and a Royal Recommendation to appropriate the funds to do so-this company will have net assets of some $68 million, if my calculations are correct and I think they are. Yet all we have heard through the news media-not from the Minister or from the agreement of sale-is that the Government expects to receive about $25 million. If that is so, we do not know, because the Bill does not tell us and the Minister does not tell us, why that does not appear in the Bill itself.
Finally, the Minister has asked the House to give an order of reference to the Standing Committee on Transport to study the role and responsibility of the Government of Canada with respect to northern transportation services and infrastructure, and the standing committee will be meeting and travelling to the North in September and perhaps October to study all of that and report back to the House. The committee will be meeting to study this issue over the next weeks and months. While it is doing that, the Minister will be selling off the primary instrument of national policy with respect to transportation in the North. Does the Minister not think that he should not, on the one hand, ask Parliament to study something and then, on the other hand, go ahead and do whatever he was planning to do in any event? June 25, 1985
Northern Transportation Company
sale until the study of the northern transportation infrastructure is completed by the Transport Committee. The Government could then proceed to implement this Bill. I believe, when all is said and done, that the Government ought not to sell Crown corporations, particularly the winners, and Parliament ought not to support such sales, generally, especially without any guarantees in legislation about just who the purchasers are going to be-and I am speaking generally here because we know who it is going to be in this case-just how much the Government-meaning the people of Canada- will receive in return for the sale of the investment they made, and what will happen in the future if the responsibilities formerly held by the Government in trust to the people of the North are not met by future owners. We are afraid that the government majority in this place will not be persuaded by logic, good thinking or anything else in its suicidal mission to rid the people of Canada of all their hard won and profitable operations, such as it did with the patent office and with Teleglobe Canada.

The Minister had an agreement in principle with a previous purchaser three or four months ago, but that sale did not go through. There is nothing in this Bill that appears to be specific as to any particular offer of purchase. Nowhere is it mentioned who will buy the corporation or which parts of it or how much of it. The Bill could just as easily be used to sell off any other Crown corporation by simply changing the name of the Bill, because the Bill is that general and vague. So the minister waited until June 12 to introduce the Bill and expected that seven days later it would be debated and passed. Of course, when we are into the dying days of a session of Parliament, the pressure is on the Minister, on every Hon. Member of this House and on the standing committees to rush through as much legislation as possible by the end of the month.
There are a number of clauses in the Bill which give the Minister the power to do practically anything he wishes with this company. If this Bill was introduced for other Crown corporations, Ministers of the Government could sell them for a song to whoever, including perhaps their friends. They could
sell our Crown corporations to someone other than the stated purchaser in press releases. They could sell them for more or less than initially indicated or for much less than the fair market value of the company. Perhaps the rush to get this legislation through is more related to giving the Minister this power than to selling the company before the summer. That is hard to say. While we agree that the purchasers we know of are going to be the best kind of purchasers, we feel that the Bill could serve as a model-all one would have to do is to change the title-for future sales of all other Crown corporations. We worry about that. If that were to happen in subsequent months or years, I can assure the Minister that he will have difficulty getting it through at the beginning of the session, let alone during the last couple of weeks.
Clause 3(3) allows the Governor in Council to exempt any parts of the corporation from sale and allows the Minister to transfer the control of those portions, so exempted, to any government agency or other Crown corporation. That is not so bad because we would like to see him keep the whole thing, but he may also give it to "to any other person or body", to quote the Bill. We find that a little disturbing. If the prospective purchasers were to decide that they do not want some portion of the company, the Minister has the authority under this Bill to let anyone else have that portion. Why has the Minister not indicated in the Bill to whom he is selling NTCL? He has a buyer. He has made various announcements. Why could he not have given us all of the details? If he wants to sell a corporation to someone, why can he not be specific? If the Bill had been specific, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), any other Minister, or the Cabinet could not change the terms. They could not dispose of some parts and not others. They could not sell off or give away parts of a corporation to any other persons known or unknown.
We do not want to obstruct this legislation, but we will want the Minister to give us more detail in committee this evening. We would like him to be a lot more forthcoming and open than he has been. Now that the Government has decided to whom it is going to sell, there is nothing wrong with making all the terms of the purchase agreement fully public. Once this Bill passes, the Minister, I am confident-I accept his word-will proceed to sell to whom he is saying he will sell. I do not know if I would be that trusting of other Ministers, but l believe this Minister and I accept his word.
Initially, the Government had accepted a bid from an Edmonton trucking company but requested some native involvement in order to soothe the native community in the North. That failed to happen and, thank goodness, bids were reopened. Another consortium of southern controlled development companies entered into the bidding. Again, the Government-and I compliment the Minister on this-decided to sell to two of the native corporations which had offered to buy, namely, the Inuit people. That agreement was announced in principle on May 17. But we must prevent this Bill, as is, to be used to sell off other Crown corporations, particularly winners, in the same manner. I can accept this sale in this instance, and in this instance only, because I trust and believe in the
June 25, 1985

Minister's intention to sell to whom he says he will, but, as I said before, Mr. Speaker, the same Bill could be used, by changing its title, to sell of almost every other Crown corporation, winner or loser. The Government is determined to make its point about privatization by selling off this corporation because it feels that since it is in the North, no one in the south will care much, but those people up North will, no matter how few they are. Either way, as a matter of general principle, our Party would be opposed to selling off Crown corporations, particularly those which are winners, and the people of Canada can share in the cost of those losers which provide an essential public service to a small market, an isolated area or a thinly and widely scattered population. However, the bid which has been accepted appears to us to be the best. While co-operation between the Inuit and the Dene would be nice, I suppose a thousand years or more of conflict is not likely to be resolved over a joint board or a split sale in the operations of NTCL.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Minister can let me know this evening, or now if he wants, whether any consideration was given to retaining a minority interest in the company of 15 per cent, 20 per cent or 25 per cent. The Government would then have representation on the board of directors and would therefore have first-hand knowledge about what is going on. Another thing, which I know the Minister would be conscious of and conscientious about, is the fact we have heard nothing about what protection there may be for the very experienced management and the employees of the company once the sale is completed and down the road a number of years. This is not an easy operation to run and it is obvious that the management and the employees of the company have been doing a darn good job. We are not suggesting it is perfect; there are always going to be some complaints, always some areas where new or additional services could be or should be provided. But, generally speaking, they have done an excellent job and we want to know what protection there is for the management and the employees of the NTCL.
I would like to close by saying that the Government will not find any obstruction on our part over this Bill for the simple reason that we know or understand who the purchasers are. Had it been otherwise, this Bill would not be going through in this session of Parliament, I can assure the Minister of that. We hope the Minister will accept some if not all of our amendments later this day. Even if he does not, we are prepared to proceed with this because it will serve as an experiment where the people of the North own and operate something which is so essential to their own as well as the general public good.
On the assumption that this will go through by this Friday, we wish the new owners well. We hope the Government will, in subsequent years, provide all the co-operation necessary, including any assistance they might want or need or ask for to help improve and make a better success of the company's operations. I hope that eventually other residents of the North, particularly the Dene, will become involved in ownership and
Northern Transportation Company operation of this corporation. That is something 1 hope the people of the North can work out among and between themselves with the assistance and co-operation of the Minister and his Department. 1 also hope, Sir, that the Minister will give serious consideration to retaining some percentage of ownership in order to maintain the national presence, not just for the sake of doing so but in support of the provision of an essential service in northern Canada. I believe everyone in Canada is willing to provide that support and participation through the Government. I do not think it was necessary to sell off 100 per cent of the company, but if that is the Government's intention,
I am confident that this Minister at least will provide all the help and assistance he can in the years ahead to make sure that those people can proceed to improve and enlarge upon this vital element of northern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure this afternoon to speak in favour of Bill C-53 which would grant to the Minister of Transport the authority to divest himself of equity in the Northern Transportation Company Limited. I guess there are two points for discussion. First of all, the Bill grants to the Government of Canada that authority; the second part is the actual sale itself. I think it will be essential at this evening's meeting of the Standing Committee on Transport, when we delve into the sale, that information requested by both the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) and the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) be made available. We should have before us the sale agreement and the memorandum of sale so that parliamentarians can be aware of what we are really getting ourselves into.
I believe that NTCL should be privatized. There is no reason why the Government of Canada should be in the business of operating barges on the Mackenzie River to the Beaufort Sea, Hudson Bay or anywhere else. It can be quite reasonably and sensibly done by Canadians in a private capacity. Why should the Government of Canada be operating trucking companies such as the Grimshaw subsidiary of NTCL? There is no reason for it. The Minister explained that the Government had got into the business by accident when it took over the old Eldorado uranium operation in the war years. Before that time, water transportation services had been provided by private companies and by the Hudson Bay company at one time. Roman Catholic missions operated their own water transport system from time to time. So the service had been provided by the private sector prior to nationalization by the Government of Canada. There is absolutely no reason why we cannot go back to the private system.
As a Crown corporation NTCL was in a very privileged position. It had certain friends in Ottawa who made sure that it was protected when it came to matters such as the issuing of water licences. Other firms which wished to get into the business found that their applications were not dealt with at the same rate of speed and with the same alacrity that NTCL's applications had been dealt with.
I think that at the same time as we are putting NTCL back into the private sector, we should take an over-all look at the

June 25, 1985
Northern Transportation Company
regulatory regime which governs water transportation in northern Canada. No longer should NTCL be in this privileged position, enjoying what is tantamount in certain areas to a monopoly. We should allow proper competition. We should allow small operators to get into the business to provide specialized and localized services. I foresee that in the immediate future we might have what you might call two trunk operators, NTCL and ATL. They would provide service throughout the whole waterway. Specialty services such as stand-by supply vessels for the Beaufort Sea oil and gas industry can be provided by others. For service into small communities there is no reason why local operators cannot get themselves smaller barges. You do not have to run 1,500-ton barges into snowdrifts. You can operate more effectively with smaller barges. This would be a good opportunity for local entrepreneurs to set up business and provide a valuable service to the smaller communities. I hope the Canadian Transport Commission will take a new view of the regime and open up the market. Let us have competition in the market for water services. Let us have flexibility so that services can be changed rapidly to meet rapidly changing demands.
Many customers of NTCL and other firms are in the oil and gas business. One year they need delivery to one point, but in the next year the market has changed and they need delivery to other locations. It is necessary to have a system which can respond rapidly to changes in demand. Small operators must be allowed to set up easily.
The Government should ensure that vessels in operation are seaworthy and that the crews of those vessels have the necessary qualifications to operate the vessels safely. However, the Government should not concern itself about what charges are made to transport goods from place to place in particular vessels. And that is not a concern of the Government of Canada.
The Hon. Member for Regina East takes a very patronizing attitude-

He says that the Government has to help us out by keeping a handle on things up there. I can tell the Hon. Member for Regina West that the operators and businessmen in the Northwest Territories are just as competent as are those in Regina or anywhere else in the country. We do not need the Government to hold our hands, thank you very much.
In the near future there will be some changes in the nature of the industry as there have been already. The resupply of communities is not as important in the general scheme of things, especially in the revenues generated for the shipping companies, as it was previously. There is no reefer service on the Mackenzie or the Beaufort Sea any more, as far as I know. Produce and groceries are not transported by water any more but, rather, by truck, air, or other quicker methods. The supply of petroleum products to some of the more remote communities is very important. They would like to be assured of having petroleum products delivered on a regular basis.
However, the future of the shipping industry is not so much in the area of community resupply as it is in the area of service to the oil and gas industry. That is the big customer of NTCL and other operators. The future may be in the transportation of heavy machinery for the oil and gas industry and there may be a greater concentration on coastal routes than on river routes. NTCL no longer has a real presence on Lake Athabasca, especially since the uranium mine there has been closed down. As roads push further north along the Mackenzie River, water supply in those areas will not be quite as important as hitherto. The centre of the industry is moving northward, with a greater emphasis on service to the oil and gas industry than there was previously when community resupply was the biggest activity in which NCTL and its few competitors engaged.
As a politician I cannot resist the temptation to make a few remarks about the inconsistency of some of my friends in the Liberal Party. Liberal policy has always fluctuated with wide swings. When the Liberal Party said one thing, one could never take for granted that that would be done as opposed to something entirely opposite. Privatization has always been the policy of this Party. NTCL was on a short list in 1979 when the Progressive Conservative Party formed the Government for much too short a period.
During the 1979 and 1980 election campaigns my Liberal competition went to places like Hay River, which is the centre of operations for NTCL, and tried to put the fear of God into the employees of NTCL. They said that the PCs would sell the industry out from under the feet of the employees and sell them down the river. The Liberal pitch was that they would not sell NTCL but would keep it as a Crown corporation guaranteeing all the jobs for life whether they were needed or not. They said that there was no way they would privatize NTCL.
Only a couple of years later when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry became the Minister of Transport, his very first act was to reverse totally the Liberal Party policy. He said that they were going to sell NTCL. That makes one wonder whether you should ever vote for Members of the Liberal persuasion having seen them swing around 180 degrees in a matter of months. Their words are not really to be believed. However, I believe the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry was correct in coming to the conclusion that NTCL was a prime candidate for privatization and that the interests of northerners and of all of Canada would be best served by having northern water transportation in private hands.

Let us look at how this policy decision has been effected in private practice. If we were to be honest with ourselves, we would have to admit that the whole issue has been a comedy of errors from start to finish. The privatization process has dragged on for well over a year. People have not known where they stood. This has been particularly hard on the employees of NTCL who did not know what was going to happen to them. They could not get a straight answer from anyone. It all started when the former Minister of Transportation appointed an American firm of financial consultants to carry out the privatization of a Canadian corporation. I cannot understand why he had to choose an American firm. Are there no Canadian financial consultants who could have done the same thing?
I have heard many prospective buyers of NTCL complain that they were unable to get the necessary information to put in a rational bid. Prospective buyers could not get that information and I know that Members of Parliament could not get it. There is no way that people in general could find out what the Government had for sale. Not only have the customers of NTCL been left up in the air for that period of time, they still do not know what will happen. The whole decision-making process during both administrations has been shrouded with secrecy. Nobody knew what was for sale or what the perspective bids were. Why could we not have had a system which would provide a form indicating what was for sale and which listed all of the assets and necessary information? In that way, there could have been a process whereby the bids were opened publicly to show who bid for what and for how much. The whole process would have been open and would have prevented any complaints about political persuasion in particular circumstances.
We saw the Northern Industrial Carrier fiasco when apparently a conditional sale was made and the prospective purchaser could not then meet the conditions of that sale. I suspect the purchaser did not know what he was getting into the first place, but that delayed matters even more. The employees, customers and others did not know what was happening.
If it is this difficult to privatize a rather small Crown corporation like NTCL, I certainly do not envy the Minister when he tries to privatize Air Canada. I hope he has learned some of the difficulties and how to overcome them when he goes to bigger and better things.

Northern Transportation Company could deal with individual people, regardless of race, who come together to form a business corporation rather than having an over-all emphasis on groups put together because of ethnic origins.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments about this Bill and the statements which have been made so far in the Chamber today. I agree with the comments of speakers on both sides of the House concerning the advisability of this piece of legislation, but I should like to take exception to some remarks which were made in a philosophical way about the policy of the former Government as it related to this Bill. I can see no inconsistency with the former Government when it initiated this legislation, but I saw some inconsistency in the comments of the Hon. Member who represents this area of the country, particularly in his argument justifying the fact that the Government brought forth this Bill. In effect, that Hon. Member said that a member of the New Democratic Party showed a patronizing attitude when he talked about the needs of people in northern areas and that those people could supply their own transportation companies, that they were well equipped to do so. I do not doubt that at all. I do not doubt the wisdom of the Government in bringing forward the legislation.
I represent a relatively northern area of the country and understand how seasons change-that sometimes it is necessary to use snowmobiles or aeroplanes to transport goods and other times it is necessary to use trucks. It must be borne in mind that the profitable part of this operation in northern Canada, as the Hon. Member outlined, is the transportation of goods and services to the oil industry.
There is another element here that I am confident would have been explained in a much more thorough manner by the former Minister of Transport had he been in the position today of having this Bill about to go through the House of Commons. It is that the Government of Canada has a real responsibility for the transportation of goods and services. It has a responsibility to make sure that when it brings in legislation like this that it is going to protect people who make use of that transportation service, whether or not it be for the transportation of fuel, as is the case with this transportation network we are talking about today. In other words, when you get down to the human element of people who are living in northern areas who depend upon a transportation system for their fuel or for their food or for any other commodity, that has to be borne in mind by the Government of Canada. What I am talking about is direct subsidization or indirect subsidization to that particular carrier.
It seems as if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) only has one thing on his mind when he talks in the House of Commons about changing the structure of transportation in this country. To him the bottom line is saving money for the Government of Canada. That goes across all boundaries of philosophy. One cannot say, for example, that this Minister of Transport or the Government of Canada is anxious to get rid of Crown corporations. When it seems that it can save money
by creating a Crown corporation for transportation purposes, it does it. For example, in the November statement the transportation company called CN Marine is being made into a Crown corporation to save the Government of Canada $20 million or $40 million a year.
The main element in legislation introduced in this House, to accomplish what the Government wants to accomplish, that should be borne in mind is how it affects people, not so much the oil companies that it serves or big business that it serves, not so much that portion of the transportation system that snows a profit to the transportation company but that portion of the system that affects people. It should also be borne in mind who these people are. These people are, in most of our isolated and northern areas, primary producers of one sort or another. They could be trappers, fishermen or loggers, but they are people.
If one adds up what the Government of Canada has done as far as the northern areas are concerned, it has to be looked at from the point of view of how much the transportation costs are being increased. How can any operator today budget, for instance, for the increase on the tax on fuel that was recently brought in in the Budget? Considering services to the general public, it was not beneficial in the northern areas to have the postal Crown corporation cut back the number of hours of the small post offices from 40 to 30.
My main interjection in this debate is that under the former Government, I am confident there would have been guarantees given to the people affected by any legislation that would have been brought forward. The Government of Canada would say that perhaps that was a waste of money and that perhaps it should be getting away from subsidizing services to the general public. That is the bottom line, is it not, of any Government, service to the people of Canada and not necessarily for a company to make a profit at the end of the year?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my friend.
Let me put it very succinctly. Bill C-32 amends the present Fisheries Act and clarifies certain powers of the Minister. The Bill has been before the House and in committee since the first week in March and, of course, it is now at report stage. An agreement has been reached between all Parties concerned that with the addition of several amendments to Bill C-32 as presented to the House there will be a further provision which will have the effect of what could loosely be called a sunset provision. The effect will be that Bill C-32 as amended and as passed by this House today, if that indeed happens and I think it will, will cease to have any force and effect on December 31, 1986. The effect also of the so-called sunset provision will be that unless the present provisions of Bill C-32 are re-enacted before that date or unless some of the provisions of Bill C-32, perhaps with other additions or deletions, are re-enacted by December 31, 1986, then the present provisions of the Fisheries Act will spring back into effect.
What it means, put very simply, is that it has been agreed that we will pass these provisions and they will have effect until December 31, 1986, unless changed by legislation before then, and that if that is not done, we will be back to where we began with the present clauses of the present Fisheries Act.
Fisheries Act
The Government has agreed to this unusual procedure on the basis of common sense. It was clear that members of the New Democratic Party did not want to allow this Bill to go through as presently constituted, and as a consequence, it would be impossible to legislate Bill C-32 before the close of this present parliamentary Session. That would mean that I as Minister of Fisheries would be in a position of leaving at risk my legal authority during the summer months and until such date as the House could next attend to this particular piece of legislation.
When I say that this procedure has been agreed to on the basis of common sense, I think that that is an appropriate way to describe it. I as Minister of Fisheries feel very strongly that it is better to have a temporary provision which at least establishes some stability with respect to the legal regime under which the Department must operate in the interests of the fishing community than it is to leave things at risk any longer. There has been some suggestion that in view of the Court of Appeal ruling which dissolved the injunction contained in Mr. Justice Collier's decision of last summer, there is no risk. It is my view and I think the view of other Members of the House that there is a risk. Mr. Speaker, before we pass Bill C-32 on third reading, I would just like to make a few brief remarks. What has been stated by the Minister is correct inasmuch as we have been able to come to an agreement for this Act to be reviewed and the sunset clause to come into effect, eliminating these amendments, at December 31, 1986. I think there is also an agreement that the Government and the committee will, prior to that date, take the Bill to the West Coast and the Atlantic Provinces to try and bring it more into tune with the realities of the fishing industry as they are today.
The fisheries policy, Mr. Speaker, should always be based on the foundation of consultation with user groups before decisions are made. I have noticed lately that decisions have been made without proper consultation. It is incumbent upon the Minister and the Government to fully consult with those most affected by fisheries legislation and policy before decisions are made. I look back to a decision made in 1979 by the then Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in the Clark Government where large trawlers were allowed in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. This affected the lives of many of our inshore fishermen. That decision was made simply because of pressure, which sometimes comes from political sources. As a result, the fishery in that area was set back for a good many years. I could go on and on about the consultation which should or should not have taken place.
In November the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) indicated the vessel insurance program was going to be reviewed and

June 25, 1985
Fisheries Act
there would be increased wharfage fees and one thing and another, but there was little or no consultation with the people who were adversely affected by the changes. Therefore, I am glad that the word "consultation" is used in this Bill so that the interests of the user groups are taken into consideration before new policies are adopted. I take the Minister at his word that this consultative process will be upgraded and we will have the opportunity to consult with all fishermen concerned. I think the Minister should heed Motion No. 3 and, as I said, I am taking him at his word.
"Monitor" is a term which has been used here quite extensively in the last number of days and we will be monitoring the situation in the future to make sure that any changes in policy or practice will be made on the basis of consultation. That includes wharfingers. In the past few months wharfingers have been relieved of their duties and I think the Minister should very carefully consider this sort of approach and not allow wharfingers to be appointed on the basis of political whim.
With that, Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that over the next year, after the committee goes to Atlantic Canada in the fall, I am hoping that a new or very carefully considered Bill will be brought forward and that the committee will have the mandate to study that Bill along with the people who were involved in the industry. I think it is incumbent upon the Minister and the Committee to travel once again to the West Coast and that the next Bill, after the sunset clause comes into effect, will be carefully written after full consideration of the best interests of the fishing community. Once again, my colleague from Comox-Powell River and I have taken the Minister at his word and we will be monitoring his progress in the future.

Mr. Speaker, the progress of this Bill through the House of Commons and committee has been a rather interesting exercise. It has consumed a large number of hours in the House, and I think one thing which should be developed as a result is the way in which Bills are introduced in order to improve understanding between the Members concerned and to try to expedite passage.
It goes without saying that this legislation has important effects on a great many people. The Minister's attention has certainly been called, in quite a number of ways, to the problems of many of the people dependent upon this industry and the expectations for solutions that they have. Early on he received a list of five important areas in the form of a letter from myself regarding the additional discretionary powers which will be given to him. As of now, those points have not been dealt with, and the position of the Minister is: "Trust me,
I will do a good job. I will live up to the election promises of this Government. I have the serious concerns of the fishing industry at heart". Well, the only reason this Bill is passing through the House today is because of this amendment being agreed to which would give the industry the necessary protection. I thank the Minister for considering it seriously and for providing a safety valve.
After several fishing seasons have passed by, we will be able to evaluate its effect in consultation with the people concerned. Our fear, of course, is that this will be the last opportunity for
Parliamentarians to involve the public in consideration of the fishing industry. Should the Minister's Cabinet colleagues or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) overrule an attempt to do the things which are required, this safety valve would at least present an opportunity for Members of Parliament and the public to provide input.
The Minister said that this legislation provides him more power than he would like to see in the hands of a Cabinet Minister, so that this rather unique sunset clause gives us an opportunity to look at the progress which has been made. Having said that, the Minister must attempt to provide a mechanism whereby the industry can be consulted and a process for making that consultation work can be put in place. There must be a mechanism for resolving disputes that does not end up in civil disobedience or a breakdown of the system. The Minister will have the enormous task of developing that.
There are many problems facing native fishermen and native communities which depend upon the fishing industry. As the committee travelled the west coast, many native fishermen indicated that they had been completely ignored by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. There is no doubt about that, Mr. Speaker. It was established time and again. The Minister has a major responsibility to ensure that the people who depend on that resource are consulted and given access to the decision-making process.
With regard to amendments, there was an interesting one for which the Minister will have to answer. The Conservative Party chose to defeat an amendment which would provide for sports fisheries within the area of federal Government jurisdiction. In light of some of the statements made in the past by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser), he will have an interesting job justifying to the sports fishing community why the Government defeated a motion which it allegedly supports. That issue must be resolved.
There are many communities in the country that depend to a very large degree on the fishing industry. Over the years we have watched the centralization of the fishing industry through the movement of processing plants to larger areas and the new phenomenon of trucking salmon from the point at which it is caught and landed hundreds and hundreds of miles to processing plants. That eventually destroys jobs and the economic base of small communities for want of an important infrastructure. Through the actions of the federal Government, a number of other factors have come into play which have made those communities economically weaker.
As the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the senior Minister from British Columbia, we ask him to study that problem which, as yet, remains unsolved.
