speakeroldname: Hon. John A. Fraser (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the remarks made by my hon. friends. It should be clearly understood that Bill C-32 was not intended to be an overhaul of the entire Fisheries Act. I know that the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) knows this to be so, despite what he has said. To argue since March that Bill C-32 should take into account every possible eventuality within the experience of fisheries on both coasts, inland, and in the north, is not an accurate approach to the amendment which has been proposed.
Bill C-32 is an amendment to provide the authority, under law, to the Minister to manage the fisheries of Canada. That authority has been cast in doubt by decisions made on the west coast a year ago. It has been put further in doubt by a court case which is proceeding in the Province of New Brunswick at this very moment. There has been the suggestion that the Government has not consulted enough. I defy anyone looking through my diary for the last eight months, and looking through the diaries of previous Fisheries Ministers, to find any Fisheries Minister who has been to more places and listened to more people than I have during the time that I have been Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
I have done that because it is my view that one cannot be Minister of Fisheries and Oceans by remaining in Ottawa. One must be where the fish and fishermen are. The vast majority of people involved in the fishing industry in Canada know that someone must have the authority to manage the fishing industry and make decisions for it.
Having said that, I was the fisheries critic for a number of years and I noticed that people within the fishing community have been concerned about decisions that are made in an arbitrary way without real consultation. To the extent that that happened, the interests of everyone may not have been properly taken into account before a decision was made. As a consequence of that, we are in the process of establishing an Atlantic Regional Council in an attempt to focus the fishing community into one place in order to have meaningful consultation. On the west coast we have the Minister's Advisory Committee which, while not perfect, is at least of assistance.
Fisheries Act
In addition to those formal structures, there is also a wide process of consultation with user groups, fishermen, and fishing communities on the establishment of fishing plans, fishing schedules, and opening dates on both coasts. To pretend that there is no consultation going on now is not accurate. Through this Bill the Fisheries Minister is now mandated to take into account the interests of the user groups, and that must be done on the basis of consultation. I believe that there is unanimous agreement among all three parties that that is an advance which reflects the wish of the fishing community. I want to assure Hon. Members that it reflects my own desire to ensure that the interests of user groups are taken into account through real consultation.
One of our difficulties has been to legislate the requirement for consultation. That has caused most of our difficulty with this Bill. It is extremely difficult to determine wording for consultation if you cannot identify the groups with which you are supposed to consult. In that respect this legislation is perhaps not satisfactory. Perhaps between now and the time when I bring further legislation into the House we can develop a consultative mechanism which can be more clearly defined.
If that is possible, then I most certainly shall put it forward and support it. However, I want to give a word of warning to my friends in the New Democratic Party. A very large degree of responsibility now lies on their shoulders not to come up with vague, rhetorical talk about what would be desirable in a perfect world but rather wording that passes the test of what is good legislation and which can be upheld as a consequence of that wording.
This spring, we sent the Fisheries Committee to the West Coast. The Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River knows perfectly well that that committee travelled because I was determined that it would travel. He also knows that I may send him, along with other Members of the committee, to Atlantic Canada. I may leave him there for months if he has any difficulty understanding the problems of that particular part of the fishery.
It must be clearly understood that 1 am going to ask the user groups to send me specific recommendations and to define the wording properly so as to improve this Bill. The search for those recommendations cannot be left indefinitely. I say to the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) and the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River that this Bill has been in the process for a long time-since March. It is my view that while the Bill is perhaps not perfect, it goes a long way to at least establishing some certainty within a legal regime until 1986 and gives us an opportunity to examine the provisions during the interim.
We will do that in order to determine if an improvement can be made. It is not my desire to be an autocrat, but it is my determination to be sure that in the interest of conservation of the fish stocks and all the people who make up the fishing communities in Canada that the fishery be properly managed.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT FEDERAL SALES TAX NOT APPLY TO CONTRACTS SIGNED BEFORE MAY 23
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the tax measures announced in the Budget brought down by the Conservative Government on May 23 is having a disastrous effect on the construction industry. Tens of thousands of jobs in the prefab concrete sector will be lost as a result of the federal sales tax imposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
This Government has no idea how the construction industry works and has levied a sales tax while failing to give sufficient notice so that contracts already signed can be carried out before the new tax becomes effective. This Government has helped to increase the cost of residential construction, and considering the way this tax is being introduced, it will cause Canadian contractors to go bankrupt and thousands of Canadians will be jobless. In many cases, the 6 per cent federal sales tax is higher than the profit margin of prefab concrete contractors. The Minister of Finance should announce immediately that the tax does not apply to contracts signed before May 23, in order to give the parties concerned a chance to adjust their prices to allow for the new tax.

Mr. Speaker, I rose in the House on December 7, 1984, and gave a statement about the troubles of the Sikh community in Vancouver after people on all sides told me that they were threatened and intimidated.
I rise today to express the shock and sadness of the Indo-Canadian community in my Province of British Columbia at the tragic crash of the Air-India jetliner.
June 25, 1985

All the facts on the crash are not in yet so I will not comment on it. However, I want to take this opportunity to tell Canadians that the Indo-Canadian community in Canada is a peaceloving community. The Sikh community is an overwhelmingly peace loving community in Canada.
Sikhs, who believe that human beings are creatures of the supernatural and therefore equal, pray every day in the temples in my city of Vancouver that God will be kind to each and every one. That includes enemies as well as friends.
Whatever the results of this crash investigation, I ask Canadians not to judge a community by a few extremists. Mahatma Gandhi once said that, if you take an eye for an eye, the whole world would go blind.

CRASH OF AIR-INDIA FLIGHT 182-SYMPATHY FOR VICTIMS' RELATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, mere words cannot adequately express the shock and sense of loss that all Canadians felt at the terrible human tragedy that occurred on Air-India Flight 182.
I know all Members of this House will join with me today to express the greatest sympathy to all of the families and friends of those who lost their lives. On a personal note, I wish to express my deep sympathy to the members of my community in Etobicoke who lost friends and loved ones.
Over the past few days the media have been quick to speculate on the possibility of sabotage aboard the Air-India flight. Extreme caution must be exercised in this situation. A complete investigation needs to be done before an accurate assessment of the cause of the crash can be determined. The last thing we need in Canada is to fuel animosities between Canadians on the basis of, as yet, unsubstantiated facts.
With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, the Government must not hesitate to tighten security procedures at all Canadian international airports. No measure should be ignored that could increase the security and safety of Canadians travelling abroad.

subtopic: NORWEGIAN VETERANS' REUNION AT ONTARIO TRAINING BASE
NORWEGIAN VETERANS' REUNION AT ONTARIO TRAINING BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute to the 2,000 Norwegian war veterans who trained at "Little Norway" near Gravenhurst, Ontario, during the Second World War. Saturday, June 22, was the fortieth anniversary of the closing of the air base. A plaque was unveiled at Muskoka Airport commemorating the airmen who trained there.
I would like to commend and thank Lieutenant Colonel Svein Aaser, Defence Attache at the Norwegian Embassy in Ottawa. Colonel Aaser brought greetings on behalf of the Norwegian Government, and a special letter from the King of Norway. It is interesting to note that many of the airmen who trained at Little Norway married Canadian girls and settled in Canada. Originally an international air show had been planned, with various types of aircraft invited to participate or be on display. Unfortunately this participation had to be cancelled a few months ago because of a conflict of dates when Trenton changed its airshow from September to June 22.
Mayor Don Holstock hosted a reception for the visiting airmen on their arrival June 14. All veterans from Muskoka formed a welcoming committee for our Norwegian visitors. The red carpet was rolled out for the visitors by Mayor Jim Lang of Bracebridge, who hosted a wine and cheese party. Mayor Sheila Hatch of Muskoka Lakes greeted the guests at a luncheon in Bala. Mayor Gorden Snell of Huntsville hosted a coffee party. Another highlight for the visiting Norwegian airmen was a boat trip on RMS Segwun, and a tour of the Ontario Fire College.

subtopic: EFFECT OF SALES TAX ON NOVA SCOTIA ROAD CONTRACTORS
EFFECT OF SALES TAX ON NOVA SCOTIA ROAD CONTRACTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Nova Scotia Road Builders Association represents the road building and heavy construction industry in my provide. Contractors who have a multi-million dollar investment in plant and equipment, and who employ more than 3,500 men and women, are small businessmen, the people the Government has claimed were ignored and unfairly treated in the past, the people the Government wants to encourage and support.
But the Government's actions belie its words. The proposed changes in the May 23 Budget with respect to the 6 per cent sales tax that will apply, among other things, to ready-mix concrete and asphalt paving mix, are a direct affront to the very principles of free enterprise that the Government supposedly espouses. Provincial and Municipal Governments will not pay that 6 per cent sales tax; the burden is falling on the small businessman. The road construction industry in Nova Scotia is one that has been battered by years of recession and is only just now beginning to re-establish any kind of a profit marging. The imposition of this sales tax is the last thing the industry needs at this time.
Already the proposal to implement the sales tax is creating chaos. There is work out to tender; concrete and asphalt will be used. Contractors do not know if they should ignore the 6 per cent sales tax and incur the Government's wrath, or to include it and not get work. A wonderful Catch-22 situation.

June 25, 1985
Surely the Government of the day can delay these tax changes until January, 1986. In the interim there will be time to get systems in place, and time for contractors to negotiate with their customers on how this tax should be collected and remitted.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian community with origins in India is transfixed with grief this week. The sudden destruction of Air-India Flight 182 off the coast of Ireland has taken the lives of 329 persons, most of them Canadian citizens of Indian origin.
It is possible that a bomb caused this tragedy. It is all too easy in such circumstances for media speculation to focus on a crime and its perpetrators. It is all too easy for popular emotions to be stirred up. People forget that individuals are innocent in our legal system until they have been found guilty in the courts, and that is is individuals who commit crimes, not whole communities.
The Indo-Canadian community has been living through very trying times. The desire by some to achieve more autonomy for Punjab culminated in the Indian Army's assault, just over a year ago, on the Golden Temple in Amritsar. The assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gradhi last October was followed by several days of fierce anti-Sikh violence in Indian cities and towns. If frustration of Sikh desires for more autonomy lead to militant action by some persons, it is clear that the community generally has paid dearly for these excesses.
Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi has aided the Sri Lankan Government in ending the violence that has gripped that neighbouring country. I call on our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to offer his assistance to the Indian Government in ending the violence that India is experiencing.

Mr. Speaker, Viktoras Petkus, a member of the Lithuanian Helsinki Group, has been arrested time and again for his visible activities and vocal advocacy on behalf of religious freedom in Soviet occupied Lithuania. Petkus was first arrested at the age of 17 in 1947, and sentenced to 10 years of hard labour for his participation in a Catholic youth organization. He was released in 1953, but was once again imprisoned in 1957 for his part in the distribution of religious books written by Lithuanian emigre writers before the occupation.
Viktoras Petkus continues to be adopted by Amnesty International as a prisoner of conscience because of his non-violent
exercise of the right to freedom of expression. The most tragic aspect of the Petkus case is his ever-worsening health. In 1978 the Soviets sentenced him to seven years in prison, three years special regime camp, and five years exile, on a charge of anti-Soviet agitation and propaganda. Those years of medical neglect, followed by an operation for a malignant tumor on his face, have cost him his health. Petkus is still alive, but in grave danger.
I call upon the House of Commons to direct the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to call upon the Ambassador of the Soviet Union to demand that Petkus be released immediately, and to send a clear reminder to the Soviet Government of its obligations as a signator of the Helsinki Accords.

subtopic: FIRST ANNUAL WORKERS MEMORIAL DAY SERVICE
FIRST ANNUAL WORKERS MEMORIAL DAY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 20, 1984, more than a kilometre below the surface in the Falconbridge mine, a rockburst occurred which resulted in the tragic deaths of four miners.
Last Thursday in Sudbury I had the honour of attending, together with the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton), the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith), the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), and the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), the first Workers Memorial Day service. The purpose of this service, organized by local citizens and the Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers' Union, was to pay respect to and to remember all those miners and others who had given their lives in the production of mineral products. It is to become a national annual event.
Representatives of labour, management, and Government consistently and thoughtfully spoke about the need for accelerated efforts for better health and safety conditions in the workplace.
In the process the Minister of State for Mines described a new, five-year, $4.2 million co-operative research program aimed at eliminating rockbursts, one of the major hazards facing underground miners. The federal Government, the Province of Ontario, Cambell Red Lake Mines Ltd., Falcon-bridge Ltd., and Inco Ltd., will each contribute $1.4 million. This is a fine example of a partnership in progress between government and industry. The threat of rockbursts will increase as Canadian mines progress to greater depths. This research is thus necessary and timely to ensure safe and highly productive mining practices.

ROLE PLAYED BY RENfe LEVESQUE IN POLITICAL, SOCIAL, AND ECONOMIC EVOLUTION OF QUEBEC

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CRASH OF AIR-1NDIA FLIGHT 182-EXPLOSION AT TOKYO AIRPORT-OFFICIAL CONDOLENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has asked me to express in the House the Government's deep sorrow over the two weekend air disasters. The destruction of Air-India Flight 182 off the coast of Ireland brought untimely and tragic death to 329 passengers and crew, the majority of whom were Canadians. An explosion at Tokyo Airport killed two Japanese citizens and wounded several others.
I cannot over-emphasize the seriousness with which the Government views these tragic and sorrowful episodes. [Translation]
Yesterday, the Prime Minister of Canada expressed his condolences to the families of those who lost their lives in this terrible accident.
The Prime Minister has announced the Government's firm resolve to do everything in its power to determine the cause of this disaster.

On behalf of the Government the Prime Minister has expressed his condolences to the families and friends of those who perished in this tragedy, and I am sure that every Canadian shares their grief in their bereavement.
Both of the flights which became the focus of these tragic episodes originated in Canada, one involving a Canadian airline, the other, of course, Air-Indian Flight 182.
[ Translation]
At this time, the Government has no evidence that the Air Indian disaster was caused by an act of terrorism.

There is at this time no direct evidence that either of these episodes is linked to the dark context of international terrorism which appears to have burst out anew in the past few weeks. Nevertheless, the course of prudence would indicate that these episodes be treated in such a context.
[ Translation]
The Government has taken steps to prevent a recurrence of these tragic episodes. Yesterday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) ordered a review of airport security.

Security measures have been intensified at all Canadian airports, with emphasis on the scrutiny of baggage.
I want to inform the House that we have begun a major investigation, involving the security forces of several countries, to determine whether indeed the two tragedies are the work of terrorists and whether there is a link between the two episodes. If that proves to be the case, every effort will be made to identify and bring the guilty parties to justice.
We will not allow this country to become a killing ground for international terrorism.

subtopic: CRASH OF AIR-1NDIA FLIGHT 182-EXPLOSION AT TOKYO AIRPORT-OFFICIAL CONDOLENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition I rise with deep sorrow to express our profound sympathy and condolences to the families of all those who lost their lives, the majority of them Canadian, in the apparent explosion of Air-India Flight 182 from Canada to the United Kingdom.
I would also like to express our sympathy and condolences to the families of those Japanese baggage handlers who were killed or injured in the apparent explosion of a bomb in luggage taken off a Canadian Pacific flight from Vancouver to Tokyo.
In addition, we express our shock not only about these tragic events but also about the strong likelihood that they are the result of terrorist actions. If that is the case, we can only have and express feelings of revulsion about conduct that takes innocent lives in this way.
We call on the Government to do everything possible to assist the families of those who lost their lives in the Air-India explosion, as well as the Japanese families affected by the explosion in Tokyo. We call on the Government to take strong and immediate action to prevent any future incidents of this
June 25, 1985

kind from taking place in connection with flights linked with Canada or with Canadian airports.
The Government must move immediately to determine how and why these tragedies occurred. The Government must join with all nations to take concerted and strong action against all acts of terrorism, not just those involving airlines, and not just after the fact, but hopefully to prevent them from taking place.
Finally, now is the time for all Canadians of every origin to unite with their fellow Canadians of East Indian origin, but not just in sympathy. We must join with them in solidarity and unity in their grief. We must join with them as fellow members of our Canadian family, all of us desiring to live in peace and harmony together in Canada and in the world.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition, we want to express our condolences to the families of those who lost their lives in these tragic accidents. We must do everything we can to prevent a recurrence of such episodes.

subtopic: CRASH OF AIR-1NDIA FLIGHT 182-EXPLOSION AT TOKYO AIRPORT-OFFICIAL CONDOLENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with all Canadians in extending our deepest sympathy at the tragic loss of life in the crash of Air-India Flight 182. When this plane, flying from Toronto to Bombay, plunged 9,500 metres into the ocean, it took 329 people to their deaths. The magnitude of the suffering is literally indescribable.
We share the grief and sorrow of the bereaved relatives and friends. Our hearts go out to the families. Many of the victims are members of the Indo-Canadian community. Disaster has shattered their peaceful lives in this their new land.
We share the deeply felt sorrow of parents and grandparents, husbands and wives, children and grandchildren. Many of the innocent victims were on a journey of family reunion, in many instances after many years spent continents apart. The trip of their dreams was tragically transformed into a deathly nightmare.
The cause of this horrible tragedy is yet to be exactly determined. Circumstances indicate strongly that there was a mid-air explosion. I would however, like to mention at this time the heroic efforts of the Irish, British, and U.S. Air Force and Navy rescue teams who, with great will and determination, and attempting to Find an answer by searching to obtain the aircraft's "black box" from the bottom of the ocean. This will be the most reliable source of information on the cause of this horrible disaster.

It is not enough to shed tears and express our sympathy. We must all work together on an international scale to prevent a recurrence of this catastrophe. Countries all over the world must co-operate in providing the best possible standard of security for innocent travellers. We owe it to the victims of this disaster to do everything in our power to allay the concerns of Canadians and people throughout the world.
Oral Questions

Steps have been taken to improve airport security. Every nation in the world faces the challenge. Increasing acts of terrorism in Beirut, Frankfurt, and possibly now on Canadian soil, make concerted international action more urgent and pressing. Our nation can and should play a leading role. International terrorism is on the agenda at the 40th session of the UN in September. The political will to fight this international blight must be an urgent priority at that session of the United Nations. We, all the peoples of the world, must see an end to this international monstrosity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in light of the statements of sympathy that have been expressed, in the usual tradition following these incidents I think you will find an inclination to agree to extend the Question Period for the normal period of time, starting now.
Question Period will therefore last for 45 minutes until 3.12 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to ask my first question to the Minister of Transport I want to express again on behalf of the Official Opposition our deepest condolences to the families so tragically affected by the terrible incident of Air-India Flight 182. We pray for them, and indeed hope that we can find ways to prevent a recurrence of this horrible disaster.
This leads me to ask the Minister of Transport what steps are being taken to protect Canadian passengers. Can the Minister of Transport guarantee air travellers that his Government has now taken every appropriate measure to protect them?

Mr. Speaker, I think first of all we should acknowledge that Canada does have one of the best safety and security mechanisms in place. That has been alluded to by international aviation authorities, by the Canadian Airline Pilots' Association, and by the American Airline Pilots' Association, but I believe it is fair to say that, in view of the activities over the last few days, and particularly the last weeks, it is important that all our security and surveillance systems be re-evaluated.

June 25, 1985
Oral Questions
To that purpose the Prime Minister has ordered a full evaluation of the safety and security of all airports and airlines.
As well, we have put in place new measures to ensure that all checked baggage will be adequately screened or inspected. We stepped up the security with respect to passengers and carry-on luggage. We put a 24-hour delay on all cargo shipments, with the exception of perishables, and we are bringing into, at least our international airports for the time being, new equipment which will assist in the inspection of baggage, which equipment we hope will be arriving before the end of this week.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Prime Minister confirmed that the Indian Government requested, apparently on numerous occasions, in the days and weeks proceeding the terrible event, increased security for Air-India flights, and for Indian diplomats in Canada. What has the Minister done specifically to respond to these pressing requests?

Mr. Speaker, from time to time there were requests for additional security by Air-India authorities. There were extra RCMP deployed both at Toronto and at Mirabel, as there has been for some time. I should point out to the House that there was no indication that there was a specific threat to Flight 182 and, as a result, the extraordinary precautionary measures were not put in place. However, whenever the Air-India people had requested additional security or assistance with regard to the surveillance of passengers and baggage, and whenever there were any suspicions and such requests had come to us, we responded on every occasion.

subtopic: STATIONING OF RCMP OFFICERS AT AIRPORTS
STATIONING OF RCMP OFFICERS AT AIRPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in light of the incident, the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association has requested that the Minister abandon his ill advised plan to remove RCMP security officers from Canadian airports. Is the Minister ready today to announce that indeed he will not go ahead with such a plan, and the RCMP not only will continue to perform at airports but will receive appropriate resources and money to do the thorough checking that they are supposed to do?

subtopic: STATIONING OF RCMP OFFICERS AT AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this was a decision that was partially implemented by the previous administration. The Hon. Member will know that there was a review in 1975, 1976, and again in 1981, conducted by the Air Transport Association of Canada, Transport Canada officials, and the RCMP. At that time it was determined that the removal of RCMP from Class 2 airports would not undermine the level of security of those airports. However,
I would like to inform the Hon. Member, and all Hon.
Members of the House, that in view of the Prime Minister's statement yesterday wherein he ordered a full evaluation of the security systems in place at our airports and the security of our airlines, we are going to defer that decision pending the outcome of this review.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subsubtopic: AIR-INDIA CRASH-REMOVAL OF BAGGAGE AT MIRABEL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the Minister that the House notes and appreciates the actions that have already been initiated by the Minister, and the announcement that he has just made.
The Minister knows that several suspicious pieces of baggage were removed from Flight 182 at Mirabel. The superintendent of airport security at Mirabel has stated that Air-India broke a basic rule by not notifying the Department of Transport of the suspicious baggage. Perhaps the Minister could clear up some confusion. He indicated yesterday that, when Transport Canada is notified of these incidents, a thorough investigation of the plane and all baggage on board takes place. On the other hand an official of his Department has said that regularly baggage is removed from planes and flights continue without further investigation. What is the proper procedure to be followed in those circumstances?

subsubtopic: AIR-INDIA CRASH-REMOVAL OF BAGGAGE AT MIRABEL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that in this particular case Transport Canada was not apprised of any specific threat against Flight 182. Therefore, the basic normal Air-India precautions and surveillance that they conduct were conducted in their usual manner. I repeat that we did have the additional RCMP security officers deployed as requested.
With respect to the specific question regarding the luggage, I would like to say to the House, and to the Hon. Member, that this is the subject of a very delicate and intensive investigation by the RCMP and others. While there has been a lot of speculation and conjecture, I would hope that the Hon. Member would agree with me that at this point in time, prior to our ascertaining all the facts, it would probably be inappropriate for us to engage in any further speculation. I can assure the Hon. Member that this investigation will be carried out with the utmost of thoroughness and, until we receive more factual information, I would appreciate it if the Hon. Member would agree with me that it would be inappropriate to comment further on that point.

subsubtopic: AIR-INDIA CRASH-REMOVAL OF BAGGAGE AT MIRABEL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the Minister that I appreciate the delicate nature of the investigation with respect to particular pieces of luggage.
June 25, 1985

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister about procedure. We are told that the RCMP in Montreal were called to investigate the luggage in question while Flight 182 was still on the ground, but when they in fact arrived the plane had just departed a few minutes before. Given the statement of the Minister that Transport Canada, when informed of these kinds of incidents, does a thorough investigation of every piece of luggage on the aircraft, why was there no procedure in place, even though the plane had left, to have either the RCMP or Transport Canada request that that aircraft return to Montreal so that a thorough investigation of all the luggage on board could take place before it continued its journey across the Atlantic?

Mr. Speaker, once again may I repeat to the Hon. Member that Flight 182 was not designated as a flight with a specific threat. As a result there were no extraordinary procedures implemented at that time. Had there been, that would have been the normal course. Furthermore, I repeat that, to the best of my knowledge, our people were not informed of this until the aeroplane had left.

Mr. Speaker, in light of the statement made by the Prime Minister yesterday, I direct this question either to the Deputy Prime Minister or the Minister of Transport. The Prime Minister said yesterday that there is to be a special investigation. I would like to know from the Deputy Prime Minister, or the Minister of Transport, who is conducting this special investigation. Is it an in-house investigation by the Ministry of Transport, is it a combination of the Ministry of Transport and representatives of airlines, or is it a throughly independent investigation?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is aware that the accident per se is being investigated under the auspices of the Indian authorities, and that is consistent with international convention. Canadian authorities, United States authorities, U.K. authorities, and Irish authorities are also involved in the investigation process. Investigations having to do with security, and any criminal investigations, are being undertaken primarily by the RCMP.

subtopic: SCREENING OF PASSENGERS AND HAND LUGGAGE
SCREENING OF PASSENGERS AND HAND LUGGAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a standard in place for a long time now, dealing with the screening of passengers and hand luggage. As the Minister well knows, the screening of checked baggage, other parcels, and all other things that are placed aboard aircraft, is left entirely to the discretion of the various airlines. Yet the Ministry of Transport owns and operates the airports in Canada.
Oral Questions
I compliment the Minister on the quickness with which he has instituted full security arrangements since Sunday. However, is Transport Canada going to return to the practices of the past, or will the Ministry of Transport now assume its own responsibility for the screening of checked baggage and all other items that are boarded onto aircraft?

subtopic: SCREENING OF PASSENGERS AND HAND LUGGAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would say to the Hon. Member, and other Hon. Members, that, as a minimum, Canada has always fulfilled the standards and recommended practices of international convention. I think the Hon. Member is aware that most of these arrangements are done through international convention. Canada's practices, have always been superior to the minimum requirements advocated by these various international conventions. In fact Canada has been in the forefront in terms of it constantly striving to improve security and surveillance in our airport system. As recently as the Economic Summit in Bonn, Canada played a very major leadership role in trying to improve our security and surveillance in the airport system.
So, Mr. Speaker, to the extent that we can upgrade those standards consistent with the international convention, we are certainly prepared to do so. In fact it will be my intention to attend the ICAO convention tomorrow in Montreal to speak to this very important issue.

Mr. Speaker, surely it is obvious that leaving this matter up to the discretion of scores of airlines which come into and leave our country is not good enough. That is painfully obvious. Will the Ministry of Transport from now on be responsible, in co-operation with the airlines, the RCMP, and other security agencies-without us becoming complacent a few weeks later-for the security, screening, and surveillance of all articles and human beings who enter aircraft on international flights and, in many instances, domestic flights, and not leave it up to the discretion of airlines which obviously try to save money every chance they get? When do we put an end to the saving of money-
Order, please. There are a number of other Hon. Members who wish to ask questions.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member heard of the very Firm declaration made by the Prime Minister yesterday and of his full commitment, and that of the Government, to deal with this very important issue. I think that is clear evidence that the Government of Canada is taking a leadership role, in conjunction with the airlines and the aviation community, to deal with this very important issue. However, I believe it is more important to deal with this matter in a co-operative way rather than simply declaring an edict, with all the inherent difficulties which may occur.

June 25, 1985
Oral Questions
The Prime Minister's commitment yesterday was to undertake a complete evaluation of Canada's airport surveillance and security system and, as well, the security and safety of our airlines. To that end we will be instituting any measures necessary in order to ensure that that is carried out.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport as well. I can sympathize and respect the kind of difficulties the Government has in trying to establish a clear set of directions on this question. But I want to ask the Minister a very important question concerning the proposed evaluation announced by the Prime Minister.
I believe the Minister would acknowledge that there have been a number of quite confusing and contradictory statements and judgments about the various roles and responsibilities of agencies under his jurisdiction, and under the Government generally. I would want to suggest to the Minister, by way of a question, that it is far more important to ensure that such an evaluation be seen as not having any vested interest attached and, therefore, should be totally independent in its point of view.
Would the Minister not agree that it would be more appropriate to have the Canadian Aviation safety Board, which is an independent agency not tied into the Government, undertake the investigation into the security system at Canadian airports, as its mandate allows, in order to ensure that it is an independent study and not one which is done by in-house agencies or organizations of the Government itself?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we will be relying upon the advice, wisdom, and recommendations which come forth from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. I think the Hon. Member has presented a good suggestion. However, I want to remind him, and Hon. Members of the House, that in the Prime Minister's announcement yesterday he requested an examination of all aspects of airport and airline security under the auspices of the Secretary of the Cabinet and senior security and intelligence officials.
I think that the element of senior security and intelligence officials surely puts that within the ambit of some independence. However, we will certainly not disregard any recommendations which the Canadian Aviation safety Board should bring forth. In fact we would welcome them.

Mr. Speaker, we certainly recognized the necessity to have a number of agencies and officials involved. However, the Aviation Safety Board is not only independent but it can make its findings public so that there can not be any ease of security.
I would again ask the Minister if it would not be more appropriate at least to have the direct responsibility for the investigation and evaluation under the auspices of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board so that it can follow its proper mandate, not only to be independent and to be able to draw upon resources, but to also make sure that the findings of that board are independent and not kept within the confines of Cabinet or behind the cabinet door.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not the intention of myself or my cabinet colleagues to keep anything behind the cabinet door. I think this is a non-partisan issue which affects all Canadians. It is something we all have to deal with in a collective way.
To the extent that the Canadian Aviation Safety Board is involved in all elements of the investigation of the accident involving Flight 182, I am sure we will not only have a full report on it but any recommendations which may flow from that report will certainly be given serious consideration by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance, or to the Deputy Prime Minister. The Minister of Finance will be meeting later this afternoon with representatives of more than one million pensioners with whom I met this morning. They made two basic points about which I would like to ask the Minister of Finance. First, they want indexation restored to all pensions and, second, they want an announcement about the timing of the Government's decision on this important matter, to be made before the end of this week. Considering that the Cabinet met on Friday, is the Minister of Finance in a position to tell the House today the answer to the two important questions to which the pensioners of Canada want answers?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is right, I will be meeting with representatives of a very important group of seniors later on this afternoon. I will be discussing with them their concerns about this matter. As I have said on many occasions in this House, I will take those concerns very much into account in arriving at any decision which might be forthcoming. However, in precise response to the Hon. Member's question, no, I am not in a position to state anything further than I have in the past.

Mr. Speaker, considering the fact that Hon. Members on the opposition side and Hon. Members on the government side have confirmed that pensioners will be in a state of anxiety over the summer-there are no two sides of that coin; everyone is in agreement about
June 25, 1985

that-and considering that one of the pensioners with whom the Minister will be meeting this afternoon said to me this morning that she would at least like an answer-
With great respect, this is becoming a preamble to a supplementary question.

-on the question of timing, will the Minister assure the House that before the House rises the Government will at least have the courtesy to inform Canada's pensioners when they will hear an answer to this important question?

Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions I have stated that there would be no changes made in the payments to senior citizens until next year, so I think the Hon. Member should be trying to allay the anxiety about which he talks by advising seniors that they are going to see the normal increase in their cheques effective July 1. Again on October 1 there will be another increase in their pension cheques. I would hope that the Hon. Member would try to put to rest some of the anxieties which have been expressed by senior citizens which, I would say, he and other Hon. Members of the House have been trying to fan.
Appropriately trying to fan.

subsubtopic: ENTRY TO CANADA-MEASURES TO STOP PERSONS WHO FACE ARREST WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Following the tragic Air-Indian disaster this weekend, many Canadians are asking questions about Immigration operations, especially in the case of persons sought by the FBI or Interpol.
Could the Minister inform the House what measures are being taken by the Department of Employment and Immigration to prevent persons for whom warrants of arrest are out from entering Canada?
Furthermore, could the Minister inform the House what kind of co-ordination exists between her Department, the Department of Transport and the new civilian security intelligence agency which is responsible for airport security?

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: ENTRY TO CANADA-MEASURES TO STOP PERSONS WHO FACE ARREST WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the policy of the Department of Immigration continues. Any investigation of the tragedy involving Flight 182 would be carried out under the aegis of the RCMP, certainly not that of the Department of Immigration.
Oral Questions

subtopic: AIR-INDIA TRAGEDY-SUPPLEMENTARY MEASURES TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
AIR-INDIA TRAGEDY-SUPPLEMENTARY MEASURES TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. In connection with the same subject, I would like to know what additional measures have been taken by the Minister and what special instructions she has given to prevent a recurrence of these acts of terrorism.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: AIR-INDIA TRAGEDY-SUPPLEMENTARY MEASURES TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again, this is not the responsibility of the Department of Immigration. If the Hon. Member thinks that what we should be doing at this point is instituting police enforcement at the borders in order to meet a demand which has not been proven, if she thinks that there are certain individuals from different parts of the world who suddenly should be kept out of our immigration stream, then I would say she is badly mistaken.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He has said, and he certainly knows the Prime Minister has said, that over the weeks I have fairly presented the views of seniors across Canada. I met with a group of seniors in Sudbury yesterday, and 12 provincial seniors' organizations this morning. Will the Minister not accept that it is fair to say that seniors across the country do have a deep anxiety about what the Government intends to do with pensions beginning next year? They fully understand what the proposal is.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says he has fairly presented the views of seniors, and I do not quarrel with that. But what I would ask him is whether he has fairly presented the views of the Government as to the reasons why we have done this.
Hear, hear!
Let me ask him whether he said to the seniors that the country's debt has been growing at 25 per cent per annum. Is he also saying to them that we are spending-
No, we didn't tell them that.
The Hon. Leader of the NDP says no, he did not tell them that. Why didn't he tell them that?

Because we don't want the pensioners to
pay for it, that is why.

June 25, 1985
Oral Questions
Why didn't he spell it all out? Why didn't he put these facts in front of them? I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker-
Order, please. We started very well today; I would like to keep it that way. The Hon. Member for Beaches.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the Minister that I have done that, and the seniors have responded by saying: "We have paid our dues".
Hear, hear!
Will the Minister, in all fairness, stand in his place and assure the seniors that the Government will remove that anxiety before the end of this week?

Mr. Speaker, let me be clear. I am very sensitive to the views expressed by seniors' groups. I have met them on a number of occasions, as has the Hon. Member. As I said many times in this House, as has the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, we are monitoring the situation. We are going to-
Oh!

Members opposite say "oh". I suggest that they pay attention to what has been happening in this country. They should pay attention to what happened during the 15 years they were in power. They should pay attention to the fact that we were left with such an enormous mountain of debt that we cannot afford to do all the things-
Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. A CP wire report which came out shortly after one o'clock says that the Japanese police and Air-India's Tokyo representative said that a Mr. A. Singh and a Mr. L. Singh, which happen to be the same initials as those of the two fugitives from justice earlier referred to, were booked on CP Air flights 003 and then scheduled to transfer to Air-India flight 301 to Bangkok. They are the only two passengers who did not show up, and their luggage appears to have made the flight. Is the Minister in a position to confirm the validity of this report and to tell us whether there may have been some security problem at our end which would have permitted this to have taken place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the release is as recent as the Hon. Member says, that being one o'clock, because I myself saw on television last night those two names being mentioned. However, I think he will agree with me that, given the wide ranging investigation that is now ongoing in order to examine every possible facet and detail of the circumstances surrounding the loss of the Air-India flight, it would not be helpful to discuss publicly any details relating to that investigation. I saw the news account on national television last night with respect to the two individuals he named, and naturally, as stated, that is one avenue of the investigation.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport has referred to the possible necessity of additional security measures. There are substantial cuts envisaged in Transport Canada, some of them arising out of the so-called Nielsen task force. Could the Deputy Prime Minister assure us that the security measures will in no way be compromised by any cuts which have been or will be announced with respect to Transport Canada, and that the Minister will be given all the resources necessary to enable him to establish that full and appropriate security is in place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Hon. Member asked the question with respect to the task force on program review. I can assure him that I, as chairman of that task force, as well as my ministerial colleagues on the task force, have approached all matters relating to the review process, in so far as they are applicable to the Department of Transport, bearing in mind at all times the need to maintain the very high and excellent standards of security which have hitherto existed in the Department, and give him the unqualified assurance that the safety and security of Canada's travelling public, both here at home and abroad, will always be a top priority with this Government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Prior to September 4, 1984, Members used to rise quite regularly and complain about the deplorable delays in war veterans pensions. When the Minister was appointed to his portfolio he promised to deal with this matter. What has he done?
June 25, 1985

speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would first like to thank the Hon. Member for his very excellent and well thought out question. The answer to his question is a resounding "yes". I will be outlining what the Government has done before the meeting of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs which will meet in exactly one-half hour in Room 269 of the West Block. All Members are welcome.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: ENQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL MODIFY PENSION
ENQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL MODIFY PENSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. We cannot let the elderly in this country go on living in their present state of anxiety. We cannot let them wait until September to know what is going to happen. Could the Minister let senior citizens know whether he will be announcing this week or before the end of this session, whether his Government intends to change its plan to de-index Old Age Security pensions?

subtopic: ENQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL MODIFY PENSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are in fact doing a number of things for older people. As an example, the spouse's allowance provisions which were passed in the House quite recently extended the Guaranteed Income Supplement to 85,000 widows and widowers who are between the ages of 60 and 64. I also remind the Hon. Member that many elderly Canadians are being favourably affected by the change in the definition of "disabled". That will affect about 120,000 Canadians in total, so I think we are doing quite a bit.

subtopic: ENQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL MODIFY PENSION
speechtext: Order, please. I asked for short questions and must ask for short and relevant answers.

senior citizens in Sudbury did he point out to them that in 1974 the previous Government of Canada-

Please relax. Please relax. That problem has deteriorated so significantly over the last 10 years that we are forced to do some things that we are not

happy about doing. However, we must do this in order to avoid having to cut total programs in the 1990s.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. A recent Canadian Press report indicated that he said that government support for science and technology was too generous. This is not my interpretation of what the Deputy Prime Minister said in the House last week, but given the importance of this issue and the importance of science and technology to the economic growth of the country, is the Deputy Prime Minister prepared to clarify the position of the Government in support of research and development?

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence

STATIONING OF RCMP OFFICERS AT AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Acting Prime Minister. Last week the President of Air Canada said in the standing committee that the screening at airports is of the best standards under the guidance and meeting the requirements of the Ministry of Transport, and upon the advice of the RCMP.
In view of the decision made by the Minister of Transport to lay off RCMP security officers in eight airports which handle international chartered flights, will he not now, in view of recent tragedies, reverse these lay-offs-not only reverse them but increase the number of RCMP security staff at these airports?
