Mr. Speaker, I rise today to make this statement with great sadness. I am sure that all Members of the House-indeed all Canadians-share with me a sense of sympathy and sorrow at the tragic loss of life resulting from the Air-India disaster and the Tokyo Airport explosion. On behalf of my colleagues and, I am sure, the entire House I would like to extend our condolences to the families of all involved.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) have previously enunciated the Government's sympathy and regret. However, I would like to repeat our expressions of sorrow and concern at this time.
The explosion at Tokyo's Narita Airport of a baggage cart containing luggage from CP Air, Flight 003 and the tragic crash of Air-India Flight 182 off the Irish coast are both tragic events of extreme concern to our civil aviation system, the Government as a whole and indeed the international aviation community.
Over the last 60 hours, since these tragedies occurred, the Government has moved quickly to ensure the security of Canadian air travellers, to reconstruct and investigate the events leading up to the incidents, and to respond in every way possible to the situation. I would like to take this opportunity to provide the House with as clear a picture as possible of some of the facts as we understand them at the present time and outline some of the actions that have been taken.
I will say that the Government has been co-operating with and has received complete co-operation from all other nations and international organizations involved. Within the Government of Canada, a number of Departments have been actively involved and have been proceeding in a co-operative and coordinated fashion.
I want to reiterate once again to the House, to Canadians and indeed to the international community that Canada maintains high standards of airport and flight security through laws requiring security action by carriers operating aircraft in Canada and through the resources of the federal Government. Under the provisions of the Foreign Aircraft Security Measures Regulations and pursuant to the Aeronautics Act, Air-India and all other carriers are required to develop, implement and table with the Minister of Transport a full security program for their flights. These measures must include the inspection of all hand carried luggage, the control of boarding passes, the establishment of sterile areas, and the maintenance of security on the aircraft. Transport Canada assist in meeting these standards through provision of proper security facilities and the training of security personnel. But ultimate responsibility for flight security rests with the carriers.
Within this context, Canada has performed admirably in the area of passenger air safety. That contention is borne out by the statements of many experts in the field.
I quote Mr. Rodney Wallace, Director of Security, International Air Transport Association. He said:
Normally, standards in Canada are very high indeed and they're particularly high with regard to Air-India so this requires a very deep study indeed.
Another quote by Mr. Wallace is as follows:
Canada has had high standards for a long period of time and of course there has been no real perceived threat against Canada and Canadian airlines or even airlines operating out of Canada. In the case of Air-India, they did increase their security a short while ago but that was because of the political situation within India.
The Director of Security for the United States Airline Pilots Association said yesterday:
Canadian airport security is of the highest quality of any system.
I want to repeat that. He said:
Canadian airport security is of the highest quality of any system. The new security measures which were implemented on Sunday are the correct response to the perceived threat but any system is vulnerable to terrorist attack, especially the sophisticated paramilitary groups of today.
Norman Foster, President of the Canadian Airline Pilots Association, said in a television interview that he feels Canadian security standards were of a very high order but that, in view of recent events, they should be reassessed. That is precisely what we are doing. I would like to outline also the
June 25, 1985

over-all international requirements governing the safety of air travellers. We are governed by international law, Annex 17 to the Convention of International Civil Aviation which requires that contracting states take the necessary measures to prevent weapons or any other dangerous devices, the carriage or bearing of which is not authorized, from being introduced by any means whatsoever on board an aircraft engaged in the carriage of passengers. The Annex further recommends that Contracting States establish the necessary procedures to prevent the unauthorized introduction of explosives or incendiary devices in baggage or cargo intended to be carried on board aircraft.
As a Contracting State, Canada is in full compliance with both the international standard and the recommended practice.
With respect to Canadian law, Mr. Speaker, the Foreign Aircraft Security Measures Regulations made pursuant to the Aeronautics Act require every owner or operator who lands foreign aircraft in Canada to establish, to maintain and to carry out security measures at aerodromes consisting of one, a system of surveillance of persons, personal belongings, baggage, goods and cargo; two, a system of searching persons and personal belongings, baggage, goods and cargo; three a system of identification that prevents baggage, goods and cargo from being placed on board the aircraft if it is not authorized to be placed on board by the owner or operator, and, fourth, a system of identification of surveillance and search personnel and the personnel of the owner or operator.
Foreign air carriers must provide a description of their security. With respect to Air-India security measures, Air-India has provided the Minister with a copy of the security program of Air-India Canadian region describing the security measures which Air-India has established and its maintenance and the carrying out of those security measures.
The Air-India station manager is directly responsible for the implementation of these security measures.
First, these measures relate to the establishment of sterile areas, the inspection of hand carried baggage, the controlling of boarding passes, the maintaining of security of aircraft, the ensuring of the security of baggage, and the ensuring of the security of cargo. The Air-India security program requires that all carry-on baggage to be checked physically by handheld devices or by X-ray equipment, and baggage for those passengers who fail to board the flight, is to be off-loaded.
At Mirabel, Air-India's cargo is handled by Mega International in accordance with Air-India security instructions.
Just to outline briefly the sequence of events, Mr. Speaker, much of the information has been provided to Canadians by radio, television and the press, but I believe I should summarize the sequence of events as we know them. I must repeat that. I think that in the course of this exercise we always submit ourselves to some danger in trying to be as forthcoming as possible, but we find that, on re-assessment or re-examination of some of the facts presented to us, sometimes these
Statements by Ministers
change and vary from time to time. Nonetheless, fraught with that danger I think it is important for us to try to reconstruct the events as accurately as possible.
Air-India's Flight 182 planned departure from Pearson International Airport, was scheduled for 1845 hours, with a connecting flight from Vancouver to Toronto carrying an unknown number of passengers. The actual departure took place at 2015 Eastern Daylight Time, one hour and 30 minutes late. It arrived at Mirabel at 2100 hours. The flight planned departure at Mirabel was set for 2203 hours. The final departure was at 2218 hours, some 15 minutes late. It picked up 104 passengers at Mirabel. The passenger manifest showed 307 passengers, with 22 crew members. The crash time, as we have been informed, was 3.13 Eastern Daylight Time.
There has been some controversy regarding the events at Toronto and Mirabel. The events established that Canada provided to Air-India all the assistance it requested for its flights during this particular period.
There was extra assistance provided at Pearson International Airport by RCMP constables who were assigned to the ticket counter, the gate and the ramp. The normal pre-boarding passenger screening occurred at the screening point. There was also a secondary search of all carry-on bags and items conducted by Burns Security personnel as monitored by the RCMP.
In the baggage area, the X-ray machine worked for a period of time and then developed a malfunction. It is estimated that 75 per cent of the baggage was X-rayed and 25 per cent was subject to a mechanical explosive sniffer.
We are informed that no bags were opened and searched. The baggage transferred to Air-India from Vancouver arrived at Toronto on a domestic flight and was delivered to the international area. Once there, it went to the checked baggage area which was then screened by security.
Air Canada's security has confirmed that these procedures were followed for Flight 182.
With respect to Mirabel, RCMP officers are dedicated to Air-India flights. There is an officer in a patrol car, one officer at the ticket counter, one at the screening check-in point, one on the arrival/departure level, and one on the mezzanine level who also checks the roof of the terminal.
Normally there would be an RCMP dog master in the baggage area but this dog was away on a training course and a Quebec Provincial Police dog served as a replacement.
RCMP officers were on the ramp, at the ticket counter, at the screening check-in point, on the arrival/departure level and on the mezzanine level.
At Mirabel, all boarded baggage was subject to X-ray scrutiny. Three suspect bags were withheld. Air-India Flight 182 departed without this luggage. It was subsequently determined that no explosives or dangerous material was contained in those bags.
With respect to CP Air Flight 003, the departure from Vancouver International Aiport was 2037 hours Zulu. The

June 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
planned arrival at Narita, Japan, was 5.55 Zulu. The actual landing at Narita, Japan was 5.40 Zulu, 15 minutes early. The ramp time was 5.47 Zulu. The explosion at Narita, Japan occurred at approximately 6.20 hours Zulu, 45 minutes after landing.
The passenger manifest showed 370 passengers and a 16-member crew.
CP Flight 001 from Pearson International Airport to Vancouver landed at Narita International at approximately 700 hours Zulu.
Flight 003 originated in Vancouver. However, the aircraft had just returned from Narita International, Japan. The aircraft did a turnaround. Normal passenger screening was carried out. Luggage was not X-rayed or searched. This is normal and meets Transport Canada's civil aviation requirements where no threat to a specific flight has been signalled.
As announced on Sunday, Mr. Speaker, we took immediate action to increase security following these tragic events. Increased security measures have already been implemented on all international flights leaving Canada for Europe, Asia and Africa as a result of the Air-India and CP Air disasters.
International authorities have been asked by the Ministry of Transport to introduce similar measures for all flights bound for Canada. In an attempt to ensure that no similar mishaps take place, all baggage on international flights is being security inspected and all international cargo, with the exception of perishable goods from known producers, will be held for at least 24 hours. Twenty X-ray security systems and new explosive sniffers are being purchased for Canadian airports to assist with the new security standards. The first of the new X-ray machines will be operational by Thursday, June 27.
_
The Government has also moved quickly to ensure full international co-operation in investigations of the Air-India disaster as well as the explosion at Narita Airport.
Representatives of the Department of Transport have been dispatched to London to assist in the investigation of the Air-India crash, and a Transport Canada security officer has been sent to Tokyo to assist in that investigation. Transport Canada is also initiating a full investigation of the quality of airport security measures in place for both flights. Investigations into Flight 182 are ongoing and the Government is taking long and short-term measures to prevent any similar occurrences. The people of Canada will be kept informed of further findings and actions respecting this very important area of government concern.
Before concluding my remarks, I should like to say to all Hon. Members of the House that this is a very serious issue. I appreciate the tone with which Hon. Members across the way have approached it. I do not think this should be a partisan issue. It is an issue which is very grave and something which requires the good will and co-operation of all Hon. Members.
There is a rumour to the effect-and I am not sure whether it has been confirmed-that Air-India will be suspending
service to Canada. I understand-and I am not sure whether it has been confirmed-it has been suggested that there will be a temporary suspension of service to Canada and other points because of the lack of equipment. However, I want to reiterate that, to the best of our knowledge, this is merely a temporary suspension and as soon as adequate equipment is made available, I believe the service will be restored.
I hope this will at least partially clarify some of the outstanding and important issues relating to this great tragedy. As I indicated, I will be keeping Hon. Members and the House informed of any further developments as they occur.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I wish to offer my sincere condolences to the families who were bereaved as a result of two tragic episodes involving, respectively, the Air Indian flight to London and the CP Air flight to Tokyo. I want to thank the Minister for the exhaustive statement he made in the House just now.
However, although this is a very serious matter in which political partisanship has no place whatsoever, the fact remains that the Canadian public must be reassured, and that consequently, we on this side of the House have a duty to ask a number of questions, not only concerning the events themselves but also about the procedures in various Canadian airports and the new methods announced by the Minister, in order to ensure that these measures will indeed be effective and provide maximum security for Canadian travellers.
The Minister stated that he had received the co-operation of the authorities of the countries concerned. I am very happy with this decision, but I wonder to what extent the Japanese authorities, especially, are allowing representatives of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board to take part in any inquiries or investigations being conducted at this time concerning the CP Air incident. I am told that representatives of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board have already arrived in Ireland. Are they going to be taking an active part in the investigation to be carried out by the Irish authorities, or will they only be called as witnesses in connection with the investigation? I believe it is essential, in order to safeguard Canadian interests, since so many Canadian families have been directly affected by this incident, that Canada's representatives take an active part in the investigation to be conducted in Ireland.
As for the investigation in Japan, I would like to have some more specific information from the Minister to find out whether or not Canadian Government representatives will be taking part in the investigation to be held in Tokyo.
The Minister referred to our high standards here in Canada. He referred to some very eloquent testimony to that effect by an authority in the aviation field. I agree that Canadian standards are very high. I recognize the Minister's good faith and I realize he is sincere in wanting to find the best way of
June 25, 1985

preventing a recurrence of such incidents. In fact, I would like to congratulate him on acting so quickly as soon as he was informed of these events.
However, Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious matter. It is far too serious for the Government to be on the defensive. From what the Minister said and from my reading of the sequence of events, it seemed to me that the Minister was inclined to defend existing procedures, Department of Transport employees, airline representatives and security officers. I think that is a big mistake, because it is clear there are contradictions.

To cite a few contradictions, I refer to articles which were published in the newspapers indicating where in fact contradictory statements were made by the Minister and by some of his officials about the two incidents involving the Air-India flight and the CP Air flight. On one hand, the Minister said that the baggage for both flights had been X-rayed. On the other hand, a Transport Canada spokesman said that only the Air-India baggage had been examined under X-ray. This is the first contradiction.
The second contradiction concerns the Minister who supposedly said that if Transport Canada had been informed that three suspicious bags were removed at Mirabel, the flight would have been held until all baggage had been searched. On the other hand, a Transport Canada spokesman said that bags had been removed from flights three or four times a month at Mirabel although planes may take off without further inspection. This statement by the Department of Transport official is frightening, in a sense, it deeply contradicts what the Minister told the press yesterday.
I do not want the Minister to look like a fool. I do not think he is a fool; I think he is a very serious, dedicated Minister. However, the contradiction between what he said and what has been said by his officials requires further independent investigation. I am afraid that if the investigation is exclusively an internal one by departmental officials, the Minister may not be apprised of what really took place.
There is another contradiction that needs to be looked at between the statement made by authorities on behalf of the Government of India and statements that have been repeated here today in the House that contradict what we have been told by officials of the Government of India. We have been told that, indeed, on several occasions prior to the incident, the Indian authorities have apprised our Government of fears, threats, and dangers and have sought the co-operation of the Canadian Government in order to protect Air-India flights and to protect Indian officials in Canada. The Minister today told us that Air-India Flight 182 was not on the alert system. Why was it not on the alert system after all those representations that had been made in recent weeks by the Indian authorities? Not only is it surprising that it was not on the alert system, but after it was brought to the attention of the Canadian authorities that three pieces of luggage were retained because they did
Statements by Ministers
not pass the appropriate tests, why was no action taken then in Mirabel to call back the flight or to make sure that before the flight left all the other luggage was properly inspected? [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I say that a complete and independent inquiry must be made, not so we can pin down the guilty person or persons but so that we can make a thorough review of security procedures being used, not just by Canadian authorities but also by the airlines whose aircraft land at Canadian airports. The point is not that individuals did or did not do a good job but that a security system or set of procedures did not work properly and should be reviewed.
The Minister must understand that it is entirely possible that luggage checked in at a small airport might be carried from one plane to another by airport employees, without going through security. For instance, a passenger leaving Windsor Airport could check in his luggage with a small airline which does not have the security procedures existing in large international air terminals. On leaving Windsor, the luggage could go to Toronto, be carried by a handler who does not know it may contain a bomb, be carried from a plane coming from Windsor, Ontario to a CP Air aircraft going from Toronto to Vancouver and ultimately to Tokyo.
There is a strong possibility that individuals who want to blow up a plane would use a small airport where security is not as great and check their luggage through to a final destination, thereby completely short-circuiting the security procedures that exist in the large air terminals. And it is possible that a person who checks in his luggage at Windsor would travel on the flight from Windsor to Toronto but not on the subsequent flight from Toronto to Vancouver and Tokyo, while the luggage containing an explosive device would remain on board the flight for which it was checked in, and so the whole security system has been completely short-circuited.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that the Minister review all these procedures in order to ensure that on all international flights, luggage checked for a specific flight can be matched with the passengers travelling on that flight, that security checks be made before an international flight leaves Canada, and that all baggage on board the aircraft can be identified as belonging to the passengers on that particular flight.
That is why I maintain that surveillance at small airports is just as important as at large airports. I agree with the Canadian Air Line Pilots' Association which is asking the Government to reconsider its decision to no longer ask the RCMP to provide for security at Canadian airports.
In reply to a question I asked previously, the Minister said that the decision had been made by the previous Government. In fact, a number of Department of Transport officials had suggested doing this to save money, but I may remind the Minister that the previous administration never accepted this recommendation by Department of Transport officials, and that in fact, the previous Government had been anxious to

June 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
keep RCMP officers on duty at Canadian airports in order to provide the best possible security.
Mr. Speaker, I would therefore ask the Minister to drop this plan and to keep the RCMP at all Canadian airports for the purpose of providing security, not only at our international airports but also at our smaller airports, because, as I explained earlier, trouble may originate from a small airport and not be identified in time.
Finally, I would like to say that the statements made by the Minister will certainly help reassure the public. I hope that the 20 new pieces of equipment that have been purchased will be in place as soon as possible. The Minister informed the House that only one piece of equipment would be a available by next Thursday, but I suppose we can expect the 19 others to be in service very shortly. In any case, until this equipment is in use, I think we will have to be very careful and provide for both visual and physical checks so that passengers on Canadian aircraft will have the assurance that every precaution has been taken to provide maximum protection.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make four recommendations.
First, I would recommend that, quite apart from the investigation made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and others conducted by Canadian authorities on security information, there is still a whole series of measures and security procedures which ought to be implemented in Canadian airports and I think that the Canadian Aviation Safety Board should be asked to investigate security procedures in our airports as soon as possible.
Second, I would want the Minister to do more than check into this and to confirm that henceforth the RCMP will be used at all Canadian airports.
Third, I would want mandatory security measures imposed by the Department of Transport to all airline companies.
And finally, fourth, I would want the Government to act as humanely and as quickly as possible to help striken families, particularly those unsure whether the bodies recovered from the see off the coast of Ireland are indeed those of their own relatives. We have learned that it is difficult to travel to Ireland to make such identifications. In my judgment, the Canadian Government musts do everything in its power to help those families, especially those that are anxious to go to Ireland to identify the victims of this terrible tragedy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my sincere feelings to those expressed by my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), and the spokesman for the Official Opposition, as well as expressions of our sympathy and sincere condolences to the families, relatives and friends of those who were lost in the tragedy
which occurred last Sunday, as well as to the families and friends, although smaller in number, of those lost, in the tragedy at the Tokyo airport. As well-and I hope members of the Press Gallery are listening-I would like to commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), for his statement about the very unfair assumptions and crass speculations made by some, including members of the media, about the possible involvement of one or more members of East Indian or other communities. That, I suggest, is reprehensible. For the sake of sensationalism, headlines, news and 30-second spots on television, those kinds of assumptions and speculations have been overdone, to put it mildly, over the last 50 or 60 hours.
Neither I nor anyone else in the house relishes having to rise to respond to an occasion such as this. However, I would like to point out that when I and other Members of the House raised issues concerning transportation safety and security under the previous administration and the current one, no sensational events were occurring and it was difficult to get the attention of members of the previous Government as well as of this one. It was difficult to get the attention of the media. Canada can no longer-if it ever could before-think that it can stand alone from and unaffected by the rest of the world and the effects of international terrorism. Regardless of the findings of the investigation of the Air-India flight and the CP Air flight, this occasion presents us with another opportunity to examine safety and security arrangements at Canadian airports.
As I said earlier today, I commend the Minister for the fast action he took to put in place substantially greater security and safety measures since last Sunday. I know that he has spent long hours working all weekend. However, and I say this without malice because it is not peculiar to this administration, we must realize that this is another instance of the barn door syndrome. Policy decisions are made and put in place, but complacency will return a few weeks from now. There will cease to be an interest in drawing the line between where saving dollars ends and appropriate measures, no matter what the cost, begin and stay in place regarding matters of safety and security.
I would remind the House that when we debated in the House, in the standing committee and before the Canadian Transport Commission the issue of deregulation, all sides agreed that there can be no compromise on safety at our airports in Canada, and by extension, safety also means security. That was agreed to unanimously even though the previous Government and the present one insisted on proceeding with the deregulation of fares, exit and entry into routes and city pairs. Even though there was unanimous agreement not to compromise on safety in the past four years there has been a move afoot to reduce the number of RCMP officers on duty at Canadian airports and to reduce their presence, both visible and invisible. I was appalled at the unmitigated gall of a member of the Official Opposition, the transportation critic, who asked about the removal of RCMP officers from airports in Canada. I would suggest that the transportation critic of the
June 25, 1985

Liberal Party talk to his seatmate, because he removed RCMP officers from 12 airports in this country-
That's not true.
You should check your facts.
It is true, and there will be eight more from which RCMP officers will be removed this summer.
This summer, that's true.

And those eight more airports include Ottawa and Victoria, an international airport. In fact, international charter flights are leaving from the so-called domestic airports on an almost weekly basis during the high tourist season.
There would have been a reliance on private security agents within a few months if it were not for the Minister's announcement today that that move will be put on hold. I suppose it will be put on hold until all this dies down and there are no more crashes or tragedies of this nature. Then the Government will proceed as usual on the grounds that it will save a few dollars.
The point is that the RCMP as well as the trained personnel of the Ministry of Transport must be in place at all times at all airports owned and operated by the Ministry of Transport. There should be no damned question about that.
Without questioning their good will, I have grave doubts about private security agents that are in place who play the only on-site role in security at our airports. They have neither the training nor the authority to deal with serious problems that may arise, whether they be problems with passengers, alerts, anonymous phone calls, hoaxes or threats. They do not have the capacity and the training to deal with a problem, even if it is only a drunken passenger who threatens physical violence. A private security agent who has no training, whether male or female, young or old, will not be able to handle that. The response time of the RCMP and the police in my city and others is 10, 15, 20 or even 30 minutes. That is not good enough. There must be on site at all times properly trained, equipped and authorized people to deal with situations when and if they arise, even though they may go for months without anything arising and it may appear to be a waste of money.
If we are going to get rid of the barn door syndrome, then that kind of an expenditure of money at the cost of taxpayers, airlines and the travelling public will have to be put in place, and I am convinced that the public will accept that and will not agree that it is an area on which the Government can cut back. As the Minister well knows, I have raised this issue on a number of occasions. I am glad to hear that he has put on hold the removal of RCMP officers.
The main problem with airport security and safety and with other issues such as the transportation of dangerous goods is that action occurs after the tragedy has occurred. Then there is a wild scramble to cover backsides, keep skirts clear and put in place all of the things that should have been in place before. There is nothing new about that. I do not condemn this
Statements by Ministers
Government only. It has occurred time and time again over the last number of years. Every time there has been a tragedy, this House and various authorities get together to try to do something about it, but within a matter of weeks or months we are back into the same rut.
There is going to be a review of procedures in handling baggage and other airline cargo. We know that in the past there has been little or no security checks on baggage which goes into the hold, in spite of some self-serving statements by some. This has been left entirely to the discretion of airlines. And it has been the case not only under this administration but also under previous Ministers of Transport. How many dozen airlines operate in and out of Canada? They all have different policies and take security measures if and when it suits them. If they receive a threat, they will notify the Ministry of Transport and, Mr. Speaker, there can be no question but that the Ministry of Transport is responsible. It has to be in charge. There can be no other way of operating. I am not suggesting, Sir, that it can be 100 per cent sure. If someone wants to beat the system badly enough, he or she will sooner or later figure out a way. But with the maximum of equipment and qualified personnel in place, it is a lot harder for them to do it. Comparisons are odious, but I do not believe that the system we have in place is any better than others in the world. There are others which do a better job and there are others which do a worse one. But any kind of complacency is out of place at this point in time.
Members of the Committee on Transport met this morning. We discussed the statement made yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with respect to a special investigation. A special investigation with respect to these incidents is fine and must take place-
It's broader than that.

-by the RCMP and the Ministry of Transport. But I think that an investigation into present and future arrangements and regulations on safety and security has to be provided by some kind of an independent body. I am not suggesting a two-year or three-year Dubin type of inquiry. We do not have that much time. I would like to suggest to the Minister of Transport that he consider providing an order of reference by this Friday to the Standing Committee on Transport and give it carte blanche in terms of staff, holding hearings, travel and reporting back with its recommendations. If there is any time at which we could support the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons, this is one instance. Failing that, however, there should be an independent inquiry with the broadest terms of reference which would make interim reports as well as a final one. And it does not have to take two or three years.
There is the whole matter of the quality, qualifications and numbers of the personnel of the Ministry of Transport and private security firms at our airports. There is the question of the sophistication, quality and numbers of the equipment.

June 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
There needs to be in place a standard for the checking, not only of checked in luggage, parcels, air cargo and air express packages, but of everything and anything that is placed on board an aircraft. 1 will not go into that issue any further, Mr. Speaker, so as to avoid creating more worry and fear in the minds of the public, but the Minister of Transport knows the areas about which I am referring.
The whole matter of inter-line baggage must be looked into. There is nothing to prevent some nut from checking something in at a domestic airport anywhere in Canada through to a destination in Europe, Africa or Asia, which would get transferred from one connecting flight to another on the same airline, or from one airline to another airline, and still not be inspected. A bomb can originate in Vegreville on a little private charter plane flying to Regina, then be put on a domestic flight to Toronto, to end up on an international flight going somewhere else.
I would like to suggest to the Minister that it is not enough to act just on alerts. I suspect that the alert regarding Air-India had more to do with the imminent arrival within two or three weeks of the President of India to the United States. I hope that was not the only reason for the Air-India alert but I suspect it was a good one. I do not blame the head of state of any country for doing so.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I hope the House and the Government will now seize the opportunity to keep in place, enlarge and replace everything with respect to cut-backs under the previous and the present administrations. They should be put back in place. I believe what the Minister has had to do over this past few days is going to require Supplementary Estimates because he just lost about $300 million out of his Department. But you do not place safety and security in jeopardy because of money. There cannot be any question about that. I hope I will never have to hear again, as long as I am in this House, that in the interests of saving a few dollars we should put into the slightest question the safety and security of our airlines and our travelling public.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to restore us back to the standards established by the Minister. I will not be partisan about his remarks and point fingers and lay blame such as, I am afraid, the last speaker attempted to do, which I believe is not called for in the circumstances. I will try to come to the way in which the Government is handling the matter.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, during the course of Question Period I posed a question to the Minister as to why, in establishing the investigation, inquiry and evaluation of our security measures, the Canadian Aviation Sefety Board was not brought in as the primary agency. I simply want to refer the Minister to the findings of the Dubin Commission in 1981. The Minister at that time was very active in this House in supporting those recommendations. The report suggested that the Bill which was introduced create a board separate from Transport Canada so that the regulatory investigative functions may be seen to operate at arm's length. It stated that removal of this potential conflict of interest should improve the
effectiveness of both the regulation and the accident investigation.
I know that things were hectic, harrowing and difficult, but we have established a major improvement in this country's safety record with the safety board. It is a quasi-judicial body, independent, with the power to call witnesses and restore confidence that any finding or judgment would not be subject to conflict of interest. I am not calling into question the integrity of officials, but I am saying that the officials responsible for managing this system should not be responsible for evaluating the effectiveness of that management. I do not think anyone in the auditing business or anywhere else would suggest that one should audit one's own performance. We are all subject to some form of critique that is more independent than that.
I know the Minister is still involved in making decisions, and I think it is wrong to dwell on history, but terrorism is becoming widespread. Therefore, would it not be more appropriate to ensure confidence in the evaluation by charging an independent body with the responsibility of making judgments and assessments of the situation? Again, I make no prior judgment, but I think there is a question of confidence over whether, both internationally and domestically, any new measures would be in full accordance with the requirement of safety and security. Therefore, I ask the Minister, would it not be more appropriate for the safety board to be given that responsibility?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's comments. I thought that my answer to the Hon. Member's question during Question Period left the impression, which I tried to give, that he had a very valid suggestion to make. To the extent that we can use the Canadian Aviation Safety Board in this process, it makes eminent good sense. As was alluded to, we are dealing with world-wide terrorism and I think it would be important to engage the most senior security and intelligence resources we have at our disposal, here and around the world, to evaluate and to ensure that any improvements in airport and airline security will take into consideration any information which can be garnered from a security and intelligence standpoint.
I will certainly take the Hon. Member's suggestion seriously-I have and I will-and to the extent we can integrate the work of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, which I agree is an independent arm, I think it would make eminent good sense and I thank him for his suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, I leave the matter in the capable hands of the Hon. Minister and we will see what arises.
The Minister indicated during Question Period that he intends to be in attendance at the International Civil Aviation Organization meetings on Thursday. IATA is also having meetings on Friday and we will have delegates there. Can he indicate whether Canada intends to put any proposals in front
June 25, 1985

of those bodies concerning the way in which various members of the international aviation community can co-ordinate their efforts? I know there have been a number of discussions in the past. I was party to some of them in my previous incarnation. But we all recognize that security has to be upgraded and improved. Time is short, but I think sufficient work has been done in the past, both in External Affairs and in Transport, concerning amendments to the international aviation code regarding registration, licencing and other procedures. Can the Minister indicate whether we will be making specific proposals? The reason I ask, and I do so out of some concern, is that we all know our country has had an extraordinarily high reputation in this area. It now may be called into question, and I think there have been a lot of comments, and I believe we should take some leadership to show that our system is open and we welcome the involvement of ICAO and IATA in helping us determine improvements in our own procedures. It also should be co-ordinated with other countries. Would the Minister care to respond to that?

Mr. Speaker, that would certainly be my intention. I think the initiatives we have taken are fairly well advanced. I know that in discussions with American authorities, we have come to the conclusion that the detection devices which have been developed are really not as adequate and proficient as they could be. I think there is a real challenge in trying to accelerate the technology required if it should be necessary to inspect all luggage carried on board an aircraft. I think we all recognize that by the actions we are now taking we are creating long line-ups and delays and perhaps some frustration. While we are bringing on equipment which will facilitate and speed up the process, we have quite a distance to go in developing the technology to put in place that kind of screening device on a massive basis. That will clearly be an issue which will have to be dealt with at the international level. However, yes, I will be making some recommendations which we believe are necessary.
I think all Hon. Members would agree that we are probably entering a new era of reality. Canadians once thought we were immune to the horrors of terrorism and sabotage, but now that it appears to have struck very close to home, it is a rude awakening for us all and we are trying to address the reality of the situation. We will do it in as positive and as straightforward a manner as we possibly can.

Mr. Speaker, I really have only one question and it flows from the statements made in the press regarding the methods currently used to check luggage and the fact that it appears as if it has been very much up to individual airlines to determine the appropriateness of the measures they themselves put in place, and the obvious effect of that kind of policy. The safety of all passengers, employees, indeed all persons in the facilities or in the vicinity of Canadian airports surely must be our primary concern. I was going to ask the Minister two things, bearing that in mind.
Quite clearly, under the present system one airline could choose to have adequate review and check-up procedures,
Statements by Ministers
while the airline immediately next to it might not. However, all of the baggage is handled in one general facility and it all goes through one main terminal. Aircraft are parked one beside the other. Notwithstanding what is accepted internationally at the moment, could we in Canada not lead the way and say that every single piece of baggage transported by aircraft must receive a proper check not only through X-ray procedures but also from the point of view of determining whether or not there may be explosives on board a plane.
Let me just preface my second question with a concern. The more things you think up, the more you alert people to a potential, and that worries me. For the first time in my life I can appreciate that it may be necessary to conduct an inquiry of this type in private; that it cannot be handled openly for fear that by the very nature of the questions you raise, new ways of creating an entree to the system are exposed for those who would act as terrorists. But it is clear that I, for example, could get on a flight in Hamilton with checked baggage and have it directed through a variety of different ways all the way to any place in the world. If it was not properly checked at the first place, chances are it would not be checked at any of the subsequent places either. Therefore, it becomes apparent to me, as a layman, that if protective measures are going to be put in place they will have to be put in every airport. There is no such thing as designated airports. They will have to be everywhere in order to provide the required protection.
I would like to suggest with some degree of trepidation that although airports are the primary targets of terrorists using transportation for their terror, they are not the only places we should be looking. There is quite clearly the option of making threats on and creating terror through any method of transportation. It might be useful, therefore, if the Minister would consider my colleague's good suggestion of some kind of parliamentary review. Perhaps we could discuss what would be an appropriate forum for this. However, there should be some parliamentary review of how transportation is conducted from the safety standpoint and how we in Canada can take whatever steps we can. I recognize that no matter what we do it will not be likely to work anyway, but we can try to provide the safest possible means for as many people as we can subject to the fertile imaginations of the terrorists of the world who always seem to be one step ahead of us.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to respond to the three questions which the Hon. Member has raised. I think it is fairly common knowledge that it is not customary for checked baggage on domestic and transborder flights to be screened through an X-ray or physically checked. Those are the established international standards.
It may not be enough.

That is a matter that we will have to consider.
With regard to the broader question of the adequacy of the standards, there are minimum standards established by inter-

June 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
national convention. The level of security of each individual airline is based upon its assessed level of threat. Because of the political developments in India it was determined by Air-India that there was an extraordinary level of threat. As a result, they have been in a high state of alert, which means that their standards are considerably higher than those required. It is based upon their assessed level of threat. For example, their security manual requires searches of baggage by X-ray, hand search, or hand-held sniffers. Air-India was following these procedures at both Pearson International and Mirabel.
When the airline determines that there is a specific threat against any given flight, which I reiterate was not the case with regard to Flight 182, there are Transport Canada procedures which call for full hand baggage inspections. That triggers a completely new process. Again, the information that I have, which has been confirmed by the RCMP, is that there was no request received for special security because of the specific threat to Flight 182. There was a request for additional RCMP personnel, but this flight was not designated as a special security threat. As a result, the extraordinary procedures, which would have been triggered had that determination been made, were not implemented at that time. I believe that probably answers most of the questions that were raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I take this opportunity to remind Members that the period allotted at this time is strictly for questions rather than for comments. The Member for Humb-er-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin).

Mr. Speaker, I have a few questions for the minister. I would like to congratulate him on the clarity of the responses we are receiving to our questions and on the quick manner in which he has acted on behalf of the Government and of the people of Canada. However, there are still a number of questions I would like to raise. The Minister has pointed out again that there was nothing to indicate to the RCMP, Transport Canada, or the Government of Canada that this particular flight required any extraordinary security measures. Are we to assume from that that the only reason a number of pieces of luggage were removed from the flight at Mirabel is that they happened to trip an electronic sensor which indicated that there were metal objects in the suitcases?
I will ask the Minister to respond to that and then I would like to continue with another question or two.

Mr. Speaker, Air-India had been in an abnormal state of alert for some time when all checked-in luggage was examined by X-ray or hand sniffer. It was in the process of that examination that the three bags were detected.

Mr. Speaker, with reference to this situation, the superintendent of airport security at Mirabel Airport said that, in his judgment, Air-India had broken a basic rule. That basic rule is that when it becomes necessary, because of electronic sensoring devices, to pull some luggage off an aircraft, Transport Canada is informed and the entire aircraft is checked by lining up baggage and people and finding out whether all the
baggage on board matches people on the aircraft. I am still a little confused.
I want to ask the Minister about the process. The Minister was quoted in the Ottawa Citizen of yesterday as saying that if Transport Canada had been informed about suspicious baggage on a flight, the flight would have been held until all the baggage had been searched. The same article in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen quotes a Transport Canada spokesman as saying that bags are removed from flights three or four times a month at Mirabel although planes may take off and continue flights without further inspection. I am sure that the Minister will appreciate that there is somewhat of a contradiction there.
I ask whether there was any recognition of any problem on the flight yesterday because Transport Canada, the RCMP, and the airline itself all had the authority to have that plane fully searched. If at any point, even after the plane had left the runway in Montreal, there was any reason to believe that there was anything amiss on that flight, there was nothing to prevent anybody from contacting that airplane and asking the pilot to return. This would have enabled a thorough investigation to be carried out which the Minister suggests would be done when Transport Canada is tipped off that there may be a problem. Can the Minister explain the contradiction between his comment and those of his officials? What is the procedure that is to be used? Why was that procedure not considered in the case of this flight, even in retrospect?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member raising that matter because I can also understand the interpretation of a contradiction. I suppose that I am partially responsible for that in that my statement was made in the context of there being a specific threat against Flight 182. If that had occurred, then the extraordinary Transport Canada procedures would have been triggered. I regret that I may have not made myself abundantly clear on that particular point. My comments were made within that context.
What is the second part of the Hon. Member's question?

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to be absolutely clear because the RCMP were called in to investigate the luggage on this aircraft and in fact I am told that they arrived minutes after the plane took off. They checked three bags in question, had a negative reaction from their sniff dogs and the aircraft continued on its way.
I just want to be clear that what the Minister is now telling us is that until that aircraft disappeared from the radar screen there was never any indication or warning whatsoever that anything may have been amiss on that airplane. I am saying that if a plane takes off and authorities in Canada, be it the RCMP or Transport Canada, discover there may be a problem, surely there is nothing stopping us from contacting the pilot as long as he is in Canadian air space and asking him to return to the airport in order to conduct the kind of thorough investigation that the Minister said would be conducted when a warning had been evident. Am I correct?
June 25, 1985

As I indicated earlier, this particular flight was not designated as a flight with a specific threat. Therefore, that procedure was not triggered.
With respect to the larger part of the question, I hope the Hon. Member and others will understand that when we get into that kind of discussion and debate we are engaged in an investigation on the floor of the House of Commons. As I said in my comments earlier, I want to be as forthcoming as I possibly can, but I believe the Hon. Member will appreciate that in our desire to be as forthcoming as possible there are facts that are updated. Sometimes there are contradictions. The Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) alluded to that earlier in his remarks when he indicated that I had been quoted as saying that the baggage for both flights had been X-rayed. That is a misquote, absolutely. It may have been misinterpreted.
The story was written by Richard Cleroux who is a very distinguished reporter. However, I can say here and now that if that impression was left, it was wrong. From the beginning I took the position, and expressed the point of view on many occasions, that the baggage with respect to Air-India was inspected either by X-ray or by a hand-held sniffing device.
With respect to the baggage on CP, it was not customary for that luggage to be examined.
The other misinformation in that same article is the fact that I am quoted as saying:
Mr. Mazankowski said that he believes dogs were also used at Toronto's Pearson International Airport on the Air-India baggage.
That is wrong. I never did say that. I did say that there were dogs available at Mirabel. I wanted the opportunity to clarify that because in this particular kind of atmosphere these kinds of contradictions should be cleared up as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, we seem to be making assumptions that whatever device was smuggled on to the plane got on through the baggage. However, many Members are often in airports, and I often wonder what security measures exist for access to the aircraft.
When the Minister's investigation takes place, would he investigate the whole question of the security of the plane while it is waiting to receive both baggage and passengers? This includes the food and mail being loaded on to the plane.
We have assumed that only airline personnel have access to the plane. It seems to me that it would be the responsibility of Transport Canada to look at the procedures that airlines have in place for personnel security.

Mr. Speaker, I genuinely appreciate the Hon. Member's comment and regret that in the course of this dialogue we sometimes draw conclusions. I regret that the assumption has been made, First, that it was a bomb or an explosive device that caused the demise of Flight 182. That has not been officially confirmed.
Second, it has not been officially confirmed that if it was a bomb, it was in a piece of luggage. I appreciate the fact that the Hon. Member has brought us back to a state of some
Statements by Ministers
objectivity. That is the problem when we become involved in this sort of discussion. In our attempt to be as forthcoming as possible, we sometimes draw conclusions.
Naturally, I think the terms of reference that were outlined by the Prime Minister clearly give us the parameters to examine airport security as well as security of the airlines, which means the airplane as well.

Mr. Speaker, earlier this afternoon I alluded to measures that could be taken by the Government to help the families who have been so badly hurt in this incident. There are a number of relatives who are anxiously waiting for news, some of whom are interested in going to Ireland to see for themselves what happened and to take whatever steps they want in order to identify the bodies or dispose of them according to their religious beliefs.
What assistance has the Minister offered to these families, and when can they expect to be accepted in Ireland? I understand that at the present time the authorities have not only not welcomed them, they have imposed what may be called an embargo for some time. Therefore, the relatives must stay home.
Will the Minister also answer a question concerning an incident that is reported in The Toronto Starl Vern Thampi, husband of Metro's Vijaya Thampi, a Toronto Star employee who was among the dead, said that he has been getting the runaround from Air-India. He told the Star, "I have phoned every half hour but I cannot get through". He told the Star, "My grief is beginning to turn into anger".
Indeed, this is something that is understandable and we should sympathize with these people who are unable to get appropriate information from Air-India, particularly if the company has decided to suspend temporarily some of its activities.
Could officials from the Department of Transport act on behalf of the airlines or assist the people who are seeking information about their relatives?

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of Sate for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has been involved in the kind of discussions to which the Hon. Member refers. I know he met with the Indian High Commissioner this morning. I am sure some of these things were discussed. I think, as was indicated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) yesterday, the Government is willing and prepared to assist in every way possible and is offering support in a general way and is assisting the bereaved families to travel.
With respect to the specific point made in the quotation from The Toronto Star as well as the general broad issue which the Hon. Member has raised, I will undertake to draw it to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. There is a co-ordinating group working between my Department, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of the Solicitor General. Indeed the Prime Minister has taken

June 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
a personal interest in this. I will certainly draw his concerns to their attention.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your indulgence in such a serious matter. I appreciate our being able to get into this matter in some detail with the Minister. I will try to put about three questions to the Minister in one and he can make note of them.
I believe the Minister mentioned the number of additional scanners that have been ordered. I did not catch the number. That is a good move. Whatever additional ones are needed, I say get them, and with the latest technology. I invite the Minister to check out what is being done at the airport in San Francisco, which is supposed to have one of the best safety and security arrangements of any in the world. The San Francisco Airport has mobile X-ray scanners. Before a plane takes off or up until its point of no return, it can return and mobile scanners move into action. I want to know whether any of those scanners were ordered.
Second, the Ministry of Transport some time ago was not satisfied with the electronic and/or chemical sniffers developed in England and in other parts of Europe. They did not meet what the Ministry thought our standards should be. The Ministry of Transport commissioned the National Research Council to develop better sniffers which it has done and has licensed a Toronto firm to produce them. I understand they will not be available until this fall. Can the Minister tell us when they will be available? Has he ordered any of those? Will there be any additional dogs trained and available, more than the present four?
I am sure the Minister and all other Members know that one can go through as a passenger with his hand luggage through three scanners in one day. The first one or two let you through and on the third one, even though you have the same amount of keys and coins in your pockets, the bells ring and the lights go on.
When will we get a standard minimum application of these machines so that if I go through a scanner in Regina, one in Winnipeg and then the one in Toronto beeps yet I have the same things in my pockets, obviously there is no uniform standard.
Does the Department have a minimum level at which the scanners must be set, or do airports with a higher risk have a tougher level than those with a lower risk? I would like to know what the score is on that.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that I can answer with precision all the questions which the Hon. Member has advanced. I can assure him that I will get him the answers and perhaps communicate with him either directly or by letter.
With respect to the X-ray equipment, and this again demonstrates the difficulty of being accurate on a day-to-day basis, I think I used the figure of $1.5 million yesterday, but the briefing notes I have today indicate that some $3.75 million is going to be spent on X-ray equipment. System Two will be
available within two weeks in some airports, an available System Three by Friday, three certainly, one at each of the following sites: Toronto, Vancouver and Mirabel. There will be five System One units. Smaller carry-on baggage units have been borrowed from manufacturers and will be flown to Pearson International Airport. The estimated cost is some $3,375 million for the time being.
As for the NRC issue, I will certainly get back to the Member with respect to the standard minimum application. 1 know there is an adjusting device. I am not mechanically proficient enough to respond, as I said, with a degree of accuracy, but I will try to get that information to the Member as soon as I possibly can.
What about the dogs?
With respect to that-

Hon. Members seeking to ask questions at this point are: The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly), and the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson). Assuming that ends it, then I will end at that point.

I will be very brief, Mr. Speaker. I want to point out to the Minister the proposal to cut at the eight airports RCMP security force. During Question Period, I asked the Minister if he would cancel that decision, not review it and not put it on hold. I asked him if he would cancel the decision. I am surprised that some Members really did not listen. I suppose that is a problem, Mr. Speaker, of Members listening to the answers and the questions that are given during Question Period.
No comment.

No comment from the Speaker. An airport can be classified domestic military, internatinal general aviation or international charter or it can be an international airpot. The point is that most of those eight airports I know of have licences for international charters, international general aviation purposes. That is why the question has been asked over and over again. Why not cancel that particular decision because then the back up security will go to the lowest bidder?
There is not much wrong with that if the low bidder is high enough to be equal to the rest of society, but for the first time in Canadian history we have the federal minimum wage at airports lower than the minimum wage in every province in Canada. A fellow can go to work one week say at the international airport in Toronto for $3.50 an hour and then go to an office building the next week in Toronto and get paid $4 an hour in Ontario, $4.58 in Quebec or $4.30 an hour in Manitoba.
And sometimes a 12 hour shift.

The Minister should tell us whether or not he is aware of this. If he is aware, then he should speak to the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) to get that provision
June 25, 1985

changed quickly because provincial minimum wages have gone up drastically since January in at least five or six provinces. The main question is that the provision of the equipment in the airport is the responsibility of the Minister's Department. The Minister's Department also pays the salaries of the RCMP officers quarterly to the Department of the Solicitor General. When an airport manager has to make a decision on a cut-back of his local budget, he should not have to make a decision on the cutting back of extra equipment or whether or not who he is going to get to repair it.
Second, the airport security staff at these eight airports should be kept on. There should be no review. There should be a greater presence of RCMP officers than less of a presence.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat again that the decision has been made to defer the withdrawal of RCMP officers from the eight airports in question.
1 want to point out once more that there were RCMP personnel removed from 12 airports earlier by the previous administration as a result of the re-evaluation in 1975-76 which was conducted by a joint review committee on Transport Canada, the RCMP and ATAC. The Hon. Member did not get up, holler and scream when the RCMP were being removed from those 12 airports.
I did.

We have stated-and 1 made it very clear in the House today-that that decision was deferred. We are going through a complete review and re-evaluation of our total airport and airline security system. I think it would be premature for me to make a definitive decision at this particular time, but I can assure the Hon. Member that in light of the new circumstances and the experiences over last weekend, he need not worry.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke privately with the Minister this morning about an issue which concerns me, and I would like to raise it publicly at this point. In the area which 1 represent and in areas surrounding it, there are at least 10 small airports from which passengers and baggage are ferried into the main terminal airport without going through the security system. One example of that would be the dirt strip in Bella Bella. People picked up on Air B.C. are ferried into the main terminal beyond the security area, providing an opportunity for them and their baggage to be moved directly into any aircraft. Will the Minister's evaluation of airport security include every point of access to main terminals or main airlines.
The people involved in the security which exists-and it is extremely minimal-are generally airline employees who have no training and very little in the way of security facilities. In the summertime, at this point in time, ticket clerks are security agents, baggage handlers and various other things. They are throwing baggage on the aircraft without ever looking at it. They are not able to frisk individuals. When there are late
Statements by Ministers
passengers and standby people waiting to board, and the propellers on the place are turning, there is no security. Would the Minister indicate whether they will look into revamping that situation?
In some areas there are security individuals. For example, TWA is one airline which contracted security from people who were former police officers or military personnel familiar with the procedures. Those people have been laid off from many terminals and apparently airline employees have been given temporary authority to do it. Given the fact that deregulation moves will result in more and more small carriers from small airports feeding the mainline and having access to those terminals, will the Minister be looking beyond major terminals and into smaller ones to ensure the presence of trained personnel to do an adequate job with security?

Mr. Speaker, let me say first of all how much I appreciate this kind of constructive contribution to the debate. The Hon. Member shared with me some thoughts on this earlier. I was looking for the sheet of paper which he presented to me; I assure him that I have it. Of course the evaluation which we will undertake will go beyond international airports. It seems to me that it would make eminent good sense, when we do that kind of evaluation, to do it on a global basis rather than simply on the basis of international, national or regional airports.
In an attempt to respond to the occurrences over the weekend, to deal with what we have perceived as an international crisis, we tried to address it by tightening up the inspection of baggage on international flights both leaving and entering Canada. We will certainly take the Hon. Member's representations into consideration.
Furthermore, the Hon. Member talked about the advent of more smaller carriers getting into the business. I think he will appreciate now, more than ever, the importance of the Aeronautics Act. It really provides a new framework for the implementation and enforcement of the necessary safety rules and regulations, another component of safety and security for the welfare of the travelling public.

Mr. Speaker, I have two related questions for the Minister. Both of them are quite short, so perhaps I might pose them together. The first one concerns the announcement in the budget papers of a new management structure for the federal airport system in Canada which will allow for the independent operation of local airports. From the Minister's last answer, can we assume that "independent" does not mean any diminution of safety and that, for instance, baggage loaded at small independent airports will have to meet certain standards so that it is not a hazard when it is transferred in larger airports? My first question concerns the nature of the independence, whether systems will still be compatible and whether there will be some regulation of it.
My second question concerns tax increases. In the space of the last five months there have been two tax increases, so that the Government will now be taking an extra $90 million per year from Canadian airline passengers. In view of the tragic

June 25, 1985
Adjournment Motion
events of last weekend, can we assume that some or all of this money will be earmarked to improve safety and security measures?

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the new proposed airport management system, I am consulting with various industry groups, aviation groups, the provinces and representatives of all regions, to examine ways and means of putting in place a more effective management and administrative system for all Canadian airports, while at the same time providing a greater degree of local autonomy or involvement by using the local airport as an important economic tool within the particular region. We think that is a sensible way to go. However, in the course of that it will in no way reflect upon the standards of safety. It will not detract in any way, shape or form from Transport Canada's responsibility to maintain a safe and reliable air navigation system across the country, control towers, light service stations and the like. It will not involve any reduction in the level of safety.
Hon. Members who have been around the House for some time will recognize that I have been involved through many years of my parliamentary career in working and helping to elevate and upgrade the level of safety in our aviation system. It was under my prior jurisdiction that we commissioned the Dubin report. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board was a product of that. The Aeronautics Act, which we recently passed through the House, is a further product of that. We have a very high level of safety in Canada, and we are always striving to improve it.
With respect to the taxes to which the Hon. Member referred, there has been some increase in the level of the ticket tax. However, I remind Hon. Members that the federal Government subsidizes every air passenger on a return trip basis to the tune of $58; in other words, every passenger who flies in Canada is subsidized at the rate of $58. I think we recognize that that is a fairly high level and that the airport cost recovery is at about 35 per cent. It was at 50 per cent in 1980. We are constantly being asked to improve firefighting services and safety, to provide better navigational services and new radar systems. This costs money, and we are attempting to address it.
I regret to interrupt the Hon. Minister, but I must make the following announcement before five o'clock.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows; the Hon. Member for
Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox (Mr. Vankoughnet) - Penitentiaries-Cost of maintaining inmates; the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor)-Sports-Baseball decision unfair to Canadian umpires; the Hon. The Minister will know that it is really not the same on the West Coast as it is on the East Coast. We have a substantial
problem with a fleet which is too large. Rather than building more vessels, we should be looking at bringing that fleet into manageable size. I wonder if the Minister might be in a position to give this House some indication of what the present status of the buy-back is right now. During the election campaign there were promises of $100 million buy-back. Now we hear the Minister talking about a $37 million buy-back. I believe it is extremely important that something be done in terms of fleet rationalization on the West Coast.
We certainly have a fleet too large for the resource at the present time and there is a major program, and a promise of the Conservative Party, to enhance the size of the resource. During the election campaign, there was talk of a $200 million enhancement program. It is our understanding now that that figure has been mentioned in committee, that there will be a program in the order of $200 million which is currently before the decision-making body of Government. I wonder if the Minister can give the House some indication as to the status of that promise before this House adjourns?
Of course, as I mentioned before, there is the problem of having an improving fishery but, certainly, when small communities which have been dependent on fisheries are being largely taken away from it by the mobile nature of the purchasing agencies, the trucking facilities to major processing operations, and the rationalizing of those facilities in the major centres, we see those communities on the coast of British Columbia being deprived of an opportunity to maintain employment in that industry. It will be useful if the Minister in his summary remarks on this legislation gives us an indication of how the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act is going to work with respect to such things on the west coast as fleet rationalization and the salmonid enhancement program.
The Minister, being aware of the employment and economic difficulties in those communities, should look at supporting infrastructure programs, through his Department, to aid fishing and processing at the local level in order to ensure that employment and economic benefits are retained in those communities. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has numerous projects in his area which require serious concern. The Minister has yet to make a statement on the Campbell River Indian band marina project, the Port Hardy freezer unit, or the Bella Coola ice plants. There are numerous areas in which we need those kinds of attention.
I would also ask the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for a comment prior to parting from this House on another critical and important issue. I think of justice. A number of individuals who were faced with, I think, indecision on the part of Government, became involved in a civil disobedience situation.
It would be hoped that the Minister would be in a frame of mind to consider whether or not the Department should maintain the charges in this matter, and, in the interests of maintaining within the industry a willingness to bargain and cooperate-and there has been an enormous amount of co-operation this year in the absence of strict authority-to bring a fishing plant into place in all aspects and keep it rolling along.
It would be my hope that the Minister, prior to this Bill being
