The Bill before us, Mr. Speaker, amends the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. As the Minister said, it guarantees loans that the banks give to the fishermen. That is an interesting proposition, Mr. Speaker. In the way the Minister said it, it is as if the banks give a loan to a fisherman for a boat or gear and that is guaranteed. In other words, if the fisherman defaults, then the bank has to then go after the federal Department of Fisheries to be paid for the difference. The Minister is shaking his head. "Take security" says the Minister. After the security is taken, it is guaranteed by the federal Government to be paid to the lender if the fisherman defaults. That is correct. The Minister is shaking his head.
Oh, no, I am only-

I want to read a brief letter from a bank manager to a fisherman. Fishermen in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, and part of Quebec are getting these letters. I would like the Minister to listen. It says:
Dear Mr. Elliott,
We advise that the Federal Government is paying no further claims against Fishery Improvement Loans advanced between 1977 and 1980. In this regard, we regret to inform you that your loans are now excluded from the Federal Government Guarantee, and as such, the accounts now revert to your sole
responsibility.
We advise that outstanding amounts on your loans are as follows: -Boat Loan, Principal-$9,602.95, Interest to May 28, 1985-$1,504.41; Gear Loan, Principal-$5,661.60, Interest to May 28, 1985-$1,824.45.
Did you notice the dates, Mr. Speaker? May, 1985. The Minister said that this particular legislation would take effect the end of this month because that would allow the Government to guarantee loans to fishermen after the end of this month. I just read a letter from a bank manager to a fisherman which said that loans granted between 1977 and 1980 are
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
no longer guaranteed by the federal Government. This is a very serious matter. We are not really debating a fisheries improvement loan guarantee program at all. Go into the bank and you will see a sign which says "See us for fisheries improvement loans guaranteed by the federal Government". They signed for the loan, they got into trouble because it was a bad fishing season from 1977 to 1980, their gear is seized and sold at public auction, they forgot about it for a few years- the Minister is getting up and going to the phone.
Phoning the bank.

Phoning the bank. I can save him the trip and tell him what is wrong.
Another gentleman says he took out a fisheries improvement loan in 1979 which was guaranteed by the "feds" as he put it. He was unable to pay so the bank repossessed his gear and sold it, the proceeds being applied to his loan. That was last week and then he received a letter from the bank saying the federal Government was paying no further claims against fisheries improvement loans advanced between 1977 and 1980 and the account was now his sole responsibility.
What has happened now for the first time, Mr. Speaker, since 1935? I will tell you what happened. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) should listen to what happened. Hidden away in the regulations, unknown to the banks, is a policy which says that the federal Government will only honour an amount of money not exceeding 10 per cent of the total value of the loans guaranteed by that bank in a three-year period. Now, this situation never arose before so the banks did not know about it.
What has happened now? A bank has exceeded the amount indicated and has been informed by the Minister's Department that the Government can no longer honour any more loan guarantees on loans from 1977 to 1980. What do the banks do? They go directly to the person they loaned the money to and say that they owe the banks the money right back to when they got the loan, including interest all along the way.
The Minister can say that was in the regulations, but my argument is this. Two years ago we had the greatest number of claims against this guarantee program, some $4 million or $4.5 million. Last year it was about $1 million. This year I suppose they are projecting it down to maybe $500,000 in claims. My point is, why can the Government of Canada not honour the guarantees that were given to the banks? It is not the bank's fault. They had never exceeded that level before. They did not know the regulation was there. I am asking the Minister, in a spirit of good will as shown by this Bill, to say to the banks that we will honour the loans made from 1977 to 1980 because the fishermen did not know the loans were not guaranteed. They were told they were. The banks did not know they were not guaranteed, they were told they were. There it is in writing.
For the sake of those fishermen, and there may only be a couple of hundred fishermen involved, a couple of hundred families, let the Government do that. Here we have a fellow who has to pay back $18,593.41 for gear that was seized back

June 25, 1985
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act in 1978, Mr. Speaker. Another poor gentleman here has to pay back $3,740.96. He was charged interest of 11.5 per cent from the beginning of the loan.
As I said, I am not blaming the Government because no action was taken, although I probably should. There are a lot of fishermen out there sitting down with their wives this evening wondering how they are going to pay this massive amount of money which they owe only because they got a loan guaranteed by the federal Government. I will tell you what they are saying. They are saying it is the Tory Government. I have heard it on the phone and I have tried to explain it to them and say no, it is not the Government of Canada at all, it is the division operating under the guarantee. I try to explain it to them. As sure as I am saying this, Mr. Speaker, they are saying it is that Government of Canada, a Tory Government, and that Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. That is what they are saying in Newfoundland. They say "He is from British Columbia, that's him! Now we have to pay all this money because the banks are notifying us in writing that the federal guarantee is no longer any good".
One fellow said to me the other day that he heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) say that we may not be able to send out any cheques any more, they may bounce. Well, this could be one of the spin-offs. The Government's guarantee is no longer any good.
My intervention was going to be very short and to the point, but you will have to agree that this is a very important subject, Mr. Speaker, affecting hundreds of people. It is not fair, either to the individual or to the banks. I never thought I would see the day when I said it was not fair to the banks, but it is not. After having introduced this Bill to extend it for a year and a half, the Minister should study this problem on an urgent basis in an effort to respect the guarantees which were signed in good faith by the banks and the fishermen concerned.

Mr. Chairman, before we move right through this, would the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans take the opportunity, during debate on Clause 1, to respond to some of the questions I raised? The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act does not stand alone as a management tool affecting the fishing fleet. During the election campaign certain commitments were made about buy-back programs. Would the Minister take a minute or two to give us an indication of the progress on such things as government investment in the Salmonid Enhancement Program and what the present status and future prospects are for the buy-back?

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to advise the Committee that with regard to salmonid enhancement and the buy-back I have submitted documents to Cabinet. As soon as they have been dealt with I will be able to advise the Hon. Member on the outcome. I want to assure him and others that I take both those matters very seriously and am pursuing them.
With respect to some other matters raised by the Hon. Member, they are important and I would be quite pleased to discuss those in detail with the Hon. Member. I believe that attempts have been made and that there is some co-operation between my staff and the Hon. Member's office to arrange a meeting on Thursday. Certainly I hope that that will be accomplished.

Mr. Chairman, could the Minister take a few minutes to respond to some questions with respect to financial assistance being made available to the Ontario region to make repairs to wharves that are suffering either from ice damage or high water which is affecting many harbours this year? Could he respond to those concerns?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot imagine what the value of improving or extending the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act will be if we are not getting the proper improvements to harbours to operate at a reasonable level. If harbours are awash and completely unusable, how are the fishermen in the Great Lakes region going to operate? What is the value of having a loan if the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is not
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act prepared to improve the harbours which are not functional in some cases because of high water? Surely we are here to deal with the over-all fishery.
For instance, in my constituency in South Bay Mouth, where a number of commercial fishermen operate, not only the perimeter wharf but all the finger wharves are completely submerged. This requires massive attention. If the fishermen operating out of South Bay Mouth do not have decent harbours from which to operate-they are completely inoperative at this time-what is the point of extending the fisheries loans legislation to them?
I saw that the Minister was prepared to respond to my representation. I am sure there would be agreement for that response to be made now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair is not convinced of the relevancy of the question. I would ask the Hon. Member to direct another question to the Minister. The Minister may reply at some time, if he wishes.

Mr. Chairman, I have one further point to make to the Minister with respect to Clause I concerning the loans that are made under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act that are not honoured by the Fisheries Department because the banks involved have gone over the figure that is supposedly stipulated in the regulations. I do not know where the figures are stipulated in the regulation.
Although most Acts are confusing, this is particularly confusing when trying to determine the amount of money the Government will respect that the banks cannot get from the fishermen, after using every method possible to get their money from the fishermen. As I stated during the second reading, the banks try every method possible to get their money and then go after the fishermen as a last resort.
I did not mention to the Minister that the Fishermens' credit has totally gone and the banks have written a second letter, pursuant to Fisheries Improvement Loans Act asking for their credit cards because they no longer have any credit with the bank. The reason is that the federal Government is no longer honouring their fisheries improvement loans. They do not point out that they have surpassed the limit stipulated by the Government.
This system was triggered for the first time in April. The fishermen were notified that they owed the banks the money plus the interest because they no longer had the loans guaranteed by the federal Government. The unfairness is that the claim of the person who took out the loan in the 1970s and worked hard to pay it back by making sacrifices will not be honoured, while someone who quit fishing after finding it difficult will have his claim honoured because he made it first.
The Department of Fisheries has no way now of knowing how many fishermen are involved in the provinces throughout this country. There is no way of knowing, unless there is a mechanism whereby the banks notify the Fisheries Improvement Loans people of the total value of their loans made as of March 31. Perhaps the Minister could then divide that total

June 25, 1985
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
figure into the total number of fishermen who received loans and arrive at a general figure of the number of fishermen who were so affected.
However, the banks are quite understandably notifying the fishermen that they are no longer covered because they were notified at the end of April by the federal Government that it no longer respects the banks' loans for that period 1977 to 1980. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that that was a bad year in the fishery.
It is also my understanding that the Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal and the Toronto Dominion Bank are fast approaching their limit from 1980 to 1983. Again, the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans may have to notify those banks that it no longer respects the claims on loans that were taken out years ago.
We do not know how many fishermen have lost all their credit and must repay up to $18,000 or $19,000 to the banks. The banks are the only ones who know the number of fishermen involved. I wanted to point out to the Minister the unfairness to the fishermen who are really trying to make it in British Columbia, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec. Members of Parliament who represent fishing ridings should be prepared for letters over the summer from fishermen who are stuck because of this particular decision. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the Minister and reiterate the importance of finding a solution to the problem.

Mr. Chairman, let me very briefly respond to the Hon. Member for Algoma. As I explained to the Fisheries Committee some weeks ago, there is an application before Treasury Board which I hope will be granted, that will give us more funds to meet some of the obligations which I think are proper to meet. I also must say to the Hon. Member, as I said in committee, that until we can persuade others to increase the funding I do not have enough money to go around. I listened with great concern to what the Hon. Member says. There is nothing that he says that I quarrel with in terms of need for these funds.
With respect to the point raised by my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, I haved read a copy of the letter from the Scotia Bank to which he referred and also a copy of the letter from his constituent. I can only say this afternoon that I am not familiar with what has lead to this. I will find out. Since this debate began, I have contacted my Department to find out exactly what the situation is and I will report back to the Hon. Member tomorrow.

Mr. Chairman, I note in this legislation, as far as I can see, that the proposal of a 1 per cent fee put in the Small Business Loans Act last fall does not apply to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act or the 15 per cent of losses which have to be absorbed by banks under the Small Business Loan Act.
I note that the Bill is being extended for only 18 months rather than the usual five years. Is the Minister planning to institute those fees in this legislation the next time the legislation is being amended? Is that why the Bill is being extended for only 18 months rather than the normal five year period? I think that kind of move made in the Small Business Loans Act has a very detrimental effect on the availability of loans.
The problem with most of these loans is that very often the small businessman, the farmer or the fisherman finds there are no funds available. The banks do not want to provide the funds because they get only 1 per cent above prime in interest and now with the 1 per cent acquisition fee being charged by the federal Government and having to absorb 15 per cent of the losses makes these loans a poor opportunity for the banks. Has the Minister considered that problem, has he rejected it, or is he keeping that open as an option when he reviews the legislation in the next 18 months when the Bill is due for renewal again?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member will understand when I say that I have presently today no firm views on what changes if any might be made to this Act many months from now. I assure the Hon. Member that I will take note of his comments and pay some attention to the representations that he has made today.
