speakeroldname: Hon. John Wise (Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-56, an Act to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Danis in the chair.
On Clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, I want to express my appreciation on behalf of my colleagues for the co-operation we have received from the two Opposition Parties with respect to the agreement to pass this piece of legislation through all stages. I thought perhaps at this point it might be appropriate for me to make some remarks on the Farm Improvement Loans Act. While we are in Committee of the Whole, perhaps I could respond to questions that more than likely will flow from Members opposite.
I am pleased today to be speaking to this legislation amending the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This Bill will extend my authority as Minister of Agriculture to guarantee loans under the Act for the 18 month period from July 1, 1985 to December 30, 1986. The extension of this Act is recognition of
June 25, 1985

its ongoing importance within the credit system of Canadian agriculture.
These days, as Members will realize, farmers pay close attention to their books as well as to their land. The successful ones are good business people who understand, among other things, how credit matters affect their operations. In examining Government programs in the agriculture credit area, you must keep in mind the farm community's special characteristics. The cyclical nature of farming demands that producers have a good handle on their cash flow requirements. The dependence of farming on weather and market prices means that producers must be highly knowledgeable about methods of stabilizing their income. The tendency to plow profits back into the business means, that, even after being in the business for years or generations, many farmers continue to require a reliable line of credit.
Finally, farming is extremely capital intensive and again has certain credit implications. It is not enough to recognize that farmers need credit. What they need is a flexible range of credit options. Without this, the sort of long-term planning so important to effective, efficient farming would not be possible.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act provides an option that meets a very specific need, that of intermediate term financing to cover capital expenditures.
The Act itself, as many Members will realize, was introduced 40 years ago. It has authorized Ministers of Agriculture to guarantee against losses term loans made to farmers by chartered banks, Alberta treasury branches and other designated lenders across the country.
Producers are able to have several outstanding loans under this program to a combined ceiling of $100,000. The maximum repayment period for loans to cover the purchase of additional land is 15 years while for all other purposes the term of repayment is 10 years. Since its introduction in March 1945, the Act has been amended several times, primarily to effect lending periods.
Just to give some idea of its impact on the farm community since the introduction of the Act until the end of last year, about 1.9 million loans have been approved worth in excess $5 billion. This reflects a sizeable capital investment in the agriculture sector.
During this period some $17 million, that is a fraction of 1 per cent, was paid by the federal Government in claims, of which $2.8 million subsequently was recovered. That is not a bad record. I think it proves farmers generally are a very, very good credit risk.
As further proof, prior to the introduction of the Act, lending institutions were reluctant to extend intermediate credit to farmers. However, during the years following the program's introduction, lending institutions came to realize that producers were indeed good risks. As a result, numerous banks and other lending organizations have entered the field with their own programs for intermediate farm loans. In this
Farm Improvement Loans Act
sense, the Farm Improvement Loans Act played an instrumental role in expanding the number of farm credit sources open to farmers, as well as raising the level of credit available to them.
I am sure every Member of the House has noted with great satisfaction the over-all decline in interest rates. This trend is reflected in FCC rates, which have dropped from thirteen and three-quarters per cent on five-year loans as of last December, to eleven and seven-eights per cent as of now, the lowest level since 1979. This downward trend is clear evidence that the Government's economic policies are on target. Declining interest rates are a sign of growing confidence in our economy and in the Government's determination to get the deficit under control.
By the way, this trend in interest rates is good news for producers who took out or plan to take out guaranteed loans through the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The ceiling on loans made under this program is equal to the prime lending rate of chartered banks plus 1 per cent. As our economy improves and interest rates reach favourable levels, this program becomes all the more attractive.
I should like to quote a few statistics to illustrate further the significance of the Farm Improvement Loans Act to the agricultural sector.
Looking back on 1984, in excess of 12,000 loans were guaranteed under the program, amounting to more than $159 million in loan capital. During the year loans were made for a variety of uses. The bulk of them, $105 million worth, went toward buying agricultural implements. The remainder funded construction or repairs of farm houses and buildings, land purchases, land improvements and irrigation, livestock purchases and equipment overhauls.
While producers in every province have benefited over the years, historically western Canada has depended more heavily on the program. For example, in 1984 loan capital guaranteed to producers under the Act in the four western provinces amounted to more than $133 million. That was about 83 per cent of the total under the Farm Improvement Loans Act last year.
It is true that FILA does not command the same share of the total farm credit market as it once did. Of course there are a number of reasons for that. For instance, provincial Governments have entered the agricultural lending field and lending institutions have set up their own programs. However, I am sure all Hon. Members would agree that it is in the best interest of the agricultural sector for this program to continue. This is especially true in rural Canada where its termination could truly spell hardship, particularly at this point in time. It is not uncommon in many less populated regions for only one lending institution to serve an entire area. Farmers in these regions see FILA as a vital resource to obtain much needed credit.
By comparison, this 18-month extension is relatively short. Of course there is a reason for it. My Department will be using this time to review the Act to ensure that it is meeting current

June 25, 1985
Farm Improvement Loans Act
needs. If necessary, changes will be introduced at the end of the extension period. Among other things, I am interested in examining whether this program could work in combination with existing and future FCC programming.
I suggest to Hon. Members that they would be acting in the interest of Canadian farmers by supporting quick passage of this Bill. I urge them to do so, and I would be happy to respond to their questions.

Mr. Chairman, we in this Party will be pleased to see the Bill pass in that it provides some assistance to agriculture. I think the Minister referred to the amount of loans last year totalling some $1.5 million.
They amounted to more than $159 million.

I should like to put that amount into perspective. We should be conscious of the fact that there are something like $20 billion worth of farm loans at the present time, and that the profit from many commodities is not adequate for producers to repay their loans or debts. This is why they are facing the worst economic crisis since the 1930s.
In its report last fall, the Farm Credit Corporation catalogued the depth and scope of the crisis when it indicated that 39,000, or something like 17 per cent of our farmers were in serious financial difficulty, were borrowing more than they were spending on capital expenditures and had equity of less than 15 per cent. Since that report came out, the Government completely fumbled the handling of the EEC beef matter. We now have something like 17 million pounds of subsidized beef entering the country, which will make it that much more difficult for farmers to repay these loans.
When I heard this afternoon that the Minister wanted to bring in emergency legislation, I hoped that he would bring in a Bill to provide for an agri-bond program such as the one recommended by the finance committee. It recommended a $96 million program which would provide 8 per cent loans. The program was recommended highly by the chairman of the committee, an outstanding chairman and government Member. Such an agri-bond program would help solve the financial distress faced by a large percentage of the 39,000 farmers about whom I just spoke.
As I understand it, the prime rate of the bank plus 1 per cent will probably be close to 13 per cent, or an interest rate which is actually higher than the present rate of the Farm Credit Corporation. Although this Bill provides a useful form of farm financing, a minuscule amount is actually available. The banks would not want to give out these loans because they would stand to make only 1 per cent above prime. Obviously they want to allocate most of their funds to other programs under which they make higher interest rates. Although some $825 million was made available through the Farm Credit Corporation last year, that amount has been slashed to some $94 million this year. There is really no hope in that regard.
In addition, producers have to face the prospect of new taxes on farm input costs; of nine cents per gallon on gasoline starting on September 3, and of a new innovation on the part
of the Government to tax the harvest of western grains. On January 1, another 1 per cent sales tax will be imposed. All these things make it very difficult for producers to repay their farm improvement loans.
In the last three or four days before the House adjourns for the summer recess, I hope the Minister will take into account the serious difficulty faced by the red meat industry and by the western grain industry, with the United States bonus program, and bring in substantial legislation to deal with the farm debt crisis. Only by doing that will we be able to come to grips with the magnitude of the farm debt problem. Extending the provisions of this Bill for a few months or a year or so, and providing a few guaranteed loans, will not really come to grips with the massive debt problem faced by many producers. As was recommended by the finance committee of the House of Commons, an agri-bond program should be established on an emergency basis. I certainly want to see this legislation passed and extended but I hope that the Minister will be bringing in more substantial legislation to really deal with the larger problem on an emergency basis later this week. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a short statement and then I have some questions for the Minister as well.
This Bill brings up an old question that I am asked, quite often when I go through my riding. Does the Farm Improvement Loans Act still exist? The answer is that it does. Most farmers are still eligible. There are some 350,000 to 500,000 farmers in Canada who would be eligible. They have to be commercial farmers who are attempting to make a living from farming. The rate is prime plus 1 per cent and the Government will guarantee part of the loan, so it should therefore be something that banks are anxious to give out.
I guess the reason they ask about the eligibility is that it extends to virtually all farm activities, anything that a farmer would want to produce on his farm. The loan can be used to purchase the breeding stock, to build buildings and facilities, to buy equipment, even to buy land and make land improvements. The term runs for 10 years on most things and up to 15 years for land purchases.
The reason I think they ask if it still exists is in part explained when you look at this particular amendment we have before us today. It is very much like two previous amendments we have had under the previous Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan. The problem is simply that for the total amount of money available for protection, because really this Bill is a form of protection to the banks, to the credit unions, to the trust companies and the Alberta treasury branches who want to participate in it, the federal Government will provide guarantees that there will be limited losses if the loans are not paid. So it is a federal Government guarantee of the loan to the farmer.
Unfortunately the Bill still reads as it read back in 1980 when I first came here. It was one of the first Bills I had to
June 25, 1985

deal with as a new Member when I came in February of 1980. The Bill at that time extended $1,550 million from July of 1980 to June 30, 1983. You can see, Mr. Chairman, how you get into a problem when you continue to use that same amount of money. Later on Mr. Whelan introduced another Bill that extended it to this June. We now have the current Minister extending it from July, 1980 to December 31, 1986. We have the same amount of money being guaranteed, not for a little over two years but over six years. There is a shrinking amount of money available for new loans as a result of this.
It has to be remembered, as I pointed out, that the loans are extended for as much as 15 years if they are for land purchases. It is small wonder then that in spite of their being something in the order of $1,550 million there in the pool that we only had, according to the Minister's statement, something in the order of $145 or $150 million loaned under the program last year. That is what I would expect, because money only becomes available to be loaned under the program as people pay off their loans of previous years.
It is not a great deal of money. It is somewhere between 3 per cent and 4 per cent of the amount of money that farmers require and use on an ongoing basis. Farmers have borrowed between $20 billion and $23 billion at any one time and this program provides just over $1.5 billion, not a very big chunk of that money.
Back when farm improvement loans meant something to the farming community they made up a much greater portion of loans outstanding. In fact, at one time they made up virtually all of the short and medium term lending that the banks engaged in. Credit unions engaged in some other lending, but banks were pretty much only in the farm improvement loans business. At that time it had been government policy to have government guarantees extended to the banks to take up a big portion of the amount of money that farmers needed.
We are quite obviously trying to shrink both the farm improvement loans through the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Credit Corporation which extends longer term loans. Along with that there has been companion legislation to attract the banks into the farm loan business, which they and the trust companies have done to some very large extent.
Farmers however have not necessarily been as well served. Those who have been in the business for more than 20 years can recall when they could get a farm improvement loan and were guaranteed both the amount of interest and the term of the interest; that gives pretty good financial control for any operation.
Gradually we got to the point where Section 88 of the Bank Act was used to supplant the Farm Improvement Loans Act. That gave the banks the right, resulting in a revolution in the farm lending field. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, when the loan was made the only item given as security was the building or the machine or the herd of cattle or whatever the loan was borrowed for.
Under Section 88 of the Bank Act, came the revolution! A farmer could buy a cow or a combine but he signed on the
Farm Improvement Loans Act
dotted line giving as security all of his grains, all of his livestock and all of the movables from that operation. We moved from there to the recent Bank Act where now a similar thing is done under Section 176, but in addition to all of this extra security Section 176 the farmer only knows on a weekly or monthly basis what the rate of interest is, and it is due on call. So this has really changed the conditions for loans. It is small wonder that farmers ask with some nostalgia what ever happened to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, because they had a firm rate of interest, they had a certain amount of time in which they knew they had to pay the loan off and the security was only the item that the loan had been granted for.
We have moved a long ways. I think this particular Act effectively protects only those people who still have farm improvement loans. I think that the chance of this particular amendment assisting very many farmers is not at all great. We will probably see a continuation of the situation, with only a few farmers succeeding in getting a farm improvement loan. It will be a somewhat different process than that which is gone through to win a lottery, but for those who make it they will consider themselves about as lucky.
I would close the remarks portion of my time today by asking the Minister if he can give us some information regarding the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and tell us how much of that $1,550 million is outstanding in loans now and how much he expects over the course of the next year to become available for such loans to farmers.

Mr. Chairman, I want to respond to the comments made by both the Hon. Member for Algoma and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre. First, I would like to indicate to them that in my remarks I did not suggest that I was coming before the House with a great, new, innovative piece of legislation. It is a piece of legislation that has been around for about 40 years.
I can well recall that about three years ago, I was not sitting here but across the way in the opposition benches. In the last 13 years, I have had two or three opportunities to speak to this legislation when it was brought forward by the previous Government for three-year extensions. I really have not changed my view about it. I want to make that point because I want to be very honest, open and frank. I can well recall that when I sat over there and made representations about this Bill, I used to make some of the same comments and observations that have been made by the two opposition critics. My remarks were probably more parallel with the latter speaker than the former.
I can recall that when I was in opposition, there was one major problem with this piece of legislation, and that was that the banks did not participate in it to the extent that we thought they should. I would like to tell my colleagues that I still have some concerns about this. Simply because I have from moved Opposition to Government does not mean that I am now carrying a flag in support of the Farm Improvement Loans Act.

June 25, 1985
Farm Improvement Loans Act
I used to say that many farmers came to me to indicate that when they approached their banking institutions, the bankers had three stock answers: one, they had never heard of this piece of legislation before; two, it was not their policy to participate in loans under this Act; three, it was their policy to provide loans under this piece of legislation but they could not extend any more loans because their allotment had been used up. It is for that very same reason that we are not coming to the House, as the previous Government did time and time again, to simply ask for a three-year extension on the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
We are coming before the House, not having forgotten the problems farmers have with this piece of legislation. We are trying to get an interim extension to this legislation because we want to take a look at it. We want to have an opportunity to assess its usefulness and to determine whether or not it is meeting the needs of today and will meet the needs of tomorrow. We want to determine if it can be approved or amalgamated with some other government program. We want to have time to find out about information of this kind so that we will be in a position to improve the Farm Improvement Loans Act if it is our finding that that is what should be done.
I am not going to take on all of the observations that have been made by the two opposition critics. I suppose I could consider myself fortunate for having the opportunity to sit through the passage of the previous Bill, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, when the Hon. Member for Algoma got so far off the Act that he began to speak about wharfingers. He did not quite get to wharfingers on this particular Bill but he did go off on an EEC tangent.
Again, I must set the record straight. It was the previous Government that turned its back on the Canadian beef industry and took no action. This Government acted. We invoked the meat import law. To refresh the Hon. Member's memory, that occurred on December 21, 1984. As a result of our invoking the meat import law the Canadian beef industry is protected to the extent that the level of EEC beef coming into this country this year is about 55 per cent lower than it was last year. I think that is a significant protection for the Canadian beef industry. In fact, about 75 or 80 per cent less beef is coming into this country from EEC countries than would have come if we had not moved. I simply make that observation to set the record straight.
The other observation of the Hon. Member was perhaps a little more on track and dealt with farm finance. A few moments ago he indicated that the Government slashed the amount of money that is transferred from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Farm Credit Corporation. He left the impression that we slashed that amount of money from $300 million to $94 million. The truth of the matter is that $94 million is what the previous Government contributed from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Farm Credit Corporation. If we are talking about slashing, yes, there was a slash, but it was not done by this Government. I wanted to set the record straight on that matter as well.
Some comments were made regarding the usefulness of the program. The Hon. Member knows where I stand on the usefulness of the program. What is our other option? Our other option is to simply terminate the legislation. If the terms of this Bill were to terminate this piece of legislation, can you imagine what we would be hearing from Members opposite, Mr. Chairman? We would be hearing the most negative comments imaginable. We are not terminating the legislation.
I think it is important to recognize that $105.7 million or 66.1 per cent of the $159 million that was lent under this program was used to purchase agricultural implements. We know about the situation facing farm implement dealers today. It is pretty serious. A great many farm implement dealers across the country are having some very great difficulties surviving. Some $14.1 million or 8.8 per cent of that money went for construction, repair or alteration of farm houses and farm buildings. We know that the construction companies and builders can certainly utilize another $14 million. As well, $15.7 million or 9 per cent of that money was used for the purchase of land.
Some $10 million was used for other improvement purchases such as clearing of land, fencing and irrigation. There was certainly some investment in land clearing, tiling and irrigation projects, all of which are certainly in the best interests of Canadian agriculture. We know that some $13.4 million or 8.4 per cent of the money was made available for the purchase of livestock. We know that when a farmer is facing a difficult financial situation, it is important to invest money in good livestock. Everyone who has been in the livestock business knows that only a rich man can afford poor cattle. There was some half a million dollars spent on major repairs and overhaul of agricultural implements.
We are not here today taking great credit, saying that this is a new innovative program which is going to be the end to all of our problems in the agricultural industry. That is not it at all. We are coming here very honestly saying that we are not perfectly satisfied with the program the way it now is, although the previous Government seemed to be. At every three-year interval we would see the same old Bill back again. The Government would ask for a three-year extension for the same old Bill. We are not doing that. We are just asking for enough time to have a look at the program to see whether or not it can be improved.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to hold up this debate, but I want to commend the Minister on what he just said. I believe it is an excellent explanation. I do not think anyone would be happy if we terminated this Bill in spite of all its shortcomings. I was happy to hear the Minister say that during the interim this Bill is going to continue and there will be a review. That is the reason I rise now.
It is not only the financial difficulties which are facing our farmers, many of whom I am not sure are going to survive until 1986. They have high interest rates and foreclosures threatened by banks. In addition, farmers in my riding have
June 25, 1985

winds, drought, grasshoppers and cut-worms to contend with. The increased costs of production are becoming so high that many farmers are almost ready to give up. They do not think they can make it. Can the Minister tell us generally what is going to be included in this review because farming in western Canada is becoming a very serious matter. Many farmers are leaving. They have given up hope. Others are on the verge of giving up hope. We must do something in order to keep our farmers there because once the farmers disappear, I tell you, Mr. Chairman, the city people will know what the price of goods will cost because it is the many farm families who are keeping the price of food down. We in Canada do not appreciate that. We do not appreciate agriculture.
My point is that there are a number of matters which should be reviewed. For instance, if farmers received a price for their produce which included the cost plus a reasonable profit, we would not have very much difficulty. Every year the farmer is receiving less and less for what he grows. He is not even getting the costs back. There is no other industry in Canada in that position. Unless we find some way of seeing that the farmer receives his cost plus a reasonable profit, we are going to lose a lot of good farmers. We are going to lose our young innovative farmers, most of whom have diplomas from agricultural colleges.
Along with a review of this Act, I would suggest to the Minister that we have to review the Bank Act as well. Section 88 is being taken advantage of. Banks have taken and frozen a whole herd of cattle, and that is pretty discomfiting and frustrating. What is entailed in the Minister's review, which I am glad he mentioned? What does he anticipate might come out of that review with regard to keeping our farmers on the land?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member for Bow River raises a number of points and, of course, they are very important and legitimate points to raise during this debate. I would love to respond to all of them, but let me only respond by saying that it is the intention of this Government to review all of the programs which currently deliver services to the agricultural community, and all of the dollars we invest, because we really do not spend money when it comes to food production in this country, rather we invest dollars in the agri-food industry. Of course, those dollars return to the general economy many, many times.
I would just like to indicate to the Hon. Member that as far as this Government is concerned, there is no question about the fact that we recognize the importance of the agri-food industry both in economic terms and as far as employment opportunities are concerned. There are many examples of this during the short period of time we have been in office. The Hon. Member knows that we have taken a number of very major steps. We are not claiming great victory here but we have taken many major steps in the farm credit, farm finance area. Other steps are being considered.
I know there was a great deal of expectation when the Budget was brought forward on May 23 that there would be some special provisions dealing with the farm finance issue.
Farm Improvement Loans Act
However, I warned Hon. Members in this House and farm organizations across the country that although there would be some very significant measures in the Budget, not to hold out any great hope that there would be any special measures in the Budget dealing with the farm finance issue. The reason for that, of course, was the fact that we have taken a number of steps. I am not going to go through them now-they are all listed and my colleagues will know what they are-except to say that the previous Government did not move in any way, shape or form in this area, but we have moved, and moved in three or four very significant ways.
I would like to indicate why I cautioned that significant measures would not be contained in the Budget dealing with the farm finance issue. Of course, there was a major provision in the Budget for which agricultural organizations have been asking for years and years and which was not provided by the previous Government. That, of course, was the measure of no capital gains. The other measure was the extension of the Registered Retirement Savings Plan. Third was the extension of the small business bond provision.
I received the report of the Bruce-Grey pilot project on May 17. The Budget, of course, came down on May 23. Since that time, I have had the benefit of the advice of both regional and provincial farm credit managers across the country. They have been acting, of course, as an appeal board in many provinces. I am receiving their advice. This week, we have a meeting with the chairpeople of the Farm Credit Appeal Board. We will have the benefit of the advice from the Bruce-Grey pilot project. We will have the benefit of the advice of our regional and provincial farm credit managers, and we will also have the benefit of the advice from the chairpeople of the Farm Credit Appeal Board. We will have to decide, of course, what further measures we can take from the federal point of view in order to deal with the farm finance issue.
I could go on-the Chairman has been very lenient with me to this point in time-but I think that most of the questions centred around this debate which can be properly procedurally talked about are those measures dealing more specifically with the farm credit issue.
In response to the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, I can tell him that I have charts and charts. I am not so sure whether I have the appropriate chart to supply him with the information for which he asked, but I can assure him that I would be happy to share the information I have. First is Table 1 which provides me with a summary of operations. It goes from the year 1945 on through to 1984 and lists the number of loans and the average loan. The next chart I have is Table 2, Loans and Repayment to Lenders. It goes through that same period of time. Table 3 shows loans classified by province and by lenders. That is interesting information. I know that when I was sitting in the Opposition, I was always anxious to receive that. I would be happy to share that information with all Hon. Members of the House. Table 3 continues for three pages.

June 25, 1985
Farm Improvement Loans Act
Now we get to Table 4, loans classified by province and purpose. I have that information here. We have Table 5, loans for implements, combines, hay bailers, trucks, tractors and others; Table 6, loans for various farm improvement purposes; Table 7, loans for construction, repair and alteration of farm houses and buildings. I have a lot of information here which I am happy to share with the Hon. Member.
I could perhaps answer him by saying that as I recall, and I may be wrong, our losses under the Farm Improvement Loans Act were next to nil, thus the observation that this is not going to cost us a great deal. Farmers are good credit risks. They will make every effort to repay their debts. Therefore, we do not really see this as a great liability. We see it, instead, as another option to provide credit to a certain group of farmers. It has served a purpose over the years. We agree with some of the comments made and that is why we are coming back here today, not to terminate this legislation, but asking for an extension so we can sit down and try to improve the Act to the benefit of Canadian farmers.

Mr. Chairman, last year some $825 million was made available for loans through the Farm Credit Corporation. This year the estimates showed only $94 million. Is the Government going to be borrowing additional funds as a result because it could not really complement the funding available through the Farm Improvement Loans Act?
I want to point out the urgency of additional credit being made available. A Bruce County independent producers' group report showed 30 per cent of their producers were in serious financial difficulty. It seems to me that, given this drastic reduction and additional funds not being put in place, it will be hard to overcome the losses and foreclosures which have been taking place. Can the Minister clarify just what percentage of the $1.5 billion guarantee provided under the Farm Improvement Loans Act has actually been utilized? Is the entire amount being utilized? That is the problem with the Act in that the banks just do not make these loans available to farmers because they do not make enough profit. It it is not being utilized, then will the Government give consideration to requiring the banks to utilize the full amount? It is useful legislation and if only a small amount of funds are being rolled over each year, then the full amount should be utilized.
In the report that the Minister referred to, one of the problems seemed to be that the FCC were very inflexible. They would not write off loans even if the banks did so. Is the Minister prepared to bring in legislation or adopt a policy which would provide for that kind of flexibility? I also wonder if we could have the Minister, since he referred to a chart, table the statistical breakdown of farm improvement loans and show how much money is being utilized, so it could be made available to all Members?

Mr. Chairman, I have tried to be as helpful as possible. If I had expected questions of this kind, then it would have been possible to have an official seated in front of me so I could receive this information. There is no question about the
circulation of the information. There is nothing confidential about that at all. It should be public knowledge and I have no reservation about making the information available to Members of the House.
I have to point out to the Hon. Member that the figure he cites might well be a combination of what the FCC could borrow from the private sector plus what it might be able to receive from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The fact is that those totals become rather unimportant because the FCC required only $94 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund last year. Therefore, when you are preparing the Estimates to be tabled, that is the basis upon which you do so; the amount required the previous year.
I have said publicly many times that if we find the demand is such that we require additional funds and we cannot get them in the private sector, then it is possible for me as Minister of Agriculture to go back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund to receive additional money. However, we have to recognize that it is highly unlikely that there will be a great demand throughout 1985 because of a number of factors, with the result that there will be many fewer transactions taking place.
The Hon. Member also indicated that loans last year totalled $1.5 million, but of course that is not correct. It was $159 million. I think the Hon. Member just made a slip of the tongue and did not do it intentionally at all. He also indicated that we might well be restricted because we are limited to $1.5 billion in total. The information I have is that would not be the case. To date roughly $900 million has been extended since 1980. Obviously I would not expect that we would be restricted by the $1.5 billion ceiling. We do have some latitude there.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister pointed out that something in the order of $159 million was lent under this program last year. That brought the total outstanding loans guaranteed under the Act into the neighbourhood of $900 million while there is $1.55 billion of loan guarantees available under the Act. Could he tell us how the system is monitored? People have gone to banks and been told that there is no more money available through that program. Is each large chartered bank allocated a maximum amount that the Government will guarantee for a certain time, or is the pool of money kept wide open so that any time a credit union, bank, or trust company wants to lend money under this program it can just do so? Surely there must be some form of communication, particularly when they are close to using up the guaranteed funds. What sort of communication system is in effect, or is it just parcelled out to various banks, some of which in fact reach their limit?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is parcelled out in any way, shape, or form. It is my understanding that in the past this Act was administered by the Department of Finance. When the previous Government asked for an extension, the administrative role was transferred from the Department of Finance to the Department of Agriculture. I believe that transfer took place three years ago. This program is now
June 25, 1985

administered by officials of my Department. We are presently considering whether the Department of Agriculture is the appropriate body to carry out that administration or whether it should be transferred to the Farm Credit Corporation.
I have received complaints that there seems to be reluctance on the part of certain bank managers to participate in this program. Elowever, some banks participate readily in the program. There is a bank in my constituency which utilizes that legislation very effectively. In fact, we would probably all be better off if we had the level of participation in this legislation which is exercised by certain banks.
With regard to administration, there are many forms which must be completed. There is a reluctance on the part of the client as well as the bank. After an application has been filled in, the banker would most likely have to seek approval from his head office in order to determine whether the federal Government was in a position to utilize the lending provisions of the Act.
That is a round-about answer, Mr. Chairman, and my terminology may not be exact, but I think you will find that that is the procedure which is followed which enables us to determine whether we have gone beyond the cap.

Mr. Chairman, would it be possible to make the seven tables referred to part of the minutes of this Committee, or to make them available to Members who would like to have them in order that they will be part of the public record?
My last question is a very simple one. The Minister mentioned a problem that appears to have been created with paperwork. Since 1980 the Minister of Agriculture has been in charge of this program. Is it his intention to simplify those procedures, or is there a policy decision to phase out the program entirely? Farmers and lenders would like an indication of the Government's intention in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, no final decision has been made with reference to the future of this program. We think this program can be improved and we want to study it for that purpose. We will be considering the possibility of making it less burdensome. I apologize for not making paper flow from my desk to that of the Elon. Member. My problem was that if this left my desk, I would not have anything in front of me from which to respond. I do not use this as a lever to attempt to get this Bill through the House, but if Hon. Members give me an indication that they are reaching the conclusion of the detailed technical questions, I will be happy to give up my only copy and have it copied and distributed.

Mr. Chairman, the Ministers answers have been helpful. He has indicated that only $900 million of the total $1.5 billion of the borrowing authority is presently being utilized by the banks. Why are the rest of those funds not being utilized by the banks? Banks are writing off hundreds of thousands of dollars in bad farm loans. If they were taking out loans of up to $100,000, which is the limit of this program, they would be guaranteed by the federal Government. Would
Farm Improvement Loans Act
the Government consider requiring banks, on a national basis, to provide a certain percentage of their loan funds under the Farm Improvements Loans Act?
With the financial situations of farmers being not as liquid as they should be, this would provide a source of reasonably priced credit. Would the Minister clarify why the full limit is not being utilized and whether the Government would give consideration to requiring banks to use a much higher percentage of the loan guarantees which are available under this program?

Mr. Chairman, I think the Hon. Member knows that according to this legislation we could not direct or unilaterally decree that the banking institutions must fully utilize the piece of legislation. I suppose that if it was the opinion of the government to take such action, that question could be put more appropriately pursuant to other legislation. However, it would appear to me that the Hon. Member is suggesting that if we took this tack, it would be a significant step in dealing with our farm finance problems. The fact is that that is not the case. I did not come to the House saying that this would be a great piece of legislation. I am as critical of this piece of legislation as I sit here as I was when I sat over there, for the very same reason.
However, when we are dealing with the farm finance issue, those old, traditional interest rate subsidies which the previous Government started but did not continue for 1984 for some reason, provide very little help and satisfaction in dealing with the crux of the matter. It is further proof that it is not only dollars that will solve our problems. It is improvements in commodity prices where the dollars really count in providing some real assistance to those farmers who face real difficulty.
The solutions will probably be found through some of the approaches and recommendations that are laid out in the Bruce-Grey pilot project. It will be through some of the recommendations that we will receive from our farm credit provincial managers across the country. It will be through some of the recommendations that we will receive from our farm credit appeal chairpeople who have been in the field. We will be getting some of those recommendations as well. It will not be achieved by those of us sitting here, throwing stones and criticizing the banking institutions in this country. That does nothing whatsoever, as we have already experienced. It serves no useful purpose at all.
It is obvious that banking institutions have changed their attitude, as they should. I believe we can take some satisfaction in that and compliment them somewhat. They are not the same group that they used to be. They are taking some positive steps in the farm finance area today.
As far as the Farm Credit Corporation is concerned, the Hon. Member indicated that there appeared to be a situation in the Bruce-Grey pilot project where the Farm Credit Corporation appeared not to be as flexible as he would like to see it. However, the Hon. Member must respect the fact that this was a pilot project. We were sitting at a table for the first time

June 25, 1985
Farm Improvement Loans Act
with clients and a group of creditors. We were in an exercise in which we had to be somewhat cautious.
In the final analysis, we had to be careful when we decided on a case in the Bruce-Grey pilot project because it had to become a national policy which applied across the country. Therefore, it led to an observation that indeed we could have been more flexible in that exercise. While that is a fair observation, those who make that observation must realize that there was a reason. We had difficulties because whatever we agreed to in the pilot project, we would have to make a national program.
Of course, there are costing factors which had to be taken into consideration. I have indicated that one useful mechanism will be appeal boards. The question we are faced with now is that there appears to be an opinion that the most effective appeal boards might not be at the federal level but might well be at the provincial level. We want to provide the best appeal process possible and we are considering very seriously the possibility of set aside, of first offers to purchase and ability to pay and ways of working out many schemes with our clients to keep them on the land if they want to stay there. Those are the directions which we must consider rather than simply dollars and a little bit of unused capital that we have here.
The other matter also deals with the Bankruptcy Bill. I have had conversations with my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. A very high priority in his legislative program is to amend the Bankruptcy Bill dealing with the farm finance issue. That is the appropriate place for it. It is not with extending the power of write downs with appeal boards, whether they be farm credit appeal boards, federal appeal boards or provincial appeal boards. The real problems develop when you extend the authority to write down and to write off. The proper legislative route to take is the one we are planning in the Bankruptcy Bill.

Mr. Chairman, I have a brief question. As you no doubt appreciate, there are not many farmers in the east end of Toronto, but I did have an opportunity recently to spend some time in Bruce-Grey county with farmers. I discovered very quickly that the resentment against the banking community largely stems from the difficulty many farmers have in making applications for funds. One reason is the distance.
Another major problem in the community at that time was that the local branch of the bank did not appoint a manager so that there was no one to whom a farmer could make an application for that Government funding. If he wanted to make such an application, perhaps he would be required to travel an extensive distance to do so.
Has the Minister's Department given any consideration to farmers in that situation and attempted to find an alternative when there may not be a branch manager at the bank or even a credit union so that farmers could avail themselves of that fund? As I say, I am not an expert but these farmers were certainly resentful toward the banking community.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the intervention by the Hon. Member for Beaches. He indicated his apologies, to some extent, that he did not have farmers in his riding. He need not apologize because he has many consumers in his riding. I want to remind the Hon. Member to tell his constituents and his consumers that if they eat, they are involved in agriculture. The Hon. Member for Beaches is very much involved in agriculture.
He points to another very legitimate problem. I thank him for focusing on something other than the federal Government or the Farm Credit Corporation. It seems that everyone wants to say it is the Government's fault and that it must come up with the solutions and the money. The fact is that we do not hold all the solutions and have all the dollars.
Some improvements can be made at the provincial level, for example. I made some observations about the appeal boards. It may well be that the more appropriate place for an appeal board would be at the provincial level. The provincial governments, through their grassroots people, have done a great job throughout the country in almost every province. They have been correctly concentrating to a great extent on increasing production and other worth-while special projects over the years. These have paid great dividends.
However, perhaps we have been lax in not recognizing that perhaps we were achieving our goals ahead of time as far as production is concerned. We have been misled, I suppose, by the so-called experts telling the world that in the 1970s we were going to have great days during the 1980s, that input costs would remain low, that we would have shortages and commodity prices at an all-time high. Maybe with those messages coming from the so-called experts, that is why provincial ministries across the nation kept going on production, production and production.
All of those observations made during the early 1970s with reference to the 1980s and beyond turned out to be completely wrong. Input costs have risen and commodity prices have fallen. Shortages are not our problem; surpluses are. They have to direct more attention to the financial problems of farmers, perhaps with business management courses and time spent there. I know that we are trying to do it, at the federal level through the Farm Credit Corporation.
The Hon. Member's observation were directed toward the banking community. I could tell some interesting stories about the observations I have made of some of the shortcomings, the shortfalls and gaps in the judicial banking community as well.
I think they have to assume a greater responsibility in providing more people at the local level with agri-food business experience. That will be helpful because the farmer over a long period of time always has looked to his banker as the financial expert for his business. Unfortunately in the past the bank manager might not have had sufficient expertise and experience in the agricultural industry. The Hon. Member makes an observation with which I agree. I added to it a little.
June 25, 1985

Mr. Chairman, might I pose a short question to the Minister following up on my colleague from Beaches? I know when I lived at the end of the Queen Street carline it was an awful problem getting farm loans under this Act. I think it was about the fourth concession of Beaches. Could the Minister tell us whether it has improved any?

Mr. Chairman, we have no problems on that concession at all, I can assure the Hon. Member of that.
Clause 1 agreed to.

Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, June 19, 1985 consideration in committee of Bill C-51, an Act to provide Borrowing Authority-Miss MacDonald (for the Minister of State (Finance))-Mr. Danis in the chair.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I owe a very deep debt of gratitude to the hon. Government House Leader, the distinguished Member for Saskatoon West for allowing me to speak on behalf of the Government. I am honoured and pleased on behalf of all the constituents of the great riding of Ottawa-Carleton to speak to Bill C-51 this evening. I would like to set this $18.2 billion borrowing requirement in its proper national economic context.
A reporter asked me the other day why I ran for Parliament. I responded by saying, because I love my country and I was concerned enough about its future to want to do something about it. I have lived and worked in the international community and have, therefore, seen Canada through the eyes of foreigners. The land is strong, but the direction in which it was heading was weak. I could see that we were going the wrong way. Therefore, I ran for Parliament and here I am. I am pleased and proud to be a part of the new crew helping to guide the ship of state on its new course through the economic, political and fiscal minefields placed by previous successive Liberal administrations.
We have had a few bumps and bruises in altering our course, Mr. Chairman, but that is part of the maturing process for a new Government. The course is now set. Economic renewal is now well under way, lead by our determination to reduce the deficit and to create an atmosphere for renewed confidence, investment and job creation by Canadian businesses.
I said during the election last year that I cannot live beyond my means, that businesses cannot that no Canadian can. Why then should our Government? 1 underlined that theme time and time again. Now we are delivering by getting our own fiscal house in order.
Borrowing Authority Act
I did a survey in my riding last December. I asked a question to which I had 2,244 responses. The question was: "Do you feel that we should take further action to reduce the deficit?" Seventy-three per cent asnwered yes, and so we are. Many people are saying that we did not go far enough soon enough.
Is it not nice to know that we are now rewarding success, instead of subsidizing effort, through the incentive of the elimination of capital gains tax to a lifetime total of $500,000? If one person with a good idea can create some jobs then we will reward that person. That is called incentive, a word my colleagues in the socialist axis do not understand. The Liberals spell prosperity "s-p-e-n-d", we spell it "i-n-c-e-n-t-i-v-e." Imagine, we are rewarding the entrepreneurial spirit, the genius of job creation in the world.
The capital gains exemption will reach all communities, not justs those the Government targets. All communities in all ridings and all Members should be applauding this giant step for Canadians.
To maintain our momentum, the Government needs to borrow some funds as a normal course of action to finance its programs. Bill C-51 is a formal request of Parliament to do that. But I want to let Canadians know that it is not money being wasted. This request for borrowing authority dovetails beautifully into the ongoing Budget debate for the following reasons. After the November 8 economic statement last fall, the opposition leaders cried that we would lose 50,000 to
100.000	jobs as a result. Well, "Holy Moses" and as our son Blair who is just over two years says "Look at that". I would like to give some statistics.
Employment increased by 159,000 in April and May, the largest two-month gain in decades. Since September, 271,000 new jobs have been created, nearly three times the job creation during the same period last year. Since January of this year,
75.000	new jobs have been created for youth. Since September, 112,000 new jobs have been created for adult women and
111.000	new jobs for adult men.
The unemployment rate declined to 10.5 per cent in May, a drop of 1.1 percentage points from September. During the same period last year the unemployment rate rose 0.4 per cent. The 10.5 per cent unemployment rate is the lowest since May, 1982.
Since September, the youth unemployment rate has declined 2.1 per cent to 16.2 per cent, which at this point in time is still unacceptably high; the unemployment rate of adult women has declined 0.6 per cent to 9.5 per cent; and the unemployment rate of adult men has declined 1.1 per cent to 8.2 per cent, the lowest rate since June, 1982.
After the May 23 Budget the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition questioned the impeccable integrity of the Minister of Finance by wondering why the Minister paid as much attention to Miami Beach as he did to Thunder Bay. The answer was quick and clear-Canadians did not have the confidence to invest their money in their own country. We

June 25, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
have changed that, and to coin an old phrase: "You ain't seen nothing yet". The net inflow of capital to Canada last fiscal year was over $2 billion, and that has not happened for a long time. That is called confidence. The more Ottawa spent, the more unemployment went up. Short-term artificial job creation has not worked, so we are going another route. We are breaking from the past. We are putting the ball in the people's court, and they are winning.
My colleague, the Hon. Minister of State for Finance, said in a speech in Toronto on May 27 that the Budget would "promote competitiveness, vitality and common sense", and that it would restore "initiative, self-reliance and personal choice". She went on to say:
One of the things we're trying to do is get out of the routine of making people's investment decisions for them.
The challenge is now on the table. Government will not do it any more. If more government is the answer, then it must have been a stupid question. Eighty per cent of deficit reduction is through imported management, program reduction and enhanced cost recovery. Twenty per cent of reduction is through increased revenue; only 20 per cent, so what is all the fuss about?
It is correct that Bill C-51 is asking for some borrowing authority, but this is a normal course of government business. Let us look at the Western Accord. "Holy Moses", as my son would say. The 1981 Budget and the hideous National Energy Program destroyed this vital Canadian industry and the Liberal Government in the process. Recently I received a letter from Miss Cooley who is with the HUDAC organization in Alberta, in which she indicated that in general the economy in the west was healthier, that the oil patch was all abustle, and that north of Edmonton accommodation was in short supply.
That is good news. An article in the June 10 edition of The Edmonton Journal read as follows:
Statistics Canada reports the seasonally-adjusted unemployment rate in Alberta dropped last month to 10.6 per cent. This time last year it was 12 per cent-
It's the type of economic news politicians, investors and the unemployed have been waiting a long time to hear.
That is also good news. We did not put balls on a Christmas tree for everyone, but what we have and are doing will solidify the future of that tree and allow more Canadians to hang whatever they want on it.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business called the Budget a block-buster, a dose of salts for our constipated economy, a requirement for a national effort to reduce the deficit so that in future years the Government would not have to borrow as much. Let us keep the Budget in its global perspective. If we borrow less, there will be more for everyone else. In economic jargon that is less crowding out of funds. This is the first time in many years that the deficit has been reduced. As an editorial which appeared in The Globe and Mail on May 27 indicated, "the Budget deserves a chance to work". We will remove $78 billion from the national debt by 1990. How can anyone question that? This fiscal year the average cost to a Canadian family will be from $1 to $1.25 per
day. That is not too much to ask in order to sustain a strong, stable recovery.
I should like to commend the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan for his strong efforts to help save and fully restore the CBC children's program, The Friendly Giant. He mentioned in a memo to all Members of Parliament on May 22, the day before the federal Budget was brought down, that across the country Canadians were demanding more control of their economic affairs. He is right. We have just given it to them. I invite him to help us sell the new prosperity which we are all starting to enjoy.
I used to live in the riding of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain when I worked as a summer student on shift work for Stelco. He indicated in debate in the House on May 28 that even if we created more jobs, produced more goods and services, where would we sell them? He is right. We all have to go out and sell what Canada has to offer, all of us in all Parties and from all provinces, and the sooner the better. If we create the right environment, Canadians will take the risks of putting some of their own money on the line to build a business. We all have a responsibility to help them do what. We have to be less critical and more positive and stop using fear tactics and vicious, thoughtless comments in the House of Commons to scare Canadians.
I should like to review a few more key economic indicators by comparing Canada with the United States. Since September last year Canada's unemployment rate has declined 1.1 per cent, while the United States unemployment rate has declined only 0.1 per cent. Since September, employment in the U.S. has increased by 1.5 per cent, while it has gone up 2.5 per cent in Canada. Holy, Moses, look at that.
We have done something which has not happened in a long time. We have brought peace to the provinces. We have strengthened our ties with the United States, which is a true sign of friendship. It sure beats kicking one's allies in the teeth. We have made energy deals with the west and with the Atlantic provinces. We have strengthened our commitment to NORAD and NATO. We have introduced the lowest rate of public spending in 17 years. We have created 271,000 jobs since September. Investment Canada has replaced that ugly FIRA feeling. Confidence and investment intentions are well up. Interest rates are down. Unemployment is down. Car sales are up. Housing starts are up. These are key economic indicators. Housing starts have increased for four consecutive months and, at 150,000 units in April, on an annual basis, were 23 per cent above the December 1984 level. There is a pent-up demand for a housing boom in the country. Retail sales jumped 3.4 per cent in March, relative to February, the seventh consecutive monthly increase. These are good signs.
When we took over government, we inherited an economically troubled country. It is now beginning to work. Tory times are employment times. Tory times are now growth times. Tory times are low interest rate times. The list goes on and on. We should not be held back. We are on a roll. What we need is more encouragement, more optimism, more positive promotion of the successes of the Government to date, more talk of the
June 25, 1985

gains Canada has made since September 1984; not doom and gloom scare tactics by the Opposition. The people of Ottawa-Carleton and the people of Canada know that we are on a roll. Business leaders of Canada, small, medium and large, feel a renewed sense of optimism. The only way to build a solid house, the only way to build a solid business, the only way to build a solid country is through a renewed sense of confidence in our ability and in our sense of direction.
I should like to quote the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada. In a speech in Toronto on May 7, he said:
Canadians should support the federal Government's determination to tackle the problem of the deficit by reducing our demands and by encouraging government to show the same sort of fiscal responsibility and prudence that we tend to show in our private lives. If we do not, we are being unfair to today's youth and are mortgaging the future of generations to come.
Mr. Galt went on to say in his same address, and I quote again:
We must accept that this means that tough decisions will have to be taken. But if we and our governments are sincere in wanting to be fair to our young people, we can, in my view, demonstrate it no more clearly than by making a determined attack on the growing future financial burden that we have been placing on their shoulders.
Mr. Galt is a man of vision, a man who is looking to the future, a man who is preparing to bite the bullet and help lower our national debt and annual deficits.
When I think of 1984 I am reminded of the successes of Canadian Olympians in Los Angeles. They won gold and silver and bronze because they were prepared. They were determined; they wanted to succeed for themselves and for their country. This new Government is also prepared. It is also determined. It will also continue to succeed so that all our people from all regions will have a healthier, happier, more stable economic, social and political future. That is what you build on, strength and successes, not weaknesses and words.
Bill C-51 is an essential component for continued Conservative creativity. The facts to date that I gave this House, Mr. Chairman, speak for themselves. The future is waiting to speak for us all, so let us get on with it.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

Mr. Chairman, just a few words to add to the subject under discussion. The fact of the matter is that there will be a lot of senior citizens who will not even sign the sheet of paper that will get them their money. It is because the $750 that they will receive is not only taxable but is taken into account the following year on the income supplement to old age pensions.
When programs like that are announced, they sound great. However, a person who is filling out that form thinks about all kinds of things. He asks how this will affect his old age pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement of his wife. The Government of Canada unilaterally removed the licences which in most cases were held by senior citizens because they were classified as part-time fishermen. Yet they had to sign for that removal. I could never figure out why they had to sign for it. In committee, someone responded by saying that in order to have the payment made to the individual the individual's signature had to be on a sheet of paper. I have noticed that both in the House and outside, there has been a tendency to misinterpret certain points, and I would like to clarify one particular point in connection with the capital gains exemption. Increasingly, people are referred to this exemption as a giveaway to Canadians. The Minister is not giving away anything, but that is what has been claimed a number of times.
1 may add that it is not an expenditure either, certainly not. [English]
It is not an expenditure or an expense.

I believe that the capital gains exemption is truly perceived by the public as an incentive to investment which is ultimately aimed at creating jobs. Of course, people may not understand how this incentive to investment is going to create jobs. It may be perceived as a foregone source of revenues badly needed by the present Government to mop up the deficit it inherited, that is to say, the cumulative deficit inherited from the previous Government.
June 25, 1985

As Hon. Members are aware, the Budget contains a proposal for a lifetime capital gains exemption of half a million dollars. This is an important initiative that is aimed at encouraging risk-taking and investment. It is a clear signal and a direct incentive to Canadians to start buying shares. Especially for small-and medium-sized businesses, realizing capital gains will provide the entrepreneurial drive that creates growth and employment which are the basis for our economic security. This measure will clearly encourage equity investment. Subsequent increases in returns on investments will encourage risktaking. Furthermore, since capital available for acquiring shares in companies will increase as a result of this measure, the balance sheet and financial health of our corporations will improve, and thus have a beneficial effect on the financial restructuring in progress since the recession. Companies will be able to develop and expand as a result of equity investment. Consolidation of their financial positions will be accelerated, and companies will be in a better position to engage in productive investment. This investment will maintain and create employment and will also help to strengthen our ability to compete on highly competitive international markets. I may also add that the full exemption will be available immediately for capital gains realized on the sale of farm property, which will increase assistance to this vital sector of the economy.
