Mr. Speaker, recently I rose in this House to ask the Solicitor General what measures Correctional Service Canada was taking and how the inmate population in Canada is helping to control the national debt, reduce expenditures and share in the economic responsibilities of this nation.
My concern stems from the fact that we are asking Canadians to participate in economic responsibility and I strongly believe all Canadians should be contributing. I believe we have a duty to all Canadians to ensure that Government exercises restraint and cut expenditures, as is being done in many areas.
Six weeks after taking office this Government cut expenditures by $4.2 billion. Various programs are presently being reviewed to determine their effectiveness and areas of duplication. This Government is serious about cutting our expenditures. We introduced measures in the May 23 Budget that will help reduce the deficit by $4.4 billion from the previous projection of almost $40 billion.
I am concerned about the costs of our correctional services. There are various costly expenditures ranging from food and clothing to visitor facilities and building maintenance. I realize that such expenditures are necessary, but they should not be incredibly expensive.
June 25, 1985

The over-all national average cost to maintain a person in a federal penitentiary rose to $109.81 per day during the year ending March 31, 1984. That is an increase from $103.66 per day for the previous year. On average, Canada spends $39,419 a year for each inmate in a federal penitentiary. Costs have risen substantially since 1979-80 when Canada spent $75.58 a day to house an inmate.
The number of inmates has also increased greatly, from 8,465 in 1979-80 to the 1983-84 total of 10,438. Women make up 2 per cent of this number. A further 1,100 federal prisoners were on parole, probation or mandatory supervision when the count was made. In 1982-83 the total expenditure on prisons cost each Canadian $42.67 a year, or a total of $1.1 billion. By 1983-84 that cost had risen to $49.13 per Canadian, or a total of $1.2 billion.
There are some programs run by the correctional institutions that give me cause to doubt the economic responsibility of the system. The conjugal visiting sessions for inmates serving life sentences does not make sense to me. These are people who have opted not to be part of our society, yet feel it is their right to have visitors with them. The costs of these visits must be borne by the average Canadian who carries on a productive, law-abiding life.
Projects such as the greenhouses and farms that the Honourable Minister mentioned in his response to my question are other programs that I am concerned about. Just how cost effective are some of these programs? We must consider the fact that supplies and equipment must be purchased for these operations, and I consider it vital that we not have the average Canadian paying for inmate activities that are not necessary and self-sufficient.
Further, there are some important questions regarding the costs of transporting inmates from penitentiaries to court houses and back. Such involvement of inmates requires elaborate preparations, a great many security personnel and costs a great deal. There is also the question of the possible danger to the community at large should the prisoner escape, not to mention the costs associated with a search for an inmate who has escaped.
At this time there are no provisions to try an inmate in a court on penitentiary grounds to save the transportation and subsequent related costs. There may be some concerns about this proposal, and some may claim that it is contrary to the Charter of Rights. However, I would like to point out that the prison population has opted not to abide by the law and by so doing have forfeited the privileges of freedom and voting. It is a person's choice and an inmate has chosen not to be part of our free and democratic society. That does not mean that inmates no longer have responsibilities. They must still lead responsible and productive lives while serving time.
I am concerned, and rightly so, that the Correctional Service of Canada is not contributing to the Government's restraint program. Are we asking our inmates to share in cost reductions to help reduce the serious national debt? We should be
Adjournment Debate
doing just that. I am not suggesting that we mistreat or abuse the prison population. I am not suggesting that prisoners are the sole cause of our present economic situation. However, I do ask that we consider treating all people on an equal and fair basis so that all people of Canada share in economic restraint.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond further to the issue raised by the Hon. Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Vankoughnet) in a question he asked during Question Period on June 10, 1985, with respect to the cost of maintaining offenders. I can understand the Hon. Member's concern, particularly in light of recently published statistics indicating a rise in the average annual cost of maintaining a person in a federal penitentiary.
The Correctional Service is very much aware that the costs of maintaining penitentiaries must be kept to acceptable levels, and is doing much to employ inmates in ways that keep them productively occupied, provide training and contribute to the daily operations and upkeep of institutions. Accordingly, inmates are assigned to cleaning duties, the preparation and serving of food, laundry services, renovation projects, farm operations, industries and so on.
In order to foster a sense of personal responsibility and thrift, inmates are required to save a portion of the money they earn while working, and in this manner funds are accrued to provide the support they need during the critical re-entry phase into the community when they are released. In other words, they can better support themselves while looking for employment and thereby avoid further burden to the taxpayer.
I must make particular mention of the fact that the Correctional Service reduces the cost of maintaining offenders through the operation of five farms and greenhouses, gardens and other operations at several institutions that collectively provide approximately 25 per cent to 30 per cent of all food required, to a total market value of about $4 million annually. Production is being expanded with the development of a sixth farm at Bowden Institution in Alberta. Since Bowden is in my constituency, this question is very important to me. The Correctional Service hopes to eventually improve self-sufficiency to the level of 50 per cent, the upper limit in practical terms given the Canadian climate and the remote location of some of our institutions.
The Correctional Service also operates almost 100 industrial shops and institutions across the country. These shops operate with inmate labour and manufacture goods that are used at the institutions or sold to government agencies and non-profit, charitable or religious organizations. Revenue generated by sales offsets the costs associated with training inmates in marketable industrial skills and the costs of operating the shops.
Finally, I would like to mention that inmates are actively employed in forestry activities carried out at five institutions, and these activities involve the production of about four million seedlings each year, spacing and thinning, log salvage,

June 25, 1985
Adjournment Debate
firefighting, campground development and parks maintenance. A joint venture of the Correctional Service and the Scott Paper Company in Nova Scotia has resulted in a tree nursery operation which provides training for inmates who are paid as Scott Paper employees and who reimburse the Correctional Service for room and board.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, there are several dynamic and original ways that have been developed by the correctional service to reduce costs, while at the same time providing inmates with training which will help them find jobs when they are released.

subtopic: SPORTS-BASEBALL DECISION UNFAIR TO CANADIAN UMPIRES
SPORTS-BASEBALL DECISION UNFAIR TO CANADIAN UMPIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 18 last I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) the following question, and I quote:
While we are waiting for the day when the world series will be held in Canada between the Expos and the Blue Jays, will the Minister ascertain why Canadians, who have graduated from recognized umpire schools in the United States, are not permitted to umpire in the minor and major leagues in the United States! while American umpires in baseball and American referees in hockey work in Canada? Should this not be a two-way street?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied as follows, and I quote:
I thank the Hon. Member for that very serious question. We are looking into it seriously. We have had discussions with officials of the United States. We are not completely satisfied as yet with the response, but it is the bottom of the seventh inning and we expect that we will win that particular game before the end of the ninth.
That was a very thoughtful answer and I am delighted that we have at least reached the seventh inning. The purpose of my remarks today is to encourage the department to bat a home run with the bases full and finish the game so that qualified Canadians may umpire in the United States in the major and minor leagues, just as qualified Americans may work in our baseball leagues in Canada.
A number of people have asked me if I have any examples. I have and I will quote them. The first example is the case of a constituent of mine who, while in the United States attending a five-week course at the Joe Brinkman Professional Umpires School in St. Bernardino, California, along with another Canadian, was astounded when told that because they were Canadians they could not be hired in the United States. An official of the Harry Wnedlestedt School for Umpires at Daytona Beach, Florida, stated in a letter to my constituent, and I quote:
Much attention is currently being given what I consider a silly law that exists banning placement of foreign candidates in jobs that can be filled by the country's own citizens. This agreement was forged between Canada and the U.S. during a time of great unemployment in both countries. Only those candidates in what is considered a critical occupation, such as science and medicine, can be placed in jobs in a country of which they are not a citizen. Hopefully if enough people complain to the politicians things will change.
Another example is the case of a young man from Surrey, B.C. who applied to work in the Pioneer League and his
request was denied. The story in The Globe and Mail on Saturday, May 11, 1985, indicated that five other Canadians have applied for work visas so they can umpire in the United States and were refused. The Americans have made one exception, a Canadian citizen from Montreal who had a brother who was U.S. citizen was permitted to work in the American league. The story also states that Canadians lost their jobs in the minor leagues after it was found out that they were Canadians.
It was reported that Barney Deary who heads baseball's umpire development program, has also appealed to have Canadians made eligible. He is reported as saying, "I am supposed to be finding the best umpires and right now I am not able to do that". I agree with him, that Canadian umpires are just as highly qualified, if not more so, as American umpires.
Another story that appeared in Referee, the magazine for sports officials, in the July, 1981 edition, told the story of a Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer living in the Northwest Territories, who in 1974 was one of the youngest umpires working in the Inner County baseball league in southern Ontario. In 1979 he worked at the Canadian National Junior Men's Championship in Richmond, B.C. In 1980 he worked at the Canadian National Senior Men's Championship in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. He was also appointed Deputy Umpire-in-Chief of Canada by National Umpire-in-Chief Ed Bitz. He is a graduate of Bill Kinnamon's Umpire School in St. Petersburg, Florida, where he received a very good rating.
I say again that this should be a two-way street. American umpires and referees may work in Canada. Surely we should have a reciprocal arrangement so that qualified Canadians may work in Baseball and hockey in the U.S.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: SPORTS-BASEBALL DECISION UNFAIR TO CANADIAN UMPIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one old ball player to another, I wish to assure the Hon. Member that we are committed to developing a mechanism which would permit aspiring and talented Canadians to pursue careers as umpires in professional baseball.
The Hon. Member has rightly pointed out that it has been some time now since major league baseball has come to Canada. As the Hon. Member knows, baseball requires anyone who wishes to pursue a career in baseball to "start at the bottom", to move through the minors into the majors. With specific reference to umpires, the United States' immigration regulations provide for Canadian participation at the major league level through the issuance of H-I employment visas, issued on the basis of merit and ability. Once a Canadian has reached this level he does not encounter any difficulties entering the United States. However, to attain that level an individual must move up through the minor leagues and, unfortunately, this cannot be done solely within Canada, as Canadian minor league teams are grouped in leagues with teams based on the United States. In order to be employed in those leagues, a Canadian requires an H-2 employment visa
June 25, 1985

which can only be issued after the United States Department of Labour has completed a labour market survey and determined there is no qualified and available American to fill the vacancy.
For many years organized baseball has had a program to develop potential major league umpires. This program is operated through the Office of Baseball Umpire Development and involves a screening of initial talent, evaluation and appraisal of development and progressive promotion up to the major leagues. We have urged the United States Department of Labour that the merit principle be incorporated in their decision on labour certification. This would provide an avenue for Canadians who have graduated from a recognized umpire school to begin careers which would hopefully culminate in the major leagues. Negotiations will continue with the United States until an equitable solution can be found.

subtopic: PENSIONS-STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA- REQUEST THAT BUDGET PROVISIONS BE WITHDRAWN
PENSIONS-STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA- REQUEST THAT BUDGET PROVISIONS BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 14 I posed a question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) regarding the restoration of full indexation of Old Age Security. On that day I quoted a statement made by, as the Prime Minister would say, a very distinguished Canadian. I wish to again quote that statement:
-it was a wrong move, I am very disappointed, I am totally against it. It was the wrong thing to do to our senior citizens. That part of the Budget was not compassionate.
That was said by the Premier of the Province of Nova Scotia. The Prime Minister responded that at the earliest possible moment he would make a statement which would be consistent with the intentions as set forth by the caveat placed in the Budget.
I suggest to Hon. Members opposite that the thrust of my question was that this Budget measure was wrong in its substance because of its negative effect on senior citizens. Unfortunately, there are far too many senior citizens in this country who live well below the poverty line. To cause them anxiety or frustration for any period of time, be it temporary or indefinitely, regarding cuts in their Old Age Security is both inequitable and unfair to those who served Canada in so many ways for so many years.
I asked the Prime Minister, as I am asking the Parliamentary Secretary, who no doubt will be answering for the Prime Minister, if the Government is prepared to make a statement forthwith, prior to the adjournment of the House on June 28, that it will restore full indexation to the cost of living, as it was before, and to right this wrong. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary with great sincerity and civility, which is another word used so often by our Prime Minister, that the measure contained in the Budget is not supported by provincial premiers, senior citizens, a vast number of members of provin-
Adjournment Debate
cial legislatures and, I venture to say, a good number of Members of Parliament in this Chamber.
I would hope that since there is no support for this measure, and since it has the possibility of causing further frustration and anxiety for our senior citizens, remedial action will be taken to restore full indexation for our senior citizens so that they will not have to live with this fear over the next number of months. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will stand in her place and indicate what the Government's intention is for the next number of days.
If the change is made there may be some commentators within the media who will write some non-favourable things about the Government. However, I suggest that if that is the case, the result of changing back to full indexation will outweigh any political fall-out that the Government may experience for a short period of time. I am quite confident that if the Government changes this measure it will receive the support of senior citizens across the country, as well as that of a large majority of Canadians who believe this regressive measure to be wrong in substance at this time for our Canadian economy.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PENSIONS-STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA- REQUEST THAT BUDGET PROVISIONS BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to deal with the very serious issue raised by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East-Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), and I congratulate him for doing so in a most civilized way.
First of all, I must remind him that the purpose of this budgetary measure is to index the Old Age Security pensions effective January 1, 1986, only for the annual increase in the consumer price index greater than 3 per cent. Mr. Speaker, we feel that this measure is a must if we want to preserve the integrity of our social programs in the years ahead. The greatest prejudice we could cause our senior citizens would be to make it impossible for the government to pay them these benefits by refusing today to make the difficult decision. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the government has never intended to ask our senior citizens to make unacceptable sacrifices, and as the Prime Minister himself repeated on many occasions, it was with no light heart that the government was forced to make those decisions. As to the Minister of Finance, on June 21, he was quoted as saying:
I do not like cutting indexation. But I look at the options that are available to us. I say to myself, to the Hon. Member and all Canadians, that we have tried to address this problem in the broadest possible way so that the load is spread as thinly as possible.
As a matter of fact, that is the reason why the government announced formally in the Budget and my colleagues and I repeated on many occasions that we would closely monitor the situation to see if the benefits were adequate and that he would increase them as resources permit.
In other words, we suggest that this budgetary step concerning the indexing of the Old Age Security pensions should be
